The Grand Master then read his annual address, as

HRl'l'HREN OF THE GRAND LODGE :
The experience of ages has convinced mankind that it is essential to the successful accomplishment of any important undertaking,
frequently to inspect its progress and the designs prepared for its consummation, in order to ascertain if the completed portion of the task
approached the ideals of the prospective plans, and to make any
changes and alterations, the necessity for which become obvious by .a
careful examination. Thus the mistakes of the past are corrected and
nvoided, all useless and superfluous matter eliminated, and the result
conforms more closely to the_aspirations of the designers.
So we have congregated to-day to contemplate the work of Masonry
in this Grand Jurisdiction during the past year and to endeavor to
discover the errors which have been committed, ~nd to formulate our
pl~ns for improvements in the future. By this means we may transform
failure from a source of humiliation ·and disgrace into a signal light to
guide us past the rocks of ignorance and darkness into the safe harbor
of knowledge and light.
Instead of indulging in vain regrets over the fact that our efforts
have not always been crowned with success, we should be inspired by
the hope that we and succeeding generations may profit by. what we
have learned, and that truth, eternal, shall eventually triumph and
reign forever over the destiny of man.
"Nor deem the irrevocable past
As wholly wasted, wholly vain,
If rising on its wreck at last
To something nobler we attain."
0

.

The present generation has witnessed the most marvelous advanc em~nt in the material knowledge of man that the world has ever known.
Science has subjugated and made subservient that potent and unknown
force which is the basic principle of so many of the inventions that
have excited the wonder· and admiration of the observers. And all this
has b~en accomplished in utter ignorance of what it is or why it existsonly its laws have been discovered and put to practical use. Masonry
possesses a subtle power and influence which it exerts in the same
mysterious way over those who study its laws and practice its pre-

8

PROCEEDINGS O.fo' 1:'HE

cepts. Its origin and the reason for its existence, while interesting, are
le,ss important than its practical application to the lives and characters
of its novitiates.
As the power and efficiency of electricity can be communicated
only through certain agencies, · so the potency of Masonry can be properly applied to certain characters. Many good men have passed through
the ceremony of initiation without benefit to themselves, and many bad
men have been made better through its lessons of truth and morality.
This fact makes extremely difficult the task of determining the question
as to the qualifications which a candidate should possess in order to
constitute him good material for membership in the Lodge, and in consequence many mistakes have been made, and will continue. The problem confronts us, then, of eliminating this undesirable element from
the organization ; and this is the most serious of our difficulties. There
is a tendency among the officers and members of Lodges to avoid the
trouble and scandal of trial and expulsion, and consequently the useless and superfluous material, the non-conductors of Masonry, remain
to mar the beauty and retard the progress of our institution. It is a
duty which each Lodge owes to the fraternity in general to rid itself
?f any vicious and immoral element which it has unwittingly admitted,
m order that our standard may be maintained and our funds preserved
for the relief of the worthy in distress.
While the mantle of charity may be used to cloak an occasional
lapse, a continued and persistent course of misconduct should be discountenanced and severely punished.
Thus only can we "preserve unsullied the reputation of the fraternity and remove every aspersion against our venerable institution."
NECROLOGY.

The grim reaper has invaded our field and garnered several sheaves
ripe with experience and knowledge for the final harvest.
Past Grand Master Wiley James Tinnin died at his home in Fresno
on the 24th day of November, 1910, at the age of eighty-one years. He
served as Grand Master of California in 1885, and was one of the pioneers of this State, having come here in 1850. It was truly said of him
that "he comprehended life deeply, studying its meaning with a guileless
heart. Realizing the limitations of human knowledge, nevertheless he
made a part of himself the fundamental truths of eternal character.
" His creed was simple. Not many days before his demise he
quietly quoted it in the words of another:
" 'Alone, and without my volition, I came into the world. Alone I
must go out of it. And alone I must appear before the judgment seat
of Almighty God.' His creed was not of words but of life."

EDMUND CLEMENT ATKINSON

p111ed away at his home in Sacramento on the 20th day of March,
1911, at the age of 73 years. He was Grand Master of California in
1886, following Brother Tinnin in the Grand Oriental chair. A con1ant attendant upon the communications of the Grand Lodge, by reason
•>f his years and experience and deep study, he was a tower of strength
In its deliberations, and his advice and counsel for the benefit of the
craft demonstrated his sincere and unselfish devotion to the principles
he expounded. He will live among us always in the spirit of his lovable
character and the lasting benefit of his works.
Thus star by star declines,
Till all are passed away,
And morning high and higher shines
To pure and perfect day.
These few words so inadequately express the sentiments we feel
upon the loss of these two great men, that we have set apart an hour
to be devoted to memorial services, and have requested Worshipful
Brother George E. "Church of Fresno, and Most Worshipful Brother
Edward H . Hart, to formulate suitable expressions of love and sympathy on this occasion.

HOM!iS.

Having implicit confidence in the ability and integrity of the Trustees of the Homes, I have deemed it the wiser course to allow them
to pursue their own policy without interference, and the present condition warrants the assertion that the confidence was well founded. Several visits to each Home have shown conditions of absolute harmony
and contentment among the residents, and an examination of their report will show that they have faithfully discharged their trust.
From a state of scepticism caused by reports based upon inadequate information as to the efficacy and economy of Masonic Homes,
I have been converted to the firm belief that we have properly solved
the problem of the care of our unfortunate brethren, with justice to
them and to ourselves.
BOARDS OF RliLI!iI'.

The Reports of the Boards of Relief reveal the fact that the practice of unostentatious charity continues, and the necessity and reason
for their existence thereby demonstrated. No practical illustration of
the universality of Masonry could be more apparent than the statements
in the reports of the various boards showing the diversity of territory
from which come many of the recipients of relief. This labor of love
has been most admirably performed, and reflects honor and glory upon
the workers and upon our fraternity.
The employment bureau at Los Angeles has proven a lasting success, and has been the means of securing work for many who might
otherwise have become a charge, and who are able and willing to help
themselves if given the opportunity.
SP:ECIAL COMMUNICATIONS.

On the 17th day of October, 1910, the Grand Lodge was convened
at Beckwith and dedicated the Masonic Temple there for Hope Lodge
No. 234.
The Brethren of this Lodge are to be commended for their loyalty
and perseverance in the face of difficulty, for this is the third temple
they have been forced to erect, by reason of fire.
October 29, 1910, the splendid temple of San Mateo Lodge No. 226
was dedicated according to ancient usage, R.'. W.'. William P. Filmer,
Senior Grand Warden, officiating.

The Grand Lodge assembled at Willows on August 12, 1911, for •
the purpose of laying the corner stone of the new temple for Laurel
Lodge No. 245. The plans give promise of a handsome and substantial
structure, and we congratulate the brethren upon their good taste.

upon the completion of this building under adverse conditions, and
wish them much pleasure in its enjoyment.
VISITATIONS.

The vast expanse of territory and the limited time to be devoted
hal made it impossible to visit as many Lodges as I wished, particularly
after the royal reception accorded wherever it was possible to go. A
spirit of harmony and a desire to further the interests of the fraternity
exists throughout the jurisdiction, and indicates a thriving condition
and a great influence for good in the community. There is a marked
improvement in the ritualistic work, due to the energy of the inspectors,
which adds much to the impressiveness of the ceremonies, and a consequently better influence upon t~e candidates.
Keep the good work up, brother inspectors, and you may yet hope
for letter-perfect work impressively rendered.
On June 24, 1911, we enjoyed the lavish hospitality of the brethren
of the San Francisco Lotlges, who joined in a celebration of the anniversary of St. John the Baptist, and entertained a large body of guests
in a royal manner. This was an event in the history of San Ftancisco
:Masonry which wili be long remembered by all who participated, and
. its frequent repetition will be of immeasurable benefit to the Craft in
this. city.
SPECIAL DISPENSATIONS.

The Grand Secretary's report shows the number and purposes of
5pecial dispensations which have been issued. Following the example
of my predecessors, no dispensations to re-ballot have been granted
~ithout a thorough examination of the reasons, and a showing that
justice would be done by such action.
A dispensation for Lodges to appear in a public demonstration was
refused, on the ground that it was not for a Mas0nic ceremony, and
was contrary to the decisions of our Grand Lodge.
nECISIONS.

Many questions have been asked to which answers might have been
ascertained by a careful examination of the constitution or decisions
and to these no further reference will be made,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

A matter upon which so many seem to be ignorant requires some
attention. Several Lodges have requested approval of amendments
which are contained in the uniform code of by-laws.
I decided that it is nO't necessary for a Lodge to adopt these provisions, as by the action of the Grand Lodge in adopting they thereby
become the by-laws of the subordinate Lodges, and should be copied
into the book of by-laws and observed.
Another matter I deemed of too much importance to render a decision upon, and which I submit to your consideratic;in, is as follows:
A Lodge in Los Angeles rejected a peti1ioner for the degrees in
May, 1910. About seven months thereafter he applied to another Lodge,
stating that he had been so rejected, and was incorrectly informed that
as more than six months has elapsed, the firs1 Lodge had lost jurisdiction. He signed the petition without reading it. After reference to a
committee and a ballot, he was elected to receive the degrees, and after
being passed it was discovered that one year must elapse after rejection before his petition could be received. On this being reported I
advised the officers to deny him advancement at least until the year
had expired; and the time is now up, and the question is how to pro• ceed further. I am of the opinion that inasmuch as he was illegally
eleated he was not lawfully initiated or passed, but as it is impossible
to take away from him what he has received, that he shat:!d be held
to be a Fellowcraft. But when this condition was discovered, he could
not be legally raised. The Lodge last receiving his petition was in error,
and should bear whatever burden may be attached. I recommend that
the latter Lodge be required to tender to the former the amount of
fees received by it for the first two degrees, and that the candidate have
returned to him the ~ee for the third, and advancement denied him,
with the privilege of again applying for the third degree, with the usual
reference and ballot. This to be a disposition of the particular case in
question, and not as an expression of the law.
Pil(RCE LIBRARY,

We are under lasting obligations to the daughters of our late
Grand Master, W. Frank Pierce, for their gift to us of his Masonico
library. This voluntary offering on their part indicates that the spirit
of this whole-souled, generous man has been transmitted 'unto them, and
that the effect of associa1ion with him has produced in them, as it has
in all with whom he came in contact, an unselfish disposition and a
desire to be of benefit to humanity.
These volumes will form the nucleus of a library for our new temple
when completed, and we trust their example will prove the inspiration
of many to display such substantial interest in the advancement of the
knowledge of our ancient Craft.

15

RECOMMENDATIONS.
JURISDICTION OF LODGl(S.

Considerable trouble has arisen over the question of the geographical
Jurisdiction Of Lodges, and the adoption of some different plan is
requisite to prevent a recurrence of some of the difficulties occasione.d
by the annexa tion of territory to cities, and the changing methods of
travel. The air line method of determining jurisdiction was proper
before the trolley car and other means of rapid conveyance, but now
1omething else seems essential.
The Grand Lodge should establish the territory of Lodges not having concurrent jurisdiction, reserving the power of cha'nging to meet
condi1tions, and the Grand Master, in issuing dispensations, should be
authorized to designate the boundaries of the territory of any new
Lodge formed.
1

ROSTl(R.

The Grand Secretary recommends the adoption of a card system
similar to that in use in New York, in order that the cumbersome and
practically useless roster may be abolished. This will save a great deal
of expense and trouble, and facilitate obtaining information as to the
standing and Masonic history of our members.
·
P1'TITIONS FOR Dl(GRl(l(S.

The form of the petition for degrees should be revised so that the
candidate shall be required to answer certain indispensable questions,
and show that he has in fact read the statement which he has signed,
in order that it may be determined afterward whether he understood
the effect of his action; and the proof would be at hand in case it
should be claimed that any misrepresentation was made by him, and
his guilt or ignorance conclusively established by his own signa:ture.
In this connection it would seem the better policy to require the
committee of investigation to ·report ithe facts they discover in regard
to a man's qualification, rather than the mere conclusion formed by
them. The favorable or unfavorable report gives only the opinion of
one member, and encourages laxity in investigation, while a statement
of facts or information obtained shows the care used by the members of
the committee making the report, and gives to the Lodge a clearer basis
for its action.
CONCLUSION.

And now, my brethren, that I am about to yield the power which
you have vested in me, to one more worthy of that trust, I thank you
for the high honor you have conferred, and to crave your kindly indulgence in all cases where errors in judgment have been committed.

Since the last Annual Communication dispensations for the formation of three new Lodges have, by order of the Grand Master, been
luued from this office, as follows:
January 11, 1911, to Kerman Lodge, at Kerman, Fresno county;
January 23, 1911, to Inglewood Lodge, at Inglewood, Los Angeles
county;
July 27, 1911, to Eagle .Rock Lodge, at Eagle Rock, Los Angeles
county.
The petitions for the foregoing dispensations, with the certificates of
withdrawal of the several petitioners from the Lodges of which they
had last been members, and the reflllired certificates as to the qualifications of the Masters and Wardens proposed, were all correctly prepared and presented; and they are her~with submitted, together with
the returned dispensations and books of record and the petitions of the
said new Lodges to be perpetuated by charter.
The charter of San Fernando Lodge No. 343 having been c;lestroyed by fire, a duplicate charter, by order. of the Grand Master, was
issued on the 1st of . September, 1911.
At the close of the last Annual Communication there were three
hundred and thirty-nine chartered L~dges on the roll of Grand Lodge,
and one Lodge (Upland) under dispensation, the total membership being 43,675." Since then three new Lodges, as shown above, have been
formed, making the total number of Lodges now on the roll three
hundred and forty-three.
Probably never in the history of Grand Lodge have. annual reports
from secretaries been prepared . with greater care1 and mailed to this
office more promptly, than this year. Of the three hundred and thirtynine chartered Lodges, annual returns from three hundred anq thirtytwo were received in time as required by law, and with minor corrections r'equired in just a few cases they were carefully and neatly prepared. The reports of two Lodges in Manila were received afte~ the
time required by law, but were mailed in time. The reports of the

have been received, the approval of the Grand Master in fifty cases
has been filed in this office. Of these, nineteen from Lodges Nos. 38,
41, 179, 187, 192, 198, 236, 245, 261, 273, 299, 321, 351, 375, 396, 414, 415,
416, and Upland U. D., proposed changes in time of stated meetings;
twelve being from Lodges Nos. 35, 110, 119, 122, 149, 156, 173, 175, 216,269,

No. 268, proposing to adopt an entire set of by-laws, was also not
approved.
The foregoing proposed amendments have been placed in the
hands of the Chairman of the Committee on By-Laws of Lodges, as required by law, and will be submitted to Grand Lodge for final action.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The books of by-laws of Lodg~s working under dispensation have also
been placed in the hands of the same committee.
The Pierce library, referred to in the address of the Grand Master,
has been boxed and stored in a fireproof warehouse near the site of the
new temple. The books fill twenty-four large boxes, and when the
new temple shall have been completed will form a splendid nucleus for
a Masonic library.
Officers of Lodges ancl brethren generally have been deluged of .
late with copies of a publication known on its face as "King Solomon
and His Followers-A Valuable Aid to the Memory." It purpprts to
contain lectures in Masonic degrees "by a system intelligible only to
the initiated," and "having been recently critically revised by competent authorities in the different Grand Jurisdictions." It is hardly necessary to call attention to the fact that it is not only of no use to a
Mason, but that the law of our Grand Lodge says that "the mysteries
of Masonry have, in all ages since the first organization of this ancient
order, been taught by tradition and committed only to the faithful
breast."
Our membership is now nearly forty-six thousand, and we are
growing at the rate of more than two thousand a year. The printed
roster last year contained the names of 43,675 members in good standing, 4,080 names of officers, 783 withdrawn, 392 suspended, 9 expelled,
632 died, or a total of 49,571 names. None of these names can be
found unless it be first known with what Lodge the brother was affiliated . Before we grow to so large membership that the task will
be beyond ordinary human endeavor, would it not .be wise to adopt a
card index of membership, and keep in the office of the Grand Secretary a card record of the Masonic history of each member in the jurisdiction. Beginning, say, with the current year, a competent clerk ought
to be able to collect data for a fairly complete index in two years or
there<.bouts, after which time the printed roster could safely be discontinued and the .present cumbersome method of annually compiling the
entire membership by. Secretaries done away with. Secretaries of
Lodges then would need only to report increase and decrease for the
year-a total of some 6,000 names, instead of nearly 50,000, as now. At
best it will require almost if not fully a year to work out the detail of this
proposed work, and at least two more years to complete it; hence I
present it for your consideration at this time.
The publication known as "List of Regular Lodges" has proved
to be valuable to Lodges-indeed, i·t ought to be in the hands of every
Tyler . and on every Secretary's table-but · unfortunately not many
Lodges buy it. I suggest that the Grand Secretary be directed to .purchase and mail to each Lodge, Grand L odge officer and Inspector one
copy yearly.

Secretaries of Ledges having life members experience difficulty in
keeping in touch with such members, and not infrequently lose all
knowledge of them. Now and then a life member is expelled. It occurs
to me that an annual life membership card should be issued, and I commend the suggestion to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
Many men-and some women-not in any way entitled to Masonic
recognition travel about the country preying on the Masonic fraternity,
tearfully telling ingeniously constructed tales of distress and too frequently securing money and attentions at the expense of our brethren
and Lodges. The Masonic Relief Association of the United States and
Canada, of which Brother Lurtin R. Ginn, of Washington, D. C., is
president, is organized for the purpose of advising as to who are frauds,
and I hope this Grand Lodge will again become a subscriber and member of the Association. '
The matter of revision of the Manual was last year referred to the
Committee on J urisprndence, and a report thereon will doubtless be
presented at this Communication. ·
The revision of the fun~ral service was- at the last Annual Communication referred to the Grand Master. I have received several communications from brethren protesting against any material change in
the present ritual for funerals, but the sentiment seems to be quite
general that it is too long and in parts too doleful and harrowing,

:Another year has drawn to a close, and in reviewing our labors to
ascertain the cause for the calls for relief, we have come to the conclusion that the unsettled condition of the labor question is responsible
for many appeals for aid; also the low rate for transportation 'to the
west, and higher rates eastward, and the increased cost of livirig.
Of .cour$.e, one o.f the principal causes is the influx of invalids who
are being sent to our delightful Southern California climate, when it
is. too late to regain health. Many of them die, and the Board of Relief is called upon to provide for burial, ·and to care for the survivors.
However!. we do our work cheerfully arid as ·o ur best judgment dic"
tates.

We think it wise to again sound a. warning, .aµd we .quote from our
last year's report a paragraph which is s.~i11 . true,• viz.:
"Brethren,. throughout the United States, who'may read .this teport:
In the name of Humanity, don't send your consumptives· and otherwise
hopeless invalids to the Pacific Coast, unless they have sufficient means
to take care of themselves. n is not doing them a kindness, and it is
positively unjust to the Craft in the West It is hard enough for
a well man to get a position, but for an invalid it is impossible.
"The large corporations and business houses require t~eir eml>loyees
to pass a physical examination before acceptln~- them...:..and rest assured
the physicians who make those examinatio?S are honest and give their
employers the benefit of the doubt. Forty years of age is also the
limit."
THE EMPLOYMtNT BURtAU.

The Masonic Employment Bureau, operated in conjunction with the
Board of Relief, and yet under separate an_d d~$tinct manageme~t, has
secured employment for many members 6! the Craft during the year.
This Bureau is supported by monthly contributions from the Board of
Relief and the other Masonic .Bodies of Los Angeles City. We would
be glad to see such a Bureau established in. every city in the United
States.

V.'. W.'. Thomas J. Baker, Grand Lecturer, presented
his annual ~eport, as follows :
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
I herewith submit to you my report as Grand Lecturer. The yeaT
which has just passed has been a most successful one Masonically.
Many new Temples have been completed by the Lodges and several
have the same under course of construction. Some Lodges are now
arranging for the purchase of lots and the adoption of plans, all of
which shows that most of the Lodges are in good financial condition.
Nothing seems to create more interest in a Lodge than the building and
completion of a new home. It seems to put new life and energy in the
officers and members and a greater desire to perfect themselves in the
work. Most of the Lodges have had a great many candidates this
year and the general c·ondition of the work throughout the jurisdiction
has greatly improved. I have visited every district in the State and
held schools of instruction, day and night sessions.
These schools have been almost invariably well attended by the
officers and brethren, all anxious to perfect themselves in the work. I
desire to thank the Inspectors for their courtesy and assistance during
the year. They have ren·dered valuable assistance to the Lodges under
their supervision.
For the purpose of stimulating interest in the ritualistic work a
series of meetings, presided over in turn by the Inspectors of San

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

63

Francisco and the bay counties, has been· inaugurated, with very satisfactory results. The first meeting was held Monday evening, Sept.ember 11th, in the Temple of Richmond Lodge, No. 375, and it proved to
be of interest and value not only to the Inspectors but to of6cers and
brethren who attended in considerable numbers. The 1next meeting
was held at the Temple of Mission Lodge, No. 169, on Wednesday
evening, September 27th, and meetings of a similar character will be
held at intervals throughout the year. It has proved two things plainly,
that the Inspectors know the ritual thoroughly and the brethren are
satisfied by practical exemplification that the system of inspectorship is
of real worth in keeping the work uniform and instilling enthusiasm
among the members.
It was my ·pleasure and privilege to accompany the Most Worshipful Grand Master on his visits to nineteen districts, comprising ninetyfive Lodges, in the northern part of the State. These visits of the
Grand Master do a great amount of good, many of the Lodges never
before in their history having had a visit from the Grand Master. On
several occasions the Grand Master conferred the Third Degree, much
to the delight of the brethren, for I am pleased to say that ou-r Most
Worshipful Grand Master conferred these degrees absolutely letter per"
feet, and the beautiful and instructive Masonic lessons which were exemplified by ·him at the banquets held after these meetings were very
much appreciated by the brethren.
Reports have been received from all the Inspectors except the
Forty-second and Sixtieth Districts, and they report the Lodges under
their care to be, with very few exceptions, in good condition, and that
quite a number of the Lodges are teaching their candidates the Third
Degree coaching lecture.
The Lodges throughout the jurisdiction are looking forward with
a great deal of pleasure to the laying of the corner stone of the new
Masonic Temple, which is to be held at this session of the Grand
Lodge.
I desire to thank the Very Worshipful Grand Secretary and his
assistant for the many courtesies extended to me in his office during
the year, and also to the Most Worshipful Grand Master for his advice and suggestions, which were of valuable assistance to me in
my work.
On Tuesday evening, October 10th, the Third Degree will be conferred and our Most Worshipful Grand Master has kindly consented
to fill the East, assisted by the Inspectors of San Francisco and the
bay counties.
On Wednesday evening, October 11th, t'1e Second Degree will he
conferred by Live Oak Lodge, No. 61, of Oakland.

The Committ€e to whom had been referr~d the address
of the Grand Master and ·the report of the Grand Secretary,
through Brother A. Bradford Webster, presented the following report:
To the M..". w:. Grand .Lodge .of California:
Your committee to whom .was assigned the consideration and distribution of the sever at matters contained in the reports of the M.". W: .
Grand Master and the v:. W.'. Grand Secretary have had the same
under careful consideration and beg leave to report thereon as follows:
Primarily we wish to commend the attitude of the Grand Master
foward the ' indifferent and vicious members of Masonry, and to voice
our hearty endorsement of his sentiment that it is the duty of the
Order to rid itself of these objectionable ele'rrients, especially where indifference has brought forth its legitimate fruit of vicious practices
which weaken the body of Masonry and bring discredit a·nd scandal
up on the Order.
The Grand Master's comment on the work of the various Boards
of Relief, and especially of the employment bureau inaugurated at Los
Angeles, is fully in accord with the most progressive standard of Masonic charity', which, if practical and efficient, must ever look to the
end of placing the needy one in a position to help himself.
It is evident from the Grand Master's report that many questions
have beert propounded to him which should have been answered by a
reference to our laws, had the inquirers possessed the necessary knowledge and perseverance in reseaTch.
In this connection your committee desires to call atterition to a portion of the report of the Committee on Correspondence rendered at
our last Annual Communication. It is noted there that in the State of
Maryland Grand Master Shryock, who has been such for more than
twenty years. has not been called upon to render a single decision
throughout that entire period, from which he argues that the Masters of
the MGryland Lodges know the law and that it must be obeyed. This

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

is no doubt an extreme case, but it is at least a sugg~stion along the
line of that portion of our Grand Master's address.
.
That portion of the addre11s referring to decisions we recommend
be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, as likewise the recommendations upon the subjects of juris.diction of Lodges and the form
and contents of petitions for degrees.
We note with appreciation the ·action of the daughters of our late
Grand Master, W. Frank Pierce, and endorse most heartily the Grand
Master's expressions in this regard.
That portion of the Grand Master's address which deals with the
establishment of a card system for the purpose of simplifying the roster
we most heartily commend, and recommend the reference of both that
portion of the Grand Secretary's report and the comment of the Grand
Master thereon to a special committee to be appointed for the purpose,
with the hope that they may see their way clear to authorize the practical adoption of some such plan.
That portion of the Grand Secretary's ·report which deals with application? for ch1nteri; and consolidatioq of Lodges we would recommend be referred to t)le Committee on Charters.
We recommend the reference to the Committee on Finance of the
Grand Secret!l'ry'i; suggestion as to the purchase by the Grand Lodge for
the use of sµbordinate Lodges of the "List of Regular Lodges,'' anµ
concur with the Grand Secretary that it is a most useful aid to proper
tiling; and to the same committee the Grand Secretary's suggescion as
to life membership cards and membership in the Masonic Relief Aswciation of the United States and Canada.
·
We commend especially that portion of the Grand Secretary'• report which deals with the use of ciphers, and concur most heartily with
him that the practice should be condemned and discouraged, if need
be even by Masonic discipline,
It is a matter of special pride to note from the Grand Secretary'•
report that the Secretaries of the various subordinate Lodges have
shown an especial degree of promptness In forwarding their returns to
the Grand Secretary, and trust that this may come to be such a habit
that only a departure from it will attract comment in the future.
The Grand Secretary'ii suggestion as to the Funeral Service seems
well taken, and we concur in an expression of opinion that, if any
change is made therein, it should be along the line of conformity to
modern sentiment, and that time-worp, hackneyed and merely heartrending features should be eliminated. The hand of the Great Reaper
falls with sufllcient force upon the bereaved without having the bitterness of' the blow augmented under the guise of a needlessly harrowing
Fune·r al Service, even though it be a fraternal upression of regard
and regret.

In conclusion, we desire to say that both the Grand Master's address and the report of the Grand Secretary reveal •a comprehensive
and inteUigent grasp of the present ptoblems of this Gtand Jurisdiction, as well as zeal and painstaking industry on the part of both of·
ficers, and we cannot but feel that during the past year we have had a
thorough and business-like administration of these high offices which
it is a pleasure to cwntemplate, and which should be a lasting source of
congratulation to the craft in general and the Masons of California in
particular.
Respectfully submitted,

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
1. It has been proposed to amend Section 1, Article IV, Part I, of
the Constitution, to read as follows :

"Section 1. The Grand Lodge shall hold its Annual Communications for the transaction of its regular business at the City of San
Francisco, commencing on the second Tuesday of October at 10 o'clock
a. m. ; provided, however, that the Annual Communication in October,
A. L. 5912, shall be held in the City of Los Angeles."
The only change made by this in the existing section is the addition of the proviso relating to the Annual Communication for the
year 1912. We tmderstand that it is the earnest desire of all our
Southern Brethren that this amendment be adopted, in order that
they may have an opportunity to entertain the Grand Lodge.

84

PROCEEDING$ OF THE

While we are not in favor of a movable Grand Lodge, we believe that it is advisable to adopt the amendment. Our new Masonic
Temple will not be completed in time for our riext Communication,
and if we are ever to gratify the desire of the Masons of Southern
California to have one Communication of the Grand Lodge in their
section of the State, the coming year is the time, for by October, 1913,
we shall be permanently established in our new home. We understand
that the additional expense of going to Los Angeles will not be great.
We feel that our Brethren of Southern _California deserve this recognition at the hands of the Grand Lodge for their faithful and efficient service in the cause of Masonry.
The amendment is so drawn that all Communications after the
year 1912 will be held in San Francisco.
We recommend that the proposed amendment be adopted.

The report was adopted and the amendment carried by
unanimous vote.
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California :

3. The facts presented by a decision of the Grand Master are as
follows:
A Lodge re~eived a pet1t1on for the degrees from one who had
been rejected by another Lodge oQn)y seven months before, electe~
him to receive the degrees, and conferred the first and second degrees.
The fact that he had been rejected only seven months before, was
made known to the Lodge by the petitioner at the time he made his
application, and he signed his petition without reading it, and acte~. i~
entire good faith . The Lodge received and acted upon the petition
upon the mistaken assumption that he, having been rejected more
than six months before, was eligible to receive the degrees in another
Lodge. Upon the discovery being made after the petitioner had re~
ceived his second degree that the Lodge h~d violated the prohibitio~
in Section 2, Article Ill, Pant III, that Jl'O Lodge sh:all '\receive such

•

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

85

application from any person who, within twelve months next preceding, shall have been rejected by any Lodge," further advancement was
refused, and the question was presented as to what was the status
of the petitioner, and what should be done.
The Grand Master held that the Lodge had violated the law, but
that the innocent petitioner, who had in fact received the fir.s t two
degrees was nevertheless a Fellow Craft; that further advancement
should be denied the candidate, with the privilege of again applying
for the third degree with the usual reference and ballot upon the expiration of the twelve months; that the offending Lodge should return to the petitioner, the fee paid by him for the third degree, and
tender to the Lodge that had rejected him, the fee paid for the first
and second degrees.
.
We are of the opinion that this was a correct disposition of the
case, and recommend that the decision of the Grand Master be approved.

•

Adopted.
·4. The Grand Master rendered a decision to the effect that the
uniform code of By-Laws, as amer)ded at the Annual Communications in October, 1883-1894, and made obligatory in subordinate Lodges
in October, 1898, became, by virtue of such action in 1898, the ByLaws of all subordinate Lodges then existing or thereafter instituted,
and should be copied into the book of By-Laws and observed; that
the only legislative power of a subordinate Lodge in regard to such
By-Laws is to fill in the blank spaces therein, left for the insertion of
the date of stated meeting, and the amounts of fees, dues iand disbursements by the Charity Committee, etc. ; that the only respects in
whiich such By-Laws may be amended . by a Lodge are those as to
which they may thus fill in the blank spaces, and that there are no
other amendments as to which approval by the Grand Master is required.
This decision is in accord with our law and we ·recommend its
approval.

Adopted.

6. As to the resolution of Brother Clement, of Calistoga Lodge,
reading as follows :
'
"Resolved, That the following be made a General Regulation of the
Grand Lodge : When a Lodge shall receive a petition for the degrees
of Masonry from anyone not residing within its jurisdiction, said Lodge
shall forfeit and pay to the Lodge within whose jurisdiction said pc- .
titioner resides the initiation fee charged by such Lodge and a penalty
of $100, unless said Lodge shall have first waived jurisdiction as to said ·
petitioner."
·

We do not believe it to be necessary or advisable to prescribe by
written law a fixed and certain penalty for a violation by a Lodge of
the prohibition referred to in the proposed resolution. Circumstances
alter cases, and it may well be that the circumstances in one case might
be such as to make the prescribed penalty just and fair, while the cir;
cumstances of another case might be such as to make the same unjust
and inequitable. ~o legislation is necessary in this matter. If a Lodge
violates the prohibition referred to, it may be proceeded against under
existing law, and such penalties inflicted as are known to Masonic
usage and for continued wilful violation undoubtedly the ch·arter of
the Lodge may be taken away. We think that the existing laws are
entirely adequate and recommend that the proposed regulation be not
adopted.

The report was adopted and the resolution lost.
7. Brother J. W . Eddy proposed an amendment to the Constitution, to be known as Section 22, Article Ill, Part III, as follows:
"No Lodge in this jurisdiction shall 1"C:Ceivi: an application for the
degrees of Masonry or for affiliation from any person who is engaged,
either as principal or agent, in manufacturing or selling intoxicating

88

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

liquors as a beverage, and every person who, at the time of the adoption of this section, is a member of any Lodge in this jurisdiction who
may hereafter engage, either as principal or agent, in the manufacture
or sale of intoxicating liquors as a beverage, .shall forfeit all rights
and privileges belonging to him as a Mason, and shall forthwith be expelled from the Lodge of which he is a member; but it is understood
that this section shall not be •retroactive."

The questi~n is solely one of policy, upon which a recommendation
by this committee. coulcl· be of no benefit to the Grand Lodge.
We, therefore, report the proposed resolution to the Grand Lodge
without recommendation.

We have always pursued the policy in this jurisdiction of leaving
to the good judgment of the subordinate Lodges the question of the
fitness of applicants for admission to our fraternity, without specific
written limitation of any kind. We doubt whether any change in this
policy is necessary or advisable to protect the craft against undesirable
members. Whether or not a change is desirable is, however, purely a
question of policy, concerning which no recommendation on the part
of this committee is essential. But if a change be considered desirable,
we are of the opinion that the proposed amendment is unnecessarily
broad in placing in the prohibited list not only those who are engaged
in "seUing intoxicating liquors as a beverage," but also all who are
engaged, either as principals or agents, in manufacturing intoxicating
liquors of any kind. If any enactment of the nature proposed be considered necessary, it would certainly seem sufficient to limit the prom-·
biti on, as is done in the jurisdiction of Nevada, to "any person engaged
exclusively in the saloon business, or following the avocation of a barkeeper." We believe the proposed amendment in its present form to be
inadvisable, and we recommend that it be not adopted.

Recommendation was adopted and the resolution
failed.

9. The Grand Master in his address said:
"Considerable trouble has arisen over the question of the geographical jurisdiction of Lodges, and the adoption of some different
plan is requisite to prevent a recurrence of some of the difficulties
occasioned by the annexation of territory to cities and the changing
methods of travel. The air line method of determining jurisdiction
was proper before the trolley car and other means of rapid conveyance,
but now something else seems essential. The Grand Lodge should establish the territory of Lodges not having concurrent jurisdiction, reserving the power of changing to meet conditions, and the Grand Master, in issuing dispensations, should be authorized to designate the
boundaries of the territory of any new Lodge formed."
We recognize that some change in our provisions as to jurisdiction
is essential. The matter, however, is one that requires considerable
time and thought, and we feel that it is impossible at this Communication to prepare and report suitable amendments.
We recommend that consideration of the matter be postponed to
our new Annual Communication, and that in the meantime it be referred
to our successors with instructions to devise and report such changes
in our existing law as are deemed advisable.
Respectfully submitted,
F. M. ANGl!LLOTTI,

The hour having arrived for the consideration of the
annual report of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic
Homes of California, M.'. W.'. William S. Wells presented
the following:

90

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

TRUSTEES' REPORT.
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The Grand Lodge, aJt its Annual Communication of 1909, having
adopted and approved the report of the Special Committee on Masonic
Homes relative to the Board of Trustees, their appointment and term
of office, and the term of Trustee Wells having expired, the M.''. w:·.
Grand Master, alt the close of the last Annual Communication in Oc~
tober, 1!)10, appointed Past Grand Master William S. Wells a Trustee
of the Masonic Homes of California, to serve for five years, vice self,
term expired. The Board, consisting of Past Grand Master William
S. Wells, Past Grand Master Motley H. Flint, Past Grand Master
Thomas Flint, Worshipful Elmer E. Stone and Worshipful E. B.
Spencer, thereupon met and organized by the election of William S.
Wells President, Motley H. Flint Vice-President, Elmer E. Stone Secretary, and as thus constituted has, during the year, conducted the affairs of the Homes, held regular monithly meetings either at Decato or
San Gabriel, and now submits its annual report for your consideration
and approval.
The reports of the Superintendent and financial report of the Secretary and accountants, herewith submitted, are full and complete and
show the general condition of the Homes and the finances, leaving but
little to be said by us.
Owing to the fact that it is almost impossible to get the September
bills audited, paid and returned in time to prepare our reports to the
Grand Lodge and have same printed on the opening day, it was determined Ito close our accounts and the year with August 31st, and hereafter our reports will cover a full year from September 1st to August
31st.
In accordance with the recommendation of the Grand Lodge, we
invested the greater part of the Endowment Fund in municipal bonds
and securities, and the fund has been increased by interest and transfer,
as shown by the financial reports of our Secretary, which is made a part
hereof.
Under Rule 16 an applicant must transfer all property to the
Home and the income therefrom may be expended for the benefit of
such applicant, but the principal shall be ithe exclusive property of the
Home and all moneys derived from such source is placed in "Special
Rule No. 16 Fund." If discharged or dismissed, the money is returned,
less the expense of care and maintenance. Upon the death of a person
having money therein the same is now transferred to the Endowment
Fund, and all moneys devised by will to the Homes is likewise placed
in the Endowment Fund, and this rule thus adoptc;:d by your Board, we

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

91

think, should be approved by the Grand Lodge for guidance in the
future.
The financial report of the Secretary shows that we have a balance
In the General Fund of $10,829.79; that the receipts from our two farms
have been $6,576.18 and our operating expenses $2,815.41, leaving a profit
of $3,706.77, and this is arrived at by charging up against each Home,
for products used, the actual market price of such products at the time
of use.
Many improvements have been made, and the work contemplated
and suggested last year has nearly all been carried out and completed.
There is still much to be done. At Decoto additional and enlarged
chicken yards are required, fences rebuilt, roads graveled and repaired,
the rooms of the second floor of the main building, annex and temple
cleaned and tinted, the barn and outbuildings painted, a new shed for
machinery and farming implements built; a reservoir for the storage
of water for irrigation purposes is contemplated, new piping is required
in many places, wooden flumes for the irrigation of the flat are to be
built, work on our plot at the cemetery is to be done and many other
minor improvements are required, all which will cost ait least five thousand dollars.
At San Gabriel the buildings must be painted outside and all interior walls on the first dormitory floor repaired, painted or tinted, general repair work on the porches, steps, railing, etc., is required, and a
different system of sewage disposal mus.t be installed, all which will
not exceed in cost twenty-five hundred dollars.
Under the rule which has been in existence for some years past,
each .Lodge in th1s jurisdiction is entitled to have one adult admitted
to .the Homes without charge. When it reaches a membership of three
hundred it is entitled to two, and when it reaches six hundred, to three,
and one for each additional three hundred in membership. A Lodge
may, if there be room and the Board approve, have additional applicants admitted upon the payment of $15 per month, these to be subject to discharge whenever the room is required to give a Lodge without full representation in the Home its quota. This rule is, in the opinion of the Board, wise, and is working well.
As yet we have not been compelled to discharge anyone for want
of room, but the time is fast approaching, and the Grand Lodge must
realize it and make preparation therefor, when the need of a new and
additional dormitory will be imperative. We are gradually increasing
in number and our rooms are nearly all occupied at the present time.
Rule 16, s·o ofiten quoted, and referred to in the applications, seems
not to be fully understood by the Lodges, and for the information of all
is here given, as follows :

92

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

"16. In consideration of his or her admission into and maintenance
in the Home, each appllcant shall, before his or her admission, execute
a tleetl of conveyance to the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Home
of California of all of his or her property, real, personal and mixed,
then owned or 1that may thereafter come into the ownership or possession of such applicant, or to which he or she may become entitled; any
life insurance, pension, or income from an organization of any kind paying benefits that he or she may be in, or that may come into his or her
possession, or which he or she may become entitled to. Any income
accruing from such property may be expended for his or her benefit, but
the principal shall be the exclusive property of the Association."

It has been the endeavor of the Board to have this rule fully and
fairly complied with, but we have not met with that co-operation and
support on the part of all the Lodges and applicants that we should.
We have been satisfied that in some cases applicants have been advised
to and have concealed the fact of having money and property. Such
cases are now being investigated and proper action will be taken when
the true facts are developed.
The Board has also held 1that this rule is likewise applicable to those
admitted from a Lodge having its quota in the Home, and that money
and property must be delivered over under this rule and the Lodge
must pay the $15 out of its own funds; that is, thait a Lodge cannot have
an applicant deliver property to it, and out of such property pay for
the care and maintenance of the applicant.
.
We have also consfrued ·the action of the Grand Lodge in 1909,
adopting the report of the Special Committee, as intending that one who
has been reinstated in a Lodge cannot be admitted to the Home within
a year, and one who has been reinstated ·or affiliated after a long demission, is investigated very carefully, and if such action was taken
for the purpose of being admitted to the Home such admission is refused.
We have thus stated 1these questions, that the Grand Lodge may
have the view of the Board on these matters and approve them if satisfactory, or make such changes or suggestions as they may desire.
The general physical condition and health of the residents has been
exceptionally good and we have had no occasion 1to use the hospital,
there having been no serious cases, but conditions are such now that it
must be operated, and all who may be confined to their rooms will be
taken there and cared for. We have a physician within call and his
services are obtained whenever needed, so that every care will be given
them under the supervision of a trained nurse. This will increase our
operating expenses the coming year, but will enable us to better care
for and control our sick and relieve them from the ministrations of
their well-meaning friends, who, as a rule, work more harm than good.

lHtAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

93

We fully appreciate the interest taken in the affairs of the Home
n~d the visits mad~ by the Lodges, members of the fraternity and
friends, and we again call your attention to this great charity and urge
upon you to vis.it the two Homes and see for yourselves what is being
done.

. In an institution like Decoto, where there are so many aged p.nd
infirm, we look for complaint, dissatisfaction and unreasonable demands
and some of you, no doubt, have experienced it. All your Board ask~
is t~at all such complaints that may be deemed by you worthy be investigaited by a personal visit to the Home, that you may have personal
knowledge of the conditions and the facts as they exiS:t, The Board and
Of~~ers will co-operate with you and extend to you every courtesy and
facility for a full and complete examination into any and all such matters: We want you to come and see what is being done for our family
and how these aged and infirm people are treated, and we have absolute ~onfidence as to the result of .such an invest.igation and what your
fi~al Judgment in the matter will be. We have been much benefited and
aided during the year by suggestions and advice of visiting brethren and
we want more of it.
'V!e ~ant to thank the fraternity and all our friends who, by their
contributions, enabled us to make ithe Christmas season at our Homes
one of •cheer, joy and happiness. Also our thanks are due to the
Lodges, Masters and offic·e rs of Lodges and brethren who have entertained our families during the year. It is a source of much happiness
to all, and tends to relieve the monotony, and we shall be glad to have
such entertainments once a month in the future, but we earnestly request. that no plans be made for any such on Sundays. Sunday is a
day of rest with us, and we prefer to have it observed in our own
quiet way with our own services, and shall discourage anything that
will interfere with such observance.
We tender our sincere thanks to the Superintendent and Matrons
for their kind assistance, their loyalty and interest in the Homes and
the welfare of the family. Their efforts and labors have all been to
the building up and best interests of the Homes.
We recommend that the usual per capita tax of one dollar be
levied and that there be appropriated, out of the General Fund, the sum
of $7,500, as we have suggested, for permanent improvements at San
Gabriel and Decoto.
W ILLIAM S. WELLS,
MOTLEY H. FLINT,
THOS. FLINT,
E. B. SPENCER,
ELMER E. STONE.

Brethren : The undersigned presents the thirteenth annual report
as Superintendent of the Masonic Homes of California.
I am pleased to report that during the past year the affairs of the
Decoto and San Gabriel Homes have been very satisfactory.
The improvements and necessary repairs have placed the buildings in good condition. The routine work in the office and details of
internal management have been systematized, modern methods adapted
to our need have been installed. The farm and grounds have been
handled on practical lines, the result being a greater return for the
time and labor involved.
Every influence at hand has been utilized to bear on the inner life
of our lar'ge family. The children at the San Gabriel Home with life
before them have been surrounded with every care and protection to
fit them for their future duties and responsibilities, while the older
members of the family at the Decoto Home are enjoying all the comforts and diversions that only those who are no longer able to fight
the battle of life can appreciate.
There are now at the Decoto Home 65 men and 37 women. Dur·
ing the past fiscal year there have been 21 admissions, 13 men and 8
women, and 8 deaths, 6 men and 2 women.
The general health of the family has been good, with the exception of several whose illness is but a gradual failing of strength, the
inevitable result of advanced age.
The residents are encouraged to volunteer in assisting with the
routine work of the Home and a number are each day giving several
hours attending to liglit duties which are assigned to them. It is by
this means that the carpenter shop, chicken and hog ranch, vegetable
gardens, .~hoe shop and barber shop are of much benefit to the Home.
The ladies assist in the mending of the household linen, also new
work. With their assistance 4,000 quarts of fruit have been preserved.
The Coleman hospital, furnished and· equipped with every modern
convenience, has solved the problem of. caring for our sick.
The opening of the men's club room was one of the most important steps taken to improve the social side of our family life. A
large room, well lighted, large fireplace, furnished with a pool table (a
gift of the Alameda Co1.1nty Lodges), 12 leather-seated chairs and two
8

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

card tables (donated by Oriental Lodge No. 144), 12 large brass cuspidors (presented by Eucalyptus Lodge No. 243), a Chelsea brass
clock (a gift of Mission Lodge No. 169), a pair of andirons (from Tehachapi Lodge No. 313), and 12 framed pictures (donated by friends).
The furnishings make it an ideal club room, well appointed, and gives
our brethren an opportunity and incentive to gather together and
interest themselves socially.
A library and reading room has been placed in the large room
opposite the Assembly Hall. The library now consists of 2,000 volumes.
The reading tables are supplied with the daily papers and current
magazines. A ladies' reading and sitting room has been provided ou
the second floor of the main building and is supplied with daily papers,
etc. A cathedral clock presented by Mission Chapter No. 155, 0. E. S.,
has been placed in the room.
The Behning foot power piano player, together with 150 rolls of
selected music, a magnificent gift of the San Francisco Lodges, was
placed in the Assembly Hall. It has filled a long-felt want, far-reaching in its influence, and furnishes music for our entertainments and
family socials.
Services are held each Sunday afternoon in the chapel. The exercises are entirely conducted by the family and consist of singing by
the Home chorus of ten voices, a Bible reading, a reading of a fifteenminute lecture or sermon by the Superintendent and at the close a recital
hy !the family of the Loi::d's Prayer. Vs1ting clergymen at times give
talks, visiting brethren and friends are often present with us and take
an active part. The services each Sunday are followed by a musical
hour which is also well attended.
On pleasant days, at times, all who are not able to walk are given
a bus ride in the vicinity of the Home.
During the past year all holidays have been observed at the Home
with appropriate exercises. On each occasion the Assembly Hall,
dining-rooms and Memorial Hall and corridors were decorated whh
garlands, bunting, bells and wreaths, the color and design in keeping
with the day celebrated. Visiting Lodges have exemplified the work
in the Siminoff Temple for the benefit of the brethren, and a varied
class of entertainments have been provided from time to time, which
brought much pleasure and good cheer to the members of the family.
Special mention of the entertainments and family gatherings are:
Thanksgiving Day: A turkey dinner, etc., an evening at home. Christmas eve : Christmas tree in the Assembly Hall, distribution of presents. Christmas Day: A bountiful turkey dinner, etc., Christmas exercises in the afternoon. New Year's Eve: Watch party, music and
parlor games. New Year's Day: A turkey d:nner, etc., an evening of
card and visiting parties. January 21: Dedication of Coleman's Hospital by the Grand Lodge of California, large numbers of brethrei1

from all parts of the State being present. Banquet in main <liningrocim January 29: The Board, of Trustees of the Odd Fellows' Home
spent the day going the rounds of the Home. Washington's Birthday:
Songs, recitations and readings. Lincoln's Birthday: Miscellaneous
program, light refreshments. March 24: Ladies' night at the opening
of the men's club room. 'The ladies were the guests of the brethren of
the Home. The evening was spent playing cards, checkers, dominoes
and chess. A championship game of pool was one of the events of the
evening. Light refreshments were served by the brethren. April 29:
Alameda Lodge No. 167 arrived in the evening and conferred two third
degrees in the Temple, after which refreshments were served in the
large dining-room. May 15: Charity Lodge No. 362 exemplified the
work in the Temple for the benefit of the brethren. May 21 : Officers
of Mission Lodge No. 169, accompanied by their ladies, made an auto
run to the Home; they attended our Sunday services, at which time
they presented the Home a Chelsea brass clock for the men's club room.
May 27: The members of Sequoia Loqge No. 349 made an auto trip
to the Home in the evening and conferred the third degree in the Temple. May 27: Ivy Chapter No. 27, 0. E. S., spent the day visiting
with the family. May 30: Memorial Day exercises in the Assembly
Hall and at Cypress Cemetery, where floral tributes were placed on the
graves of all members of the family who have passed away since the
Home was founded. .June 3: The celebrated Pasmore family gave
one of their most excellent concerts, which was thoroughly enjoyed by
the residents of the Home. June 10: The me;nbers of Doric Lodge
No. 216 and their ladies arrived on a special train, bringing with them
thirty children, accompanied by the teachers of the State Normal
School; after luncheon in Palm Grove, a most pleasing program was
given in the Temple, consisting of songs, fancy dancing by the children, etc., with music by their orchestra of fifteen pieces, a day long to
be remembered. June 13: Jewell Lodge No. 374 and Jewell Chapter
No. 238, 0. E. S., spent the day at the Home; after enjoying their
basket luncheon in the grove, an afternoon open-air concert was given
by a band of thirty musicians which they brought with them; a most
happy day for all. July 4: Patriotic exercises in the Assembly Hall,
consisting of songs, recitations and readings; an exhibition of fireworks
in the evening in the presence of the entire family and visiting friends.
July 8: Live Oak Lodge No. 61 made a trip to the Home on a special
train; after a basket picnic in Palm Grove, with ice cream and cake
for all, a splendid musical and literary program was rendered in the
Temple, which was much enjoyed by the family. August 19: Eucalyptus Lodge No. 243 conferred the third degree for the pleasure of the
brethren of the Home. August 23: The Board of Trustees of the
Hebrew Home for the aged, at San Francisco, made an inspection tour
of the Home and grounds. August 27: Mission Chapter No. 155,

0. E. S., spent the day visiting with the family. At our Sunday serv-

able to the occasion. Cadet drills by the boys, wand drills by the
girls, catchy songs with gestures or movements, and games with songs,
furnish much pleasure not only to the children but to visitors who
witness their work. The children have advanced much .in their music,
particularly with the piano and singing, but the mandolin quartette is
necessarily being reorganized on account of the larger girls leaving the
Home. This quartette is a favorite feature at entertainments of Lodges
and Eastern Star bodies, and while the new one is not proficient enough
to take part in programs they are working faithfully and will have
substitutes waiting, so the quartette may not again be disturbed by departures from the Home.
The entertainment~ of the year deserving particular mention are:
November 4-Reception to Grand Master Dana Reid Weller, the
children taking part in the program.
December 21-Christmas entertainment, given by Acacia Chapter,
0. E. S., the children giving the program and being remembered by
Christmas presents.
December 25-A beautiful Christmas tree and appropriate program
was held in the Assembly Room on Christmas Day. The room was
very bright and cheerful, with holly, corn strings and ribbons arranged
by the older girls. The generous fund donated by the several Lodges
and members was used to meet the individual tastes, desires and needs
of each child. A more happy culmination of a year's anticipation of
holiday time could .not have been arranged.
March 5-Meeting of Los Angeles Board of Relief, 52 members
present. The children gave a good program and members of the
Board viewed .the building and grounds.
March 31-A splendid musical recital by Mrs. Runkel.
April 16-Visit of members of Palestine Lodge and Palestine
Chapter, 0. E. S., about 70 in number. Good program and treats for
the children.
May 21-Character reading and splendid address adapted to the
understanding of the children by Brother Frank F. Pratt.
June 2-Esperanza Chapter, 0. E. S., had lunch under the trees
and furnished program for the children. 1
June 11-"South Gate Day" about one hundred members of South
Gate and their families visited the Home. A most enjoyable day both
for the children and the visitors.
June 17-Los Angeles Chapter, 0 . E. S., gave a picnic under the
trees, with basket lunch, inviting all the children and employees of
the Home to take part. The program alternated with numbers between
the children and visitors. The boys' ball team beat a select nine from
the men visitors.
June 24-The children took part in St. John's Day celebration, given
by Signet Chapter No. 57, R. A. M.

ices, which they attended, a beautiful cathedral clock was presented
to the Home for the ladies' reading room.
All the stores and supplies of the Home have been centralized.
The large half basement of the Annex building has been made the
storehouse of the Home and is now partitioned into eight rooms. In
addition to the storerooms, an office, dispensary, shoe shop, barber shop
and bakery have also been placed there in rooms adapted for the purpose. A large carpenter shop has been opened up in the basement of
the main building, also a paint shop. A large room has also been
partitioned off for storing · furniture, trunks, etc.
The woodwork and fences at the springs have been repaire.. new
water boxes were made to replace the old ones. The supply of water
has been ample and the reservoirs are now almost up to their full
capacity. The septic tank system has been completed and now furnishes water for the irrigation of the flat in front of the Home, part
of which has been planted to alfalfa.
The chicken ranch supplies the Home with eggs, the hog ranch
with pork and the gardens with all vegetables · except potatoes. The
orchards supply all fruit for preserves and table use; a ready sale for
the surplus is found in the San Francisco market. The prunes are
now being gathered and sent to the dryer; the vineyard is in good
bearing and will yield good returns.
·
SAN GABRIEL.
The Home at San Gabriel has enjoyed a particularly successful year.
Our children are all perfect in health, happy in their surroundings, and
exceptionally good in discipline. No visitor at the Home leaves without
being much impressed with the general behavior and courtesy of the
children. There are now at San Gabriel 50 children-30 boys and 20
girls. During the year there have been 19 admissions-11 boys and 8
girls-and 14 departures. Of the departures some have returned to
mothers who have remarried, two whose father regained his health and
the others placed in: good surroundings, the girls receiving advanced
education and the boys learning trades.
·A cheerful atmosphere of home-like influences surrounds the children at all times. The Sunday school, undenominational in teaching, is
condncted by neighbors in the chapel on the grounds, the children of
the entire district surrounding uniting in the service. Church service is
held in the morning pnly, by some pastor from the Los Angeles
churches.
The children have been well entertained many times by visitations
from the Lodges and Chapters. All holidays and anniversaries of historical or other incidents are appropriately observed by programs suit-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNLh

August 8--Halcyon Chapter, 0. E. S., gave a watermelon party, the
children being a feature of the program.
·
August 26-The children, as the guests of East Gate Lodge, were
given an auto ride through the streets of Los Angeles. It was the first
time many of the smaller ones had seen the streets lighted, which gave
them new impressions of the city. The latter part of the evening was
spent on the spacious grounds of Brother Spaulding's home, where the
children enjoyed an interesting vaudeville entertainment provided for
them.
August 29-Professor B. R. Baumgardt gave his lecture on "Legends
of the Rhine," with illustrations of views from Germaqy.
Many other affairs highly interesting in their character in the
way of social gatherings with neighbors, birthday parties, etc., occupy
the time pleasantly and no notice is necessary to provide a jolly evening
any time.
No greater enjoyment or benefit has been provided the children
than their vacation at Camp Wells (so named by the children as a
compliment to Judge Wells, the President of the Board of Trustees).
The camp equipment was safely stored in the camp company's warehouse and we trust such a trip to the mountains may be made .an annual treat. A certain sum apportioned from the Christmas donations
would cover the expense easily. The task of moving this body of children with all necessary bedding and supplies is no small one, but is
well worth the effort.
The improvements made during the year are practically those recommended in our last report. A good dairy barn pas been built, with
necessary fencing and equipment. A new concrete oil reservoir has
been constructed for the heating plant, also a brick smoke stack to replace the old steel one, which became useless on account of age and
rust. A new reservoir connected with the irrigating pipes has been
built. This we housed over, built in dressing rooms and use as a
swimming tank for the children, making a very popular improvement
for both uses. A new roof was put on the main building and new
plumbing fixtures have replaced the old ones in every department. Many
other improvements, minor in themselves but in the aggregate add much
to the general benefit of the property, have been made as convenience
would permit during the year.
The fruits this year produced well and the garden has supplied
p~iJ.ctically all the vegetables used except potatoes.
About an acre
ha~ been set out in table grapes and another acre in a variety of berries,
all the plants doing exceptionally well. The ornamental garden in front
of the buildings has been much improved with new walks, shrubs and
flowers.

Grand Master Dana Reid Well er and officers of the Grand Lodge
have made a number of visits to both Homes, and during the year a
large number of the brethren have spent many pleasant hours with us.
I desire to express my appreciation of the efficient and conscientious work on the part of the Matrons whose earnest efforts have been
a potent factor in maintaining a high standard of service throughout
their departments.
On behalf of the Matrons and myself I wish to thank the members of the Board for the kindly assistance given and the many acts
of courtesy received. ·
We again wish to assure you of our heartfelt appreciation of the
confidence placed in us. We have endeavored to bring to our work
a good understanding of the responsibility of the duties devolved upon
us and with unfaltering trust in the ideals of the Home, our hands
strengthened by past experience, we look forward with faith to the
coming year.
Fraternally submitted,
FRANK B. HARTMAN,
Superintendent.

WH:ERl\AS, This Grand Lodge views with approval and satisfaction
the present administration of the affairs of the Masonic Homes of Cali~
fornia, realizing that in the prop'er conducting of the same Masonry
necessarily places itself before the world in its most practical as well
as one of its most commendable forms; and
WHl\RJiAS, Considering the rapid growth in the. membership of subordinate Lodges in this Grand Jurisdiction, and the urgent necessity of
fulfilling every obligation laid upon us to suitably provide for -0ur worthy
needy of both sexes ; and
WHl\Rl\AS, The limit of our accommodations at Decoto is now almost
reached ; . therefore, be it
Resolved, That this Grand Lodge requests the Board of Trustees of
the Masonic Homes of California to submit to the next Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge such plans as they may deem necessary for
the proper enlargement of the Home at Decoto, in order that our need
for further accommodations may not find us unprepared to fulfill the
duty incumbent .upon us.

The resolution was adopted.
