Afternoon Session.
Wednesday, October 11, A. L. 5911.
The Grand Lodge was called on at 1 :45 o'clock, the
Grand Master presiding.
In the presence of a house seated to its fullest capacity
W.'. Brother Albert G. Burnett delivered his annual oration, · and every delegate present will bear witness that it
did real good, not only to the ear-for its delivery was as
sweetest music-but to the heart and mind and conscience.
A motion by Brother Ernest C. Bonner, amended by motion
of R.'. W:. Brother A. J. Monroe, that 5,000 copies be
printed and distributed to Lodges by the Grand Secretary,
with a like number of copies of the Grand Master's address,
was unanimously carried.

The full text of the oration is as follows:
Any man might well hesitate to deliver an address upon an occasion like this. The nature of the theme that must engage our attention, the high character and attainments of those who listen, and the
e·xpectations that have been aroused by the rhetorical efforts at past
Convocations are rather discouraging to pretentious ambition, and they
operate to increase any speaker's distrust of his ability to say anything
worthy of the time and of the ,audience. How often have you been
instructed, entertained and charmed by the learning and eloquence of
the most gifted men of the State. Their utterances have undoubtedly sunk deep into your minds, and, like good seed sown in good
ground, have produced an abundant harvest of inspiring thoughts and
noble deeds .
. I know n ot whether I shall be able to add anything to your mental
e·quipment or to assist you in garnering more of the real substantial
fruits of Masonic teaching, but may I not hope at least to convince you
of my conviction that this venerable Institution is one of the. greatest
instrumentalities in the world for the moral regeneration of mankind;
that we cannot love it with an affection too ardent, nor can we too generously devote our time and attention to the practice and promulgation
of its principles.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

137

We naturally ask : What is it about Masonry that challenges
our admiration, excites our interest and justifies the labor and sacrifices
that we furnish in its behalf? Do we not devote to its convocations and
the duties imposed by its laws and ritual much time that we can illy
spare from our business? Do we not deny ourselves a portion at least
of the j oys of home life in order that the work of the Lodge-room may .
not be neglected?
Do we not contribute freely of money that we sometimes need
for other purposes, that the boundaries of the order may be extended,
1hat its power in the land may be increased and its influence enlarged
and multiplied? Do we not spend hours of anxious thought and
1emain awake at night, concerned lest through our indifference or inattention we hinder the mighty work in which the Craft are engaged?
What is it that prompts this keen interest? Why should we be
so deeply concerned in the development and growth of the Order?
For our conduct and attitude can we justify ourselves in the forum of
enlightened conscience?
Do we revere Masonry, pay homage at its shrine, and profess ad~erence and devotion to its tenets because of its antiquity, because
H has come down to us from the dim and mysterious past?
Tbis
feature, my brethren, cannot be ignored; it is not to be minimized.
It appeals strongly to the imagination and awakens the interest of
every one who is not entirely engrossed with self. The fact that this
institution has survived, for hundreds of years, the mutations of human
affairs, that it has withstood the assaults of a thousand tempests of
factional strife, that it has successfully resisted the persistept attacks
of perfidious foes with!n and misguided and fanatical foes without,
that the mighty conflicts of men and of nations for self aggrandizement, the wars of conquest and devastation, the revolutions in government and the storm and stress in the social and the political world
which history reveals, have not disturbed the foundations of our "an~
dent and honorable institution" is a circumstance of tremendous moment and a persuasive argument in favor of the validity of its claims.
upon the attention and admiration of mankind.
I need not remind you, however, that this alone is not sufficient
tn justify the esteem in which we hold this institution.
Do we glory in our membership because of the number and character of those who have allied themselves to the Order? We are associated, indeed, with a vast company of men, growing more numerous every year. Counting those on this and on the other shore
they are almost as numerous as the sands of the sea. In number~
there are majesty and strength and influence and we have a right to
be pro.ud of our connection with such a mighty host. But infinitely

138

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

of more importance is the high quality of the men who have been and
are identified with this organizati0n.
Confining ourselves to the history of our own country, it is the
language of truth and soberness to declare that its most brilliant
pages have been the result of the genius, patriotism, courage and industry of members of the Order. Our brethren, indeed, have been in
the very vanguard of progress in every department of human activity.
They have acquired and maintained leadership in peace as well as
in war.
What a splendid galaxy of inventors, of artists, of poets, of historians, of orators, of statesmen, and of warriors, could be summoned
from our rolls since the days of the Revolution! What a tremendous
ti1sk it would be to discover and to name the great leaders in our
history, beginning with Washington, who have enlisted under our banners and who have considered themselves blessed of Providence because they were permitted to be members of our Order !
But of equal o·r of more importance are the thousands "to fortune
and to fame unknown" who may not be considered great by those who
are dazzled by the artificial standards of the world, but who, in the quiet
walks of life, have been animated by a high purpose, have gone on
faithfully discharging their duties to their fellow-men, developing those
traits of character that ally us to the Infinite and becoming living
epistles of the utility and beauty of Masonic principles.
Again, my brethrep, if we could comprehend the great field of ,
benevolence and philanthropy that has felt the kindly touch of our
ministration, if we could have indelibly impressed upon our minds a
faithful picture of the distress that has been relieved, of the burdens
of sorrow and despair that have been removed, of the misfortunes
of crime and of poverty that have been alleviated, of the wayward
steps of weak and sinful men that have been turned to paths of peace
and righteousness, of the new song of hope that has been put into
the hearts of the discouraged and the despondent and of the courage
irnd inspiration that have been implanted in the lives of thousands of
the "weary and heavy laden"-all through the influence and efforts of
Masons working in the spirit of Masonry and under the guidance of
its prinCiples, we would have no occasion to inquire further whether
our Order is worth while and whether it merits sincere affection and
unqualified support.
Men and institutions are and ever will be judged by their works.
"By their fruits you shall know them." As an Order we are willing
to submit to that test. Blot out the contribution of M asonry to the
cause of civilization and of humanity and the world would be poor
indeed. Take away from our lives the influence of its principles and
we would be fit associates for barbarians and savages.

139

This last statement, after all, gives us the suggestion of the source

?f t_he ~onderful power of this institution in the world and of the
)usttfu!at1on for our zeal in its behalf. The fountains of idealism
that give character to all our teachings have their origin in the highest a~~ noblest conception of moral truth. They are replenished by
th~ l~vmg waters that flow from the eternal throne of God. These
prmc1ples represent the crystallized product of the best thought of
the. best men of the ages. The wisdom and experience of the cent_u nes have demonstrated the infallibilty of these moral sentiments
as a guide to success and to happiness. No cine, indeed, can achieve
success. worthy of the name, no one can experience enduring happiness without at least an earnest effort to bring his life under the
domination of these divine principies.
Changing s~~ewhat the figure of speech and paraphrasing the
language of P h1hps Brooks, may it not be said: That we are fed
here ;-rith counsel when we are in doubt, with inspiration when we
sometimes falter, with caution when we would be rash, with calm, clear,
trustful cheerfulness through many an hour when our hearts are dark.
The hungry souls of men all over the country are fed with sympathy
and consolation. There is spread before us an abundant feast of
great ?uty and devotion on which we may all grow strong. W e are
fed with solemn, solid truths. W e learn the sacredness of governr.:ent and ~he wickedness of treason. Our . souls become glad and
v 1gorou~ with the love of liberty. We learn to love truth and yet
be charitable-to hate wrong and oppression and yet not treasure one
personal inj1uy or insult. We acquire a reverent and genuine religion.
We are taught the love and fear of God in the shape in which we
ueed tpem most. We may indeed became men worthy of any mission
and prepared for any duty that may arise.
But the one supremely significant and vital principle that lies at
the basis of all our activity and development is the value that we
place ?n the individual. Our institution does not regard men so
much m the mass, but it exalts the individual man as the most imP?rtant object o_f al~ crea~ion. It is not concerned particularly about
J-.1~ ra~k or station m society but it recognizes him as fit to associate
with km~s and to become the ·heir of all the ages. It looks upon him
a~ the child of God and destined to live forever.
This is the tenet of our Order without which all the 'others would
be as "sounding. brass or ~inkling cymbal." If our brethren, generally,
would accept this truth without reservation, if the belief in the inestimable value of man and the conviction that he was made in the image
o~ the Creat~ r and shall live through eternity were a living, active,
vi~al, compelh~g force in the minds of Masons everywhere, what a
mighty revolution would soon be effected in human affairs ; what tre-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

mendous strides would be taken by us towards the realization of the
ldty ideals of our ritual! If the 45,000 Masons in _California be!ie~ed
with all the power and fervor of sincere and undisturbed conv1ct1on
that this earth is not our abiding place, that man is. more deathless
than the stars that he is capable of infinite development, that we are
f!estined to b: associated through eternity with the spirits of the i ust
made perfect, would not our influence for higher things be multiplied,
and through our efforts would not the State soon become a much
Letter place in which to live?
What we need more than anything else is steadfast faith in these
!undamental principles. We are comparatively weak and our influence is impaired because many of us do not believe with the whole
heart the great vital doctrine that we profess. If we would, and could
only accept it with full conviction and unchangeable purpose, we
would have like power with those men of old, who the apostle says:
"Through faith subdued kingdoms wrought righteousness, obtained the ·
i:romises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of hre,
escaped the edge of the sword, out ·of weakness were made strong,
waxed violent in. fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens."
If we had tire full measure of this faith in man and his Maker
we should realize and we should teach our neighbors to realize that
while we seem to be standing on the borders of an awful gulf which
is swallowing up all things human and there appears to be, amid this
universal wreck, nothing stable, nothing abiding, nothing immortal on
which poor, frail, dying man can fasten, this seemin~ darkness of. the
tomb disappears before the illuminating light of faith and, sustamed
by its gracious influence, with joy and courage in the place of fear
arid despair, we approach the cold waters of death.
Everything else will disappoint you; everythi~g else is . mut~b.le;
tverything else will fail you in the hour of severe tnal. But this ab1dmg
faith in the value. of man and in the existence and providence of God
will never fail you. It may be represented as a citadel against which
the storm may rage and spend its force in vain. It will stand firm
amid the ruins of all material things and it will endure forever.
If we had this faith as an inseparable part of our daily life, if
it were ingrained into the very fibre of our being, we could not be
satisfied with . our present indifference towards the misfortunes and
misery of our fellow-men. How complacently, indeed, do we view
the wretchedness that is all about us. H ow easily we persuade ourselves that we are not r~sponsible for the unhappy condition of our
neighbors and· that we are powerless to alleviate it. Blessed probably
with good health, possessing the means whereby we ~ay sec~re for
ourselves and families "the comfo rts and even the luxuries of life and

c.ccupying, it may be, positions of honor and usefulness in the com. munity, we wrap about ourselves the cloak of self-righteousness and
\1-onder how anyone can find anything to complain about in this beautiful world.
If we had this faith as we ought, my brethren, we would rather
be and feel like Tolstoy after the great change came into his life. This
great philosopher of Russia was born in the ranks of the nobility
and he enjoyed every possible social distinction. It is said that "He
sounded all the depths and shoals of honor in so far as honor could
be derived from society or from literature and yet, at the age of fortydght, life seemed so vain and empty to him that he wanted to die."
But he became a new creature through the inspiration of higher
ideals and for thirty years living the simple life of a peasant, he
preached and practised a philosophy based upon the doctrine of the
great commandment : "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all
thy heart and thy neighbor as thyself."
Nor could we be content to donate a part of our money to re!ieve the distress of our neighbors. Such assistance, of course, is to
he commern!ed, but we cannot so easily discharge our whole duty
to those in need. No doubt, the donors of pretentious charity often
apply to themselves the pleasing unction of "duty well done" though
their gifts are like that of Sir Launfal, when starting upon his search
for the "Holy Grail" he encountered the leper at the gate of the castle,
beseeching aid. Sir Launfal was filled with loathing at the appearance
of the afflicted man, but to salve his conscience he tossed, in disdain,
to the beggar a piece of money. The unfortunate mendicant needed
money, but he needed sympathy and affection more, and with scorn
he rejected the gift,

But how different is the story when Sir Launfal returned from
his search and saw the leper again. His gift then was of the humblest character, but back of the gift were rove and compassion. A~
Lowell has so bctautifully expressed it:
"Then the soul of the leper stood up in his eyes ;
And looked at Sir Launfal and straightway he
Remembered in what a haughtier guise
He had flung an alms fo lepi:osie
When he girt his young life up in gilded mail
And set forth in search of the H cily Grail.
The heart within him was ashes and dust,
H e parted in twain his single crust ;
H e broke the ice on the streamlet's brink,
And gave the leper to eat and. drink; · ·

'Twas a mouldy crust of cocuse brown bread ;
'Twas water out of a wooden bowl,
Yet with fine wheaten bread was th.e leper fed
And it was red wine he drank with his thirsty soul."
Indeed, the world needs the red wine of sympathy and love more
than it needs the chilling gifts of formal charity.
If we had faith my brethren, even as a grain of mustard seed,
we should studious!~ refrain from spreading a.nY snares, digging any
pitfalls or placing any stumbling blocks for the wanderin_g feet .o~ our
weak, erring neighbors. Are not .the inducements to sm s~ff1C1ent1y
alluring? Are not the temptations to abandon the wa~ of virtue sufficiently strong? Are we not all in danger of bec~mmg ~nally "Cajtaways? And shall we, with knowledge of the pen! that lu~ks even
for the strongest and best, do anything to encourage the evil beasts
oi passion or of appetite to impair or destroy the moral fibre of our
brother's character?
We may be strong, but we must help to bear the burdens of the
weak. We may be able to resist temptation, but we must put no
"must eat
temptation in the way of our broth er who may fa11· We
no meat" even, if. it cause our brother to stumble.
If this faith and our profession mean anything to us will we n?t
be restrained from defaming the character of ·o ur brother and will
hold his character in our affection as a treasure worthy of
Th" d
we not
preservation just as we regard our own good nam~? . is . oes not
demand compromise with flagrant vice or fellowship w1.th dishonesty
or corruption, or that we shall ignore or excus~ pers1st~nt . wrongdoing or that we abate our opposition to everythmg that 1s m_decent
or debasing in public or private life or that we shall waver m our
demands that Masons shall observe the moral law and discharge as a
-sacred trust the duties of citizenship. But it does mean t?at the reputation of every man, especially of this "Household of Faith," shall be
a precious thing in our sight, that we shall scorn to destroy or to detract from it unless we are compelled by a high sense of duty to
society or the interests of justice require that we speak the truth.
Brethren may we have this day a stronger faith than ever before
in the everla~ting efficacy of these great ideas upon which our Order
is founded. May our strength .be renewed, our vision darified a~d
may we have a highe.r conception of the importance of the work 1?
"'hich we are engaged. May we realize more fully the debt of gratitude we owe to the munificent Author of our being for the gifts of
mind that He has bestowed upon the children of men and for the possibilities of moral and intellectual progress and development that are
ours without distinction of outward circumstance. May we never for-

Ket that not only is it our imperious duty to cultivate and develop
those gifts, but that the emplo:r.ment of them in the service of our
fellow-man must ever be the source of the greatest gratification and
the surest guarantee of their ultima·te perfection.
Let us not be satisfied with our past achievements nor content
with what we are now doing for the welfare of mankind. There is
:m urgent demand everywhere for more aggressive efforts to stay the
hand of injustice, to oppose the usurpations of tyrannical power, to
cripple the wings of avarice and to bring to naught the ambitious
~chemes of selfish aggrandizement
But the only way possible by
which the destruction of wrong may be effected and needed reforms in
government and society may be accomplished is through the acceptnnce by the masses of the people of these moral sentiments to which
we have pledged our allegiance.
·
As Mr. Bancroft has said: "It is alone by infusing great principles into the common mind that revolutions in human society are
brought about. They never have been, they never can be effected by
superior individual excellence." He refers to the age of the Antonines
as the age of the greatest glory of the Roman Empire when men, distinguished by every accomplishment of culture and science, for a century in succession held undisputed sway over more than one hundred
millions of people, until Marcus Aurelius, the noblest of all the emperors, ascended the throne. He could do nothing. His philosophy,
though of the highest type, did not and could not stay the downward
tendency of the Roman Empire, nor did it accomplish a single great
beneficent reform. It is a solemn truth that Bancroft uttered when
he declared that "Society can be regenerated, the human race advanced, only by moral principles, diffused through the multitude."
And we must do our part, my brethren, to induce the multitude to
believe and to accept these principles.
The task we have before us is, of course, a stupendous undertaking, but the reward will be commensurate with the effort required.
We shall not work alone, but we are to be associates and co-workers
with all the forces of righteousness, and it may not be in our day, but
in the near future, as the splendid result of all these good influences
the world shall know the truth and "the truth shall make them free."
And men shall believe, and act as they believe, that "there exists," as
Washington said, "in the economy and course of nature an indissoluble
union be~een virtue and happiness, between duty and advantage," "and
the prop1t1ous smiles of Heaven cannot be expected on a natkin"-and
he might have added, on an individiual-"that disregards the elemental
rules of order and right which Heaven itself has ordained."

Let us never doubt for a moment, my brethren, that these principles are eternally right, that if we faithfully practise them they will
bring us peace and happiness here and glory in the Hereafter.
ALBERT G. BURNETT,
Grand Orator.

The parade was thus formed on Sutter street near
Steiner, and numbered about eight thousand Masons. The
line of march was along Steiner street to Post, thence to.
Van Ness avenue, and thence to Oak street and Van Ness ·
avenue the site of the new Masonic Temple. The Grand
officers' of the several Masonic bodies were seated on a
raised platform erected near the northeast corner of the
building, and the ceremony was commenced with prayer
by Sir Reuben Henry Sink, Prelate of the Grand Commandery, as follows:
Reverently, o" God, we undertake any of our human projects, and
we would seek, first of all, in the beginning, God, Thou,. who art ~he
Supreme Architect of the Universe, who art seeking to bmld for Thme
own glory a spiritual temple, not made with hands, a temple of ~uman
character in which Thy spirit dwells. We look to Thee for gmdan.ce,
and we p~ay that Thou wilt in this undertaking give us wisdom to gmde
us, strength to support us, and the beauty ?f holines~ to adorn our
labors and to render them acceptable in Thy sight; and m the ceremo~y
in which we are engaged of laying a corner stone in this city to M~somc
work and Masonic honor, may Thy blessing descend upon us m the
undertaking.
So order the lives of those who profess the great principles of ~he
Masonic Order that, within the walls here to be erected there may h~e
and act those men who have the honor of God and the good of their
fellow-men at heart, that they may feel their mission, and discharge
their duty as u.nto Thee. And may it be that, when the children of those
who lay the corner stone to-day sh~ll aris~ ~nd ask, What me.ans
this building? that it may be said, It 1s a bu1ldmg where the sublime
principles of humanity are inculcated, and where men meet to plan the
good of their fellow-men.
Bless, we pray Thee, this Convocation. Bless, we pray Thee, every
Lodge represented here. And may all our work be done so that Thou
mayest give unto us the approval of Thine own righteous judgment.

165

A song by the Grand Lodge quartette under the direction of our veteran Grand Organist Samuel Mayer followed.
Brother William H. Crocker, President of the Masonic
Temple Association of California, then addressed the
Grand Master as follows :
We are assembled here to-day to take part in one of the oldest
ceremonies known to history. This ceremony has taught the same lesson
to all the peoples of the earth for five thousand years.
The implements we use are the same-the stone, the line, the
plummet, the mortar, the trowel.
If we follow the precepts of the ancient builders we cannot go
wrong, because the voice of God was very close to them in their building:
"Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a
precious corner stone, a sure foundation.
"Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the·
plummet." (Isaiah XXVII-16.)
Mankind are swayed by many ambitions-the pursuit of riches, the
lust of conquest, the fight foii thrones. All these are but baubles compared to the spiritual force within the heart of the humblest Masonthat force which guides his hand and causes him to lay each stone
to the line with judgment and to use his plummet in righteousness. Be
it a home for the family or be it a temple dedicated to our faith in the
eternal verities of the Almighty, the nobility of his vocation surpasses
all others allowed to mankind in the narrow span of mortal life.
We are gathered together to-day to build anew, for we have been
taught a great lesson by a great disaster. The same lesson was taught
to the children of Israel three thousand years ago. They had forgotten
the covenant and had worshiped false prophets, and the wind and the
earthquake came.
"And after the earthquake a fire, but the Lord was not in the fire;
and after the fire a still small voice." (I Kings, XIX-12.)

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGl.!l OF CALIFORNIA

If we but follow the dictates of the still small voice our foundation
will be secure and our temple everlasting.
Most Worshipful Grand Master, I deliver into your hands this
trowel-'-in form, the same that has been used for ages past. I do this
on behalf of the faithful brotherhood of Masons here assembled. We
know that in the laying of this corner stone you will give expression to
our undying faith in the great truths of Masonry, and that in this
temple, when completed, we will find a shrine where Faith, Hope and
Charity shall abide for all generations hereafter. (Applause.)

The Grand Secretary then read the record of the contents of the casket as follows:

166

The Grand Master accepted the pleasant duty of laying the corner stone in the following words:
Mr. President and Brethren: This is a proud and happy event in
the history of Masonry in California. It marks the commencement
of the construction of the building which will not only be a home for
the Grand Lodge of California and the subordinate Lodges here, but it
will be a monument to the fraternity and a credit to this community,
and we will thereby contribute our fair share to the reconstruction of
this gre.a t city. (Applause.)
As the materials which will be used in its construction are gathered
from the various places whence they originate, and shall be brought
here and placed in position, they will demonstrate the practical applica•
tion of Masonry as it was practiced by our predecessors. As we assemble here from the various parts · of the State and attempt to perfect
a structure for the upbuilding of man, we demonstrate the practicai
application of the moral principles as we work in Masonry to-day.
These same materials, taken in their rough and imperfect state, sepa-rated from each other and with no unity of design, accomplish nothing.
It is only through the organization of men banded together for the
purpose of upbuilding the morality of the community in which they
reside which accomplishes what our Fraternity aspires to perform.
And so long as we practice those virtues which are inculcated in our.
Lodges, and apply the principles of this institution to our lives and
actions, just so long are we taking part in the construction of that moral
edifice and entitled to craftsmen's wages.
The temple of Solomon, great and magnificent as it was, has
crumbled away and disappeared from the earth. This building which
we are starting to-day will not escape the ravages of time. But this
spiritual building which we are erecting will not .perish. The characters which are formed through this association will not die. They enter
into the construction of that spiritual building, that house not made with
ha.nds, eternal in the heavens. (Applause.)

The Grand Treasurer, with the assistance of his
brethren, then took the casket, a heavy copper box 20
inches in length, 16 inches in width and 12 inches in depth,
and descending to the corner, placed it in the cavity
which had been prepared in the lower stone. (This stone,
by the way, is the largest and heaviest corner stone ever
laid in California, it being of granite, weighing twelve
tons.) The Grand Master and his officers then performed
the usual ceremonies of the Craft, and after the completion
of the ritualistic work returned to the platform and listened to the following eloquent oration delivered by Brother
Samuel M. Shortridge:
Most Worshipful: .Humbly and bowed low before the Great Architect of the Universe we are come to lay the corner stone of a temple to
be erected_to His honor and glory. From all sections of our imperial
and beloved State-from wondrous northland and miraculous southlandfrom snowy mountain and violet valley-from village and metropolis:__
we come as Masons of all degrees, but equals all, brothers all, and all
dedicated, all consecrated to the same eternal and divine principles and
faith. (Applause.)
The corner stone has been squared and leveled and adjusted properly by the craftsmen, and on and above it shall rise a temple which will
stand for all that is good and pure, for all that is noble and sublime, for
all that is to be des~red by the sons of men. (Applause.)
My brothers, we come with proud memories of what our beloved
Order has done for mankind. This twilight hour will not permit me
to enlarge upon that glorious record-glorious in deeds of charity, glorious in acts of loving kindness, glorious in steadfastness of faith, glorious in fidelity to the holy cause of •righteousness and peace. (Applause.)
N.ot arrogantly, but in lofty pride, we may this day say that we
belong to the greatest fraternal organization that has ever existed or
exists among men, an Order whose emblem is the cross of Christ, whose
hope is the crown of immortality-which was born before the dawn of
history and has seen the •rise and fall of dynasties, the birth and decay of nations-which wrought marble into forms of beauty. before ever
the columns of the Parthenon were reared or Carthage rose to splendor
-which lighted the sacred torch of science before Rome was founded or
her conquering eagles flew across the Alps-which adorned the cities of
the old world with her masterpieces of architecture and whose genius
reverently displayed itself in erecting temples to the living God-which

•

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

171

flourished before Jerusalem had fallen, and, later, !l)arched and suffer.ed

and died to redeem the Holy City and rescue the sepulchre of the
l,ord-the Order which has joyfully followed the Cross and on whose
celestial banner flame the words, "In Hoc Signo Vinces." (Applause.)
From the days of the son of David, from our immortal Grand Master King Solomon, down the ages, through the darkness and the light,
through all the centuries gray, the banner of Masonry has COflsoled the
sorrowing and inspi-red the despairing, and has been a hope and a blessing to all who sought and found shelter beneath its heavenly folds.
(Applause.)
Our Order is indeed ancient and venerable ; but it is full of the
vitality of youth, it is strong in the strength of immortal truth; and
though this temple may crumble and fall, though you and I may soon
pass away and be remembered not, though every Mason alive to-day
will go to his last abode, Masonry will survive triumphant over the
death of individual members, and live on and on, under the blessing of
Almighty God. (Applause.)
These pious and "impressive ceremonies-the laying of this corner
stone-the beginning of this great architectural work-tum our thoughts
in gratitude to our predecessors, to whom we are indebted for whatever
makes our Order symmetrical and enduring, beloved and beneficentthe ancient Operative Masons, the craftsmen of genius and industry who
toiled with brain and hand, who in their daily lives taught and still
teach the dignity of labor, the beauty of harmony, the blessing of union,
the virtue of obedience, and the necessity of law. The splendid structures, the majestic temples, the glorious cathedrals, scattered over Europe
were and are the consummate work of their master hands. They were
artisans and artists. They wrought in sad sincerity; they builded bet•
ter than they knew, and their glory endureth forever. And we, their
successors and heirs, we, Speculative Masons, like them, Free and Accepted, hold fast to the same principles and subscribe to the same faith
which they exemplified in their lives and cherished in their hearts. (Applause.)
•
·
If our Order stands for anything, it stands for law, it stands for
orde-r, it stands fo.r harmony and peace, it stands for the equality in
rights of all of God's creatures. (Applause.) It stands for law "whose
seat is the bosom of God," and without which chaos would reign in the
social as in the material world. It stands for order, essential to progress and on which all government rests. It stands for peace and harmony among brothers and among States, without which neither a·rt nor
science can flourish. It stands-and may it ever stand- for equality.
W e teach obedience to law. We teach the value of order. We rejoice
in the glories and victories of harmony and peace. We proclaim the
equality of man. Lofty and lowly, prince and peasant, king and sub-

172

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ject, president and citizen, all, all men of whatever rank or station meet
as equals within the temple of Masonry and kneel as. equals before her
sacred altar. We believe that the men who toil with hand or brain, on
the bench or in the shop, in high or low station, who are obedient to law
and faithful to their country, should be equal in the sight of the law, as
we know they are equal in the sight of God.. And over and above all
these holy and beautiful and needful things we openly and reverently
avow our belief in the immortality of the human soul and our firm faith
in the justice of an omnipotent and omniscient God. (Applause.)
My brothers, as Masons we can look heaven in the face without a
fear and without a blush. Our Order not only uplifts and dignifies
human labor; it teaches and practices charity toward all men, cjlarity of
the heart, charity of the lip, charity of the hand-that charity which
"suffereth long and is kind," which "envieth not," which "vaunteth not
itself, is not puffed up," which "doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh ho evil"-that charity
which "rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth." (Applause.)
Masonry teaches men to be charitable, upright and true, faithful,
generous and brave in the battle of life. And every man who is a good
and true Mason will be a good and true citizen of California and of the
Republic. (Applause.)
We are this day laying the corner stone of a temple which will
stand for the virtues and principles of our Order-a temple dedicated to
humanity, to charity that knows no race or creed, to peace whose garlands are unfading, to righteousness which ennobleth man and exalteth a
nation.
Upon the corner stone has been poured the corn of nourishment,
the wine of refreshment, and the oil of joy. May this temple be a home
of nourishment for the poor, the weary and heavy laden. May it be a
refuge of refreshment for the footsore and feeble. May it be a place
of joy for eyes dimmed by tears, for hearts bowed down by grief, for
the distressed in body and in mind. May the gladsome light of morning play upon its walls; may the lingering rays of evening reflect its
glory. May it stand for generations yet to be, immune from fire and
shock, welcoming to its fraternal hospitality the Masons of California
and of all lands. (Applause.)
But, oh, if it should fall, like that other beloved temple, if it should
be consumed by fire or overwhelmed by disaster, the principles and
truths for which it stands will not perish in its ·ruins. Those principles
are immutable, those truths are immortal, and being of celestial origin
they cannot die ; they will survive the wreck of matter and the crash of
worlds. Oh, may this temple stand, watched over and guarded by the

173

approving stars of heaven, and when it falls, if fall it ·must, may our
children-brothers yet unborn-erect another and even more glorious
and worthy temple to Masonry and to God. (Applause.)

At the conclusion of the oration, "Old Hundred" was
sung by the choir, accompanied by the band and joined
in by the whole assembly. The ceremonies were terminated with a benediction by the Grand Chaplain.

Prior to the execution of the contracts for the erection of the temple, and pursuant to the approval of this Grand Lodge, a mortgage of
$250,000 was executed with the Savings Union Bank of San Francisco.
It has not yet beconie rtecessary to use this fund, and no interest will
be paid on the loan until -it ·shall ·be used for the payment of contracts.
Work was commenced on the temple on the first day of August,
and it is expected that it will require about two years' time to complete the structure. ·
As has already beeri shown by the list of subscribers, the Masonic
bodies of the State have· ·enthusiastically endorsed the building of a
monumental temple for our Order by liberally subscribing for stock,
and many individual Ma·sons have also generously subscribed from their
private resources ; yet in order to complete and furnish the building it
is necessary to sell additional stock to the amount of $75,000; exclusive
of the mortgage indebtedness.
We venture to express the hope that a few of our• brethren' to
whom the Almighty has been generous in Jlis bestowal of this world's
gifts w'ill find it in their· hearts to assist i11 the finishing of this magnificent temple. ·
The splendid and enthusiastic outpouri·ng of Masons, displayed in ·
the great pageant of·yesterday, at the laying -o f the corner stone, indicates that the brethren ·of our fraternity are proudly looking for.ward
to the time when the finest Masonic Temple of the West shall be completed, and we confidently believe that many Lodges and brethren who
have heretofore withheld their subscriptions, will now come forward
with their generous assistance.

By Brother Eddy: "Resolved, Tha.t the following general regulation be, and the same is hereby adopted: ( l) All Lodges i111: this jurisdiction are forbidden to receive of any party for the degrees of Masonry
or the application of any Master Mason for affiliation who may be engaged 'in the business of saloonkeeping, either as proprietor or employee. (2) Any Master Mason who shall hereafter engage in the
business of saloonkeeping, either as proprietor or employee, shall thereby
forfeit his membership in the Lodge to which he may belong; and it
shall be the duty of the Master of said Lodge to declare such Master
Mason suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry."

This was defeated, as previously reported.

an application for affiliation of any person engaged exclusively in the
saloon business or as a bartender. Any Mason who may hereafter engage in such business exclusively or as a bartender shall be expelled."

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee, to whom was referred the trial record of Brother
J. J. Q., a member of Yosemite Lodge, No. 133, charged with unmasonic
conduct, beg leave to report as follows:
Brother Q. was charged with being often under the influence of
intoxicating liquor for the past three years and using language on the
streets unbecoming a Mason; receiving money from a member of his
Lodge in payment of dues and not accounting te> the Lodge for the
same, and also refusing to deliver up the keys to the Lodge room in
order that the Lodge might meet, thus preventing the members from
holding a meeting.
There does not appear in the transcript any evidence of a notice
being sent to the members of the Lodge stating the pur~ose for
which the meeting was called, as required by law. The minutes of the
meeting, however, recites "due notification was given to the brethren."
The record is in fair shape up to the serving of the summons,
which was served by one of the Commissioners. While there is no law
agairn>t this, yet it would seem better to have the summons served by
the Tyler, or the Master should authorize some person other than
one of the Commissioners. The next error occurred when two of the
· Commissioners were called as witnesses-in fact, they were the only witnesses. The testimony wa·s sufficient to establish the guilt of the
accused on the second and third specifications and of the charge. All
of the seven Commissioners found the accused guilty of two of the
specifications, but made no finding as to the charge, and voted to
expel the accused. The failure ito make a finding of guilty on the
charge is error, but if the accused was guilty of the specified acts he
was also guilty of unmasonic conduct.
G. W. Alexander acted as secretary pro tern during the trial, S. D.
Hobron acted as secretary at ithe meetiI)g when the Commissioners were
elected, and was alse> elected one of the Commissioners; he also signed
the summons. Alexander certified to the actual trial record, but Hobron (one of the Commissioners) certified to ithe balance of the proceedings; this is also error. Alexander should have acted throughout
the entire proceedings. There is no Tecord in the transcript of the presentation of the matter to the Lodge, but the certificate of the secretary
pro tern shows that some result was announced in the Lodge.
The Master directed the Junior Warden to prefer the charges,
hence, under our law, if objection were to be made, he would have
been disqualified to •receive the charges or to preside at the trial. The
Junior Warden was also elected one of the Com.missioners.
From the record it appears that the charges and summons wer.e
properly served on the accused; · the Master wrote to the accused and

This charge grew out of a dispute as to who was responsible for
the disabling of an engine at Stanford University under charge of
Brother J. Brother J. had accused Brother H. of being ·responsible inqirectly for the · placing of "emery" in the lubricating oil used on the
said engine.
Brother H. tried to convince Brother J. that he (H.) knew nothing
about the alleged placing of "emery" in the oil, J?ut Brother J. ·refused
to listen to him or to disclose to H. any proof that H. was responsible
for the so-called crime :or had anything to do with or any knowledge
thereof; then Brother H. preferred charges of unmasonic conduct against
Brother J. for slandering Brother H.'s character.
• The evidence produced at the trial did not disclose in the least one
fact tending to prove that Brother H . knew, either directly or indirectly,
anything about any "emery" being placed in the said oil until told so
by Brother J., but there was some t~stimony to the. effect that there

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee, to whom was referred the trial recOTd in the case
~f Brother A., expelled by Lodi Lodge, No. 256, having had the same
under con sideration, respectfully report as follows:
Brother A. was brought to trial on charges preferred against him
for shooting a Master Mason with a revolver. He was convicted and
expelled from the Lodge.
'
A reversal is asked upon two grounds:
l"irst-That prior to the last stated meeting, prior to the trial of
the accused, the accused had presented his request for a <limit, which
he had failed to receive, and that he was without the jurisdiction of the
,
Lodge, being confined in the county jail at Stockton.
Second-That the Master erred in deny~ng the motion of the accused for a continuance until such time as he could be present.
The issuance of a <limit would, of course, have been no bar to the
charges against the accused and the trial thereon, and under the circumstances of the case, the accused then being incarcerated in the county
jail, we think Lodi Lodge still retained jurisdiction to try him; this
particularly so in view of the fact that the <limit was not asked for until
after charges had been presented and the Commissioners elected.
As to the second ground, the accused is, of course, entitled to be
present and to be confronted with the witnesses against him; and a
continuance for a reasonable time ought never be refused.
It appears from the record in this case that the accused was in
jail awaiting trial. There is nothing in the record and nothing was ~
presented in support of the motion for a continuance to show that there
was any likelihood that the accused would ever be able to appear before
the Commissioners.

191

Strictly construed, the showing made at the time by oounsel for
accused in support of his request for a continuance was neither strong
nor persuasive ; yet in view of the facts as now detailed to your come
mittee, that proceedings were then being taken in the due course of the
law to proceed against the accused in the proper courts of the State for
a trial upon the cha rge of murder, and it further appearing, the homicide having occurred on the 16th of June last, that the case will come
up for trial in the Superior Court of San Joaquin county on the 24th
of the present month, we think the Master of Lodi Lodge, in the proper
exercise of the discretion conferred upon him, conceding the technical
insufficiency of the showing made, might well have continued the hearing over until after the conclusion of the trial in the Superior Court.
We believe it to be a proper and just exposiUon of Masonic jurisprudence to hold that where one is accused in the courts of the land of
a criminal offense and is also charged in the Masonic tribunals with
the same offense, and it appears to the Master of the Lodge before
whom the trial is to be held that the trial of the accused in the courts
is reasonably imminent, in such event the proper and usual course of
procedure should be to defer the Masonic trial until his tr.ial in the
courts shall have been held. This we hold, not that the result of such
trial in the courts, whatever its termination, is to be regarded as controlling or binding upon Masonic tribunals, but merely that the accused
may not suffer or be compelled to suffer any prejudice in the courts
of law by reason of action had against him by the Masonic brotherhood.
This particular case exhibits peculiarly, we think, the necessity for
such a reasonable rule of procedure, for it might well have been that
the accused, charged with the high crime of murder in the courts, felt
constrained to refuse to make public his defense, if any, to such charge
until actually brought to trial. T o compel him to do otherwise, by
opening up his defense before the Masonic tribunal, might result in
serious prejudice to his rights in the courts of law; in fact, a conviction
by his Masonic brethren might reasonably be expected to influence the
verdict of the jury sitting in judgment upon him; on the other hand,
to force him to a trial at a time when he could not safely present his
defense would be to commit a most flagrant injustice.
We feel therefore constrained to offer and recommend the adoption of the following resolution :
ResDlved, 'l'hat the action of Lodi Lodge, N o. 256, in expelling
Brother A. be and the same ls hereby reversed and remanded to Lodi

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Lodge for a new trial, said trial to be ha.d after the trial of said Brother
A. shall have been concluded in the Superior Court.
Respectfully submitted,

knowledge :of what his duties as a Mason required of him in that behalf, appellat11t on at least two occasions thereafter paid such public attentions to the lady in question as to cause public comment. No testimony was offered in explanation by appellant, and we must therefore
judge the case upon the record made. These proven facts in our opirti:on were sufficient, without giving any wnsideration to the filing of the
complaint in the divorce proceedings or the published article, to sustain the finding of the commissioners that the acts of the appellant
produced "much scandalous talk and comment at said town of Mill
Valley and in that neighborhood," and that appellant was guilty of
unmasonic conduct.
We therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution:

Resolved, That the action of Mill Valley Lodge, No. 356, in this
matter be sustained.
Respectfully submitted,

The resolution of Brother Hugh J. Owen relative to
the restoration of members suspended for non-payment of
clues, was reported by the Committee on Jurisprudence
without recommendation. The resolution was then, by
rnte of Grand Lodge adopted by unanimous vote. It
reads as follows:
To restore Section 11, of Article III, Part III, of the Constitution,
to read as it was prior to October, 1909, and reading as follows:
No Lodge shall expel a member for the non-payment of dues; but,
in case any member shall have refused or neglected to pay hh; regular
dues during a period of twelve months, he shall be notified by the Secretary, either by registered letter or by actual service of notice duly
certified by the Tyler, that unless at the next stated meeting either his
dues be paid or sickness or. inability to pay be shown as . the cause of
such refusal or neglect, he will be suspended from all the rights and
privileges of Mason·ry. If neither of these things be done, he shall at
~uch stated meeting be declared by the Master to be suspended, unless
for special ·reasons shown, the Lodge shall remit his dues or grant
him further time for their payment. But any Mason thus suspended
who shall at any time pay the arrearages due at the time of his suspension, together with such further dues as would, had he retained his
membership, have accrued against him to the date of such payment, or
who shall have ha'd such arrearages and dues remitted by his Lodge,

204

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

shall by either- of these acts be restored; Provided, that should any
member suspended for non-payment of dues neglect for the period of
two ' years to pay ms dues, or have the same remitted by his Lodge,
said member shall not be restored except by a three-fourths vote by
ballot of all the members present at the next stated meeting after tke
petition for restoration is presented.
I
Any Secretary failing or neglecting to comply with the requirements -of this section relative to notifying delinquents, shall be subject
to discipline by his Lodge for neglect of duty.

Wiley James Tinnin was chosen Grand Master of Masons of
California at the Annual Communication of this Grand Body held in
this city in the year 1885. In the brief, business-like annual address
which he delivered the following year he made mention of the remarkable fact that in each of the preceding twenty-nine years he had attended every Communication of this Grand Body. To this remarkable
fact it is meet that we add another !liO•t less remarkable: That during
the quarter of a century after he laid aside the robes of his high office, which he honored not less perhaps than it honored him, he attended every Communication down to the year 1910, the year of his
death. Fifty years of constant attendance arnl. faithful service! What
a record is that, my brethren! Tell me how dould it have been unless
prompted and inspired by a heart filled with the spir.it of Masonry, and
a mind penetrated with its lofty ideals.
Born at Jackson, Mississippi, October 7tih, 1829, at the time of his
death, November 24th of last year, Past . Grand Master Tinnin had
lived more than eighty-one years. During that long life he never fully

may write of him, as it did of another, that he likewise was one who
loved his fellow men.
An a rdent lover of literature, a devotee of the poetic muse, Past
Grand Master Atkinslon was wont · to quote on occasion many gems of

verse from the great masters of poetry and prose whom 'he loved so
fondly and with whom many 'Of his happiest hours were spent. Of these
master thoughts none seem so appropriate, at this moment, nor fraught
with such sublimely poetic significance as these stanzas from Letitia
Barbauld:

216

217

"Life, I know not what thou art,
But I know that thou and I must part;
Or when, or where, or how we met,
I own to me's a secret yet.
Life, we've been long together,
Through pleasant and through cloudy weather.
'Tis- hard to part when friends are dear,
Perhaps 'twill cause a sigh, a tear.
Then steal away, give little warning;
Take thine own time ;
Say not 'good night,'
But in some brighter clime
Bid me 'good morning.'"

Resolutions relative to the death of V.". w:. George
Johnson, who passed from this life Tuesday, October 10,
1911:
Once more we a re reminded of the departure of a good man and
brother to that Celestial Lodge above.
Ver.y W orshipful George Johnson is now numbered among pur
honored dead. He received his Masonic degrees in California Lodge,
No. 1, during the year 1872, and was Master of that Lodge in 1878-79.
Brother Johnson was appointed Assistant Grand Secreta·ry in 1887,
in which capacity he served until the death of the Grand Secretary,
Brother Alexander G. Abell, which occurred in December, 1890, at
which time he was appointed to fill the vacancy in the offi ce of Grand
Secretary, and in October, 1891, was elected to that high office and
served continuously until August, 1908, ill health forcing him to retire.
While Grand Secretary of this Grand Lodge he was faithful to every
trust reposed in him, diligent and conscientious in the discharge of the
duties of his office. Therefore, be it

Resolved, That this Grand Lodge ex tends its sympathy to his bereaved family who loved him, believing that the record he has left behind
·
will and must be a great solace to them.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Brother Johnson was a true man and Mason, and passed to the
Great Beyond loved and honored by his brethren. While we extend I
sympathy to his bereaved family, we feel that our dear brother has
reached a happier. goal, where he lives, a!nd lives most truly, in those
deeds of kindness that were enacted toward his fellow men; for, after
all, our good deeds are the only assets we take with us. And be it

Adopted October, 1911.
Part I, Article IV:
"Section 1. The Grand Lodge shall hold its Annual Communications for the transaction of its regular business at the city of San Francisco, commencing on the second Tuesday of October at 10 o'clock
n. m.; provided, however, that the Annual Communication in October,
A. L. 5912, shall be held in the city of Los Angeles."
Part I, Article VII:
"Section 1. The following Regular Committees, to consist of five
members each, shall be appointed by the Grand Master at each Annual
Communication, as soon as practicable after its commencement, viz.: On
Charters and on By-Laws of Lodges, the duties of which committees
shall cease at the close of such CommunicaHon.
"Sec. 2. The following Standing Committees, to consist of five
members each, shall also be appointed by the Grand Master at each
Annual Communication just before its close, viz.: On Jurisprudence,
on Finances, on Accounts, on Grievances, on Correspondence, on Returns, on Credentials, and on Pay of Members, the duties of which
committees shall continue during the year thereafter, and shall cease
at the cLose of the next succeeding Annual Communication."
Part III, Article III :
"Sec. 11. No Lodge shall expel a member for the non-payment of
dues; but, in case any member shall have refused or neglected to pay
his regular dues during a period of twelve months, he shall be notified
by the Secretary, either by registered letter or by actual service of
notice duly certified by the Tyler, that unless at the next stated meeting either his dues be paid or sickness Q>
r inability to pay be shown as
the cause of such refusal or neglect, he will be suspended from all
the rights and privileg~s of Masonry. If neither of these things be
done, he shall at such stated meeting be declared by the Master to be
suspended, unless, for special reasons shown, the Lodge shall remit
bis dues or grant him further time for their payment. But any Mason
thus suspended who shall at any time pay the arrearages due at the
time of his suspension, together with such furt)ler dues as would, had
he retained his membership, have accrued against him to the date of
such payment, or who shall have had such arrearages and dues remitted
by his Lodge, shall by either of these acts be restored; provided, that
&hould any member suspended for non-payment of dues neglect for

PROP(;>SED AMENDMENT TO THE
CONSTITUTION.
At the Annual Communication in October, 1911, the
following amendment to the Constitution was proposed,
VIZ. :

•

Part III, Article III, Section 20:
"No Lodge shall receive an application for the degrees of Masonry,
or for affiliation, from anyone who is engaged, either as principal,
agent or employee, in the saloon business, except in connection with,
and as part of, the operation of a bona fide hotel or restaurant, or who
is a barkeeper; and any Mason who may •hereafter enter upon and engage in the saloon business, either as owner, agent or employe~, except
in connection with and as part of the operation of a bona fide hotel or
restaurant: or who shall become a barkeeper., shall be deemed guilty of
unmasonic conduct, and shall, upon due trial and conviction of said
offense; forfeit all Masonic rights and privileges, including membership
in any Lodge."

The above was reported by the Committee on Jurispnidence without recommendation and received the vote of
a majority of the Grand Lodge, and now awaits the constitutional vote of two-thirds at the next Ann~al Communication.

ALABAMA, 1910.
Number of Lodges, 526. Present ~embership, 23,303. Net gain, 984.
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted
Masons of Alabama held its Ninetieth Annual Communication in the
city of Montgomery, December 6th and 7th, 19l~M.". w:. Lawrence
11. Lee, Grand Master, presiding.
From the opening parag'r aphs of the Grand Master's address we
quote as follows :
"Masonically and materially the year has been a good one, and we
ure under every obligation to return profound and grateful thanks to
the Grand Master of us all for the many evidences of His continued
favor in the blessings bestowed up on us, personally and as a frater·
nity.
' ·
"To the end that man may rightfully develop along God-intended
lines, Masonry has ever stood for the highest and broadest individual
education and the inculcation of strict and scientific moral principle. It
points with unerring directness to light and truth, that its votaries, seeing the light and knowing. the truth, may so order their ways as not
only to walk uprightly before God and man, but to assist others to plant
their feet in the pathway that leads to happiness and knowledge here,
and to a glorious immortality in all fhe glad afterwhiles."
Concerning the work of the year,. he reports the constitution of
f mrteen new Lodges, which received charters at the preceding Annual
Communication, etc.
Numerous dispensations were granted, and a large number of
Special Communications of the Grand Lodge were held for purposes
nf placing corner stones, dedicating buildings, etc,
I a

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

The Grand Master embodies in his address the following from
the Special Report of the Committee on Correspondence, concerning
the controversy between New Jersey and Mississippi over the so-called
"Negro Masonry" question:
"I had a personal interview. with the then Deputy Grand Master,
and in that interview learned that the practice of initiating negroes was
indulged by one Lodge in that Grand Jurisdiction, but that it was being ·
discouraged and, in his judgment, would be discontinued. Before
reaching a decision as to what ought to be done I deemed it advisable
to make inquiries as to similar conditions in other Grand Jurisdictions.
I did this for the reason that it would be unjust and discriminatory to
act as to one jurisdictioi+ and not as to others where the conditions
were similar.
"I find similar conditions to exist in several of the Grand Jurisdictions with whom we hold fraternal relations. Such a condition exists
in Nova Scotia, in Washington, possibly in the Philippines, where California has several Lodges, certainly in several Lodges under the juris:
diction of the Mother Grand . Lodge of England. To have begun the
severing of fraternal relations on that account would have led to results
not at all desirable, in iny judgment.
"If our proud boast be true that Masonry is universal (and the
writer is firmly convinced that it is), then its viewpoint is necessarily
as broad and universal. From this viewpoint the objection to continui.ng fraternal relati.ons fo.r the reasons stated is untenable, because based
upon a racial and social prejudice1 or at least a racial and social distinction. While this prejudice or distinction is as firmly grounded in
the writer as in any other living man, 1 am of the opinion that it should
not be allowed to bias our judgment or control our actions in matters
affecting the rights of others, who may conscientiously entertain othet'
views.
·
"This decision should not be construed in any sense as committing
the Lodges in Alabama to the doctrine that negroes who are regularly
made Masons in other jurisdictions with which we are in fraternal relation are to be received in Lodges in this Grand Jurisdiction."
The Committee on Cotrespondence is in error in its supposition
that in any of the California Lodges in the Philippines negroes are.
admitted, or, in fact, any but white men, and any so-called Masonic
Lodges in the Philippines, outside of those holding charters from the
Grand Lodge of California, are not generally recognized as regular,
their charters having, as a rule, been issued by the Grand Orient of
Spain. We are certain, also, that there are no Lodges' in the State of
Washington admitting negroes, and we believe that Alpha Lodge, in
the Jurisdiction of New Jersey, and Union Lodge No. 18, Nova Scotia,
formerly 598 registry of England, established January, 1856, ten years
before the formation of the Grand Lodge of Nova Scotia, and therefore inherited by the latter jurisdiction from England, are the only
two Lodges on the American Continent wherein negroes are initiated
as Masons.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

4

That he is a man of personal independence may be judged from
his issuing a dispensation to conduct the Masonic funeral service in
the case of an Entered Apprentice, also one in the case of a Fellow
Craft, and his comment upon this action is as follows:
"I am aware many will disagree with .me in this, but I hold an
E. A. or F. C. are brother Masons, not entitled to all the privileges of
a M. ·. M. ·. but a brother Mason just the same, and surely you would
not withhold from him the last sad rites of our fraternity."
That the Fraternity in Alberta is in a prosperous condition may
be judged from the fact that the Grand Master reports an increase
in membership over the preceding year of 33 1-3 per cent, this coupled
with the assurance that the material making up the increase was of
excellent character.
Dispensations were issued during the year for nine new Lodges.
The young jurisdiction is apparently performing its functions in a
truly Masonic manner, its charity obligations being in no sense overlooked.
From the report of the Finance Committee one observes that the
sum of $500 was transferred to the Alberta Masonic Home ~nd School
Fund with a statement that a further sum of $500 is to be donated
durin~ the year if the cash balance in the Grand Treasury will justify
the withdrawal of such additional sum.
At the annual Grand election M.". w:. Thomas McNabb, of Lethbridge was chosen Grand Master, and M.". w:. George Macdonald, .
M. D,. Calgary, Grand Secretary.

The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of Arizona held its Twenty-ninth Annual Communication in the Masonic Hall in the city of Tucson on the 14th and 15th of February,
1911-M.". w:. Frank Thomas, Grand Master, presiding.

5

The following amendment to the Constitution was adopted at this
Communication, thereby establishing a practice concerning the matter
referred to in harmony with the practice of our own and certain other
Jurisdictions :
"Any member of a Lodge who is in good standing and whose dues
nre paid, who desires to affiliate with another Lodge, may apply for and
receive from the Secretary of his Lodge a duly attested certificate of
his standing in the Lodge. By presenting such certificate with his petition, a member may apply for affiliation with another Lodge. If such
applicant be elected to affiliate with a Lodge, he can become a member
thereof only by filing with the Secretary at a stated meeting a <limit
from the Lodge of which he was last a member."
The Grand Lodge gave approval to the proposition placed before it
by the Grand Lodge of Virginia, ·concerning th~ creation of a Memorial
to Washington, the Mason, at Alexandria, and the Grand Master was
authorized to appoint a representative for Arizona to the proposed Memorial Association.
'
Arizona is creating a widows and orphans' fund, and already has
accumulated to the credit of that fund the sum of $7,396.95.
The Grand Lodge enjoys a substantial income, with total resources
at this time of $28,086.65.
The Thirtieth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Arizona will be holden in Prescott, commencing on Tuesday, the 13th day
of February, 1912.
Henry Alfred Morgan, Grand Master, Willcox.

ARKANSAS, 1910.
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of Arkansas met at. its Sixty-eighth Regular Annual Communication in the city of Little Rock on the 15th day of November,
1910-M.". w:. A. ]. Witt, Grand Master, presiding.
Seven Emergent Communications of the Grand Lodge were held
within the year for the purpose of laying cornerstones of public buildings, etc.
Eloquent passages abound at the opening of the Grand Master's
address, one of which we quote as follows :
"When we look down the corridors of time into the dreamless past
and search through the centuries gone for the basic principles upon
which our Order is founded, we find that liberty and freedom of conscience have impressed themselves upon humanity in every clime where
Masonry has found an abiding place. Centuries ago, when warring
factions sought supremacy, when nations sought the overthrow of each
other through internecine strife, when the arts and sciences struggled
in their infancy for attention, and when civilization first assumed shape
a!ld commenced that development which has resulted in its present
high standard, we find that Masonry, through all these vicissitudes,

6

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

through all these struggles, was silently but surely and firmly impressing its great lesson upon humanity in every clime-the fatherhood of
God and the brotherhood of man."
The Grand Master feelingly refers to the death. of Past Grand
Master William K. Ramsay, who answered the call of the Death Angel
on ·March 18, 1910, at his home in Camden, Ark., in the sixty-seventh
year of his age.
He also mentions with regret the death of Brother R. H. McCulloch, who was for many years connected with the Grand Lodge, serving
upon various committees, being at the time of his death a member of
the Committee on Appeals and Grievances.
Some five or six rulings by the Grand Master during the year are
dignified under the heading "Decisions," one of which, on account of the
peculiarity of the questi~ and the novelty of the answer, we quote as
follows :
"Q. Is it proper or prudent, at public installations, or laying of
cornerstones under the auspices of a Masonic Lodge, to have or to
approve of having speculative stands, such as shooting matches, doll
racks, knife boards, swings and other devices, etc., for speculative purposes? Ans. No ; but quite unmasonic. A Lodge which connives at,
permits or encourages such devices on any Masonic occasio[\ deserves
censure and severe discipline."
The work of the year was represented by dispensations to form
ten new Lodges ; by the numerous Emergent Communications referred
to above ; by a limited number of official visitations, etc.
The Grand Master refers to the Masonic Orphans' Home and expresses his gratification that the institution is progressing favorably and
the conditions surrounding the same are of a satisfactory character, and
that it promises to perform in an efficient manner the work it was de~
signed to accomplish.

there was no discourtesy intended or implied by the California Lodge

Reference is made by the Grarid Master in hi:i ~rldress to the proposed Washington Masonic Memorial to be created at Alexandria, Va.,
and inasmuch as his comments upon the subject are unique we quote
them in part as follows:

"In view of the fact that all of the great achievements of Washington were along military, statesmanship and political lines, he having
become famous in statecraft and in military achievements as perhaps
no other man whose public and private acts grace the pages of history,
but having rendered no distinguished Masonic services, I can not give
the pro,iect my personal endorsement. Should the object sought to be
obtained be accomplished, in after years, or even in our own time, the
Masonic fraternity might be called upon to commemorate the memory, in like manner, of any other distinguished statesman who had endeared his memory to the· hearts of the American people by deeds of
valor upon fields of battle, or by acts of statesmanship in the service of
our beloved country. Therefore, once the precedent is set, it might, in
justice and all candor, be said that it should be followed in similar
instances from mere matter of sentiment."
American Masons, we apprehend, will take issue with the Grand
Master of Arkansas in his statement that Washington was not distinguisheq for his Masonic services, for Washington certainly was distinguished as a Mason, having been continuously identified with the
great Fraternity from the time that he was less than 21 years of age to
the very last day of his illustrious life, and having exemplified in his
unexampled career and character, Masonic precepts and teachings, and
these things are so well and universally known, particularly by well
informed Masons, that to argue to the contrary is to betray a strange
lack of correct and authentic information.

He makes a quotation from Brother W. R. Davis' eulogy upon
our late Grand Master, the M.". W.". Brother W. F. Pierce, and comments as follows:
"Brother William 'R. Davis also voiced the general feeling of affection, and from his remarks we copy the following gem:
"If anything is true, it is true everywhere and forever that the
sum of the angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles; that
greate•r means more than less; that convergence is different from divergence; that every point is the center of an infinite sphere. But
these are no more a part of the constitution of things than that sympathy and antipathy are opposite; that malevolence and benevolence
part ways; that the giving of a cup of cold water is one thing and a
stab in the dark is another; that selfishness deserts, unselfishness cooperates and sacrifices, mercy forgives, and the torches of sentient intelligence give light to other kindred understandings. This constitution of things makes me think that the abstract laws of space and
quantity are not the only perpetuities, There is no reason why greater
should be more than less forever, and yet have benevolence, forever
good, perish; nor why convergence should be different from diver!fence
forever; and yet have unselfishness perish from constituted th1ngs;
nor why light should be different from darkness forever, and yet there
comes · a time when all sentient lights are extinguished from the cosmos, leaving its abstractions alone, the unconscious perpetuities to endure. The mathematical perpetuities of tbe cosmos, perceived by the
awareness of the intellect are true through no greater lanse of time or
wider reaches of space than are the other laws perceived by the awareness of the understanding which takes hold of them, call it what you
will. This thought makes me think we do not perish. A cosmic jest
it is, if the laws of quantity and direction are eternal, and the laws of
sentient consciousness run out. The iTony of swallowing up in the
vortex of annihilation all these conscious intelligences, one by one,
leaving to remain in perpetuity only insensate abstraction and insensate matter could only mean that life and the earth are but the trick
in the universe and that man, the summit of terrestrial creation, is only
a cosmic plaything. But the splendors of the universe bear upon their
face no leer as of a trick and the glories of the cosmos bear upon
their countenance no grimace as of a jest."

The work of the year was represented by the constitution of two
new Lodges which received charters at the preceding Annual Communication; in dispensations to form five new Lodges; in -certain
Special Communications for the purpose of laying corner-stones of
public buildings, etc.
The Grand Master closes his excellent address as follows:
"As we contemplate the past, let us draw from it the great lessons
it teaches, the mighty inspiration it affords, and with minds and hearts
thereby strengthened let us turn with hope and confidence to the future, and e:o on to still higher growth and still greater achievements,
ever humbly acknowledging the superintending control and imploring the
divine aid and guidance of the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe.."
From the report of the Grand Treasurer, it appears that the income of the Grand Lodge reaches the substantial amount of $14,568.20.
There is no Masonic Home,in this jurisdiction, in lieu thereof the
Grand Lodge maintains a benevolent fund from which disbursements
are made to worthy distressed Masons, their widows and orphans.
The Grand Orator, Brother Fred E. Angone, delivered an oration
for which he was duly thanked, and the oration printed .by order of the
Grand Lodge in the Proceedings.
If Brother Angone had surrounded more of his oration with quotation marks it would have been in order, the first three complete
paragraphs of his effort being lifted bodily from the annual address
of the Grand Master of California in 1907.
The following resolution, which was duly adopted, in reference
to the use of "keys," affords matter for reflection to those of us who
find it impossible to reconcile the use of ''keys" with the obligations
all Masons assume.
"Resolved, That this Grand Lodge prohibit the use by any one of
any 'key' while opening or closing a Lodge or conferring the degrees,
or while posting a candidate; and that the Grand Lecturer be instructed
to insert in the receipts for these 'keys' words of this import : 'I hereby
agree not to use this 'key' in the Lodge room during the opening or
closing of the Lodge or while conferring the degree, or while posting
a candidate."
M.'. W .'. Brother Henry M. Teller, Ex-United States Senator and
Senior Past Grand Master of the jurisdiction, made an excellent address
of a historical and reminiscent character in the afternoon of the second
day.
The Committee on Foreign Correspondence makes a splendid
report, reviewing with rare judgment and discrimination the Proceedings of American and Foreign Jurisdictions.
California, 1909, is very fully considered with extracts from the
address of the Grand Master, reports of committees, etc.
Albert B. McGaffey, Grand Master, Denver.
Charles H. Jacobson, Grand Secretary, Denver.

CONNECTICUT, 1911.
Total Number of Me~bers, 22,351. Gain, 499. Number of Lodges, 105.
The Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of the Most
Ancient and Honorable Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons 0£ the
State of Connecticut was 'held in the Masonic Temple, City of New
Haven, January 18th and 19th, 1911, the Grand Master, M:. w:. Fred
A. Verplanck, presiding.
Two Special Communications. of the Grand Lodge were held in
the previous yea·r, one for dedicating the new Masonic Hall at Windsor, the other for the purpose of unveiling and dedicating a monument
to the Masonic dead, erected by Olive Branch Lodge No. 84, at Westville.
In accordance with the usual custom in this jurisdiction, the Grand
Lodge, immediately after it had been .opened in Ample Form and at
the outset of the Grand Master's address, was called up, and in the
language of the Grand Master, as a tribute to those "who had borne
the burden and heat of the day and gone to their reward,'' listened to
the'reading of the Roll of the beloved Dead, being a list of those eminent
in the Councils of the Craft in this and other jurisdictions, a•d who
had died during the year.
The year was apparently a busy one with the Grand Master, who
reports numerous visits to .subordinates of his jurisdiction; dispensations for various purposes were granted; certain local questions of law
were decided, and the ordinary duties incident to his office were
capably performed.
He attended the meeting held at Alexandria, Va., on February 22,
1910, for the purpose of organizing the Washington Masonic Memorial
Association.
He reports the Masonic Home of Connecticut to be in excellent
condition, and has the following remarks to make as to the wisdom and
~ighteousness of Lodges increasing dues, etc., in cases where necessary
to meet their charity and other obligations, and concludes that where
this is done fearlessly, the effect has been salutary upon the membership.
He·re is what he has to say:
"A careful study of the returns from the subordinate Lodges shows
that those L?dges 'that. boldly raised their fees to meet the require,
ments of their own treasury and the treasury of the Masonic Charity
Foundation have met with no diminution of work. Men have cheerfully paid the fees. In many Lodges an increase in dues and initiation
fees has been coincident with an increase in Lodge membership. Masonry should not be cheap. It should not make an appeal to cheap men.
The strength of a Lodge does not lie in numbers but m the character of
its membership. I believe that those Lodges which have not as yet
raised their fees to meet the new requirements should do so at once
and that the result will soon justify the wisdom of the step."

The First Stated Communication of the Grand Lodge, Free and
Accepted Masons, of the District of Columbia, for ~?e ye.ar 1910 was
held in the city of Washington, March 12, 1910-M. · W. · George C.

This being a Communication prescribed by the Constitution for

the· degrees of Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Mason
were exemplified.

A Special Communication of the Grand Lodge was held March
24 1910 for the purpose of paying the last honors of the Craft to dece~sed Past Grand Master Eldred Griffith Davis.

held May 11, 1910, at which business of a routine character was
