17

The Third Stated Communication of the Grand Lodge was held
September 24th, 1910, at which matters pertaining to the new Masonic
Temple were considered and certain other ordinary business transacted.
The One Hundredth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of the District of Columbia was held December 21, 1910.
At the opening of his address the Grand Master felicitates the
Grand Lodge upon its condition of prosperity, etc., in the one hundredth
year of its existence in the following language:
"The one hundredth year of our existence as a Grand Jurisdiction has been fraught with much happiness and peace, harmony and a
truly Masonic comity having prevailed in our midst and our fraternal
relations with other jurisdictions have not been marred by a single
unpleasant incident. It has been a busy year, and a spirit of progress
has been inaugurated which will redound to the credit of the Craft and
place our jurisdiction on a higher plane of excellence. The end of our
first century, in my judgment, finds us better equipped for the duties
and responsibilities of a Grand Lodge than we have ever been before,
and I feel that we can confidently look to the future with gratification
and assurance."
His report is a business-like statement of the activities of the
Grand Lodge during the preceding year.
He refers especially to the divine service at Mount St. Albans, at
which there were assembled more than 35CO Master Masons, and the
cccasion being of a somewhat unusual character we quote his report of
the event, which was the event of the year, so far as District of Columbia Masonry is concerned, as follows:
"At the Stated Communication _of the Grand Lodge held September

Sunday, September _25, 1910, .the. largest number of Masons ever known
to have assembled in the District of Columbia.

The Annual Grand Festival of the Grand Lodge of England was
held at Freemasons' Hall, London, April 27, 1910, Lord Ampthill, Pro
Grand Master, presiding.
A Special Grand Lodge was held at Freemasons' Hall, May 19,
1910, being a Memorial Service in honor of his Late Majesty King
Edward VII, and this event overshadoweq everything else in English
Freemasonry during the year, Lord Ampthill, Pro Grand Master on the
Throne.
This special Grand Lodge was convened :
"First-To vote a loyal and dutiful address to His Majesty the
King, tendering the respectful sympathy of the Craft on the death of his
late Majesty, King Edward VII, Past Grand Master and Protector of
the Order, and assuring His Majesty of the earnest prayer of the Fraternity that Almighty God may bless his accession to the throne.
"Second-To vote a humble address to Her Majesty the Queen
Mother, declaring the profound and abiding sorrow of the Fraternity
at the death of their Protector and former Grand Master, and assurfnlf Her Majesty that all the brethren unite in the prayer that Almighty
God may give strength and comfort to Her Majesty and the other
members of the royal family in their deep affliction.
"Third-To pass a resolution assuring the M.'. w:. Grand Master of the fraternal sympathy of the Craft, and of their deep condolence
with His Royal Highness in the loss of his royal brother, and begging
ills Royal Highness to lay at the foot of the throne the loyal and
dutiful address of the Fraternity, and to convey to Her Majesty the
~)ueen Mother, and the members of the royal family, the respectful
11ympathy of his obedient and devoted brethren."

FLORIDA, 1911.
Membership, 9,501. Lodges, 197. Increase During the Year, 423.
The Eighty Second Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons of Florida was held in the city of Jacksonville January 17, 1911, M ." . w:. Lewis C. Massey, Grand Master,
presiding.
The. Grand Master announces in his annual address the death of
Past Grand Master Thomas M. Pleston, and pays a fitting tribute tO
his memory and worth.
The year was one of activity, six Lodges, which received charters
at the previous Annual Communication, were duly constituted.
He granted dispensations for seven new Lodges. He laid the
corner-stones of six or seven public buildings, and various ceremonies
of dedicating halls took place.
On June 26, 1910, the Grand Master received notice from the
R." . W:. Grand Secretary of Alabama that the Grand Lodge of that
state at its Grand Communication in December, 1909, had adopted certain resolutions concerning the jurisdiction of Lodges located near
the lines of adj oining states, and these resolutions being in harmony
with the views of Florida upon the subject, may be considered as settling, so far as those states are concerned at least, the ofttimes perplexing question of jurisdiction of Lodges near state lines. The resolution
is as follows :
"First: That persons residing in this or any adjoining State within •
five miles of the State line may petition and be made a Mason in the
nearest Lodge, measured by straight lines, to their residence; whether
that Lodge is in this or another Grand Jurisdiction, provided that such
other Grand Jurisdiction now has or shall hereafter enact a similar law.
"Second: That profanes who while residing in this State have
heretofore been made Masons in adjoining Grand Jurisdictions be ancl
they are hereby healed and hereafter recognized as regular Masons in
this Grand Jurisdiction."

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

21

The Grand Master refers to the Washington Masonic Memorial

and expresses his approval of the undertaking and voices the hope that
the Grand Lodge of Florida will give the project its favorable endorsement.
We quote from his address upon the subject, as follows:
"I sincerely hope that the movement will receive the endorsement
of the Grand Lodge and .that we shall be represented at the meeting.
As Broth~r George Washington stands out as by far the greatest citizen of this coui;try, before, during or since his time, so to American
Masons he continues the best proof of the claim of our fraternity that
'the wisest and best of men in all ages have been encouragers and promoters of our art.' Great soldier, statesman and man of affairs as he
was, he nevertheless found time to visit the military lodges during the
Revolutionary War, and afterwards to become the first Master of
Alexandria Lodge No. 22, the gavel of which he wielded for nearly two
years."
Seventeen so-called decisions upon questions of Masonic Law
within his jurisdiction were rendered by him, and from the seventeen,
we select the following:
"If a bro.ther under char_ges is in prison, the Master should appoint
a representative to act for him, and the brother's statement of his case
should be obtained, either verbally or in writing.''
" If, on the petition of a candidate, the ballot shows one black ball
and the ballot is spread a second time with the same result the ballot
cannot be reopened even by dispensation from the Grand Master and
even though the dark ballot was cast by mistake, as the second passi~g of
the ballot is the final Masonic method of guarding against mistakes."
"The Master of a Lodge ought not, in his official character and
over his official signature, to join in an invitation to a reception and
picnic extended by a Grand Officer of the Order of the Eastern Star
residing in .his. town, ~o o.fficers of the General Grand Chapter of the
same orgamzation, which 1s not and cannot be a Masonic body though
'
some of its members are Master Masons."
"~he. ceremony of layii;ig a corner stone cannot be performed when
the buildm~ has been practlcnlly completed, or when its walls have been
already built over the place provided for the corner stone; much less
when a mere space has been left into which the corner stone is to be
slipped. Neither will a corner stone be laid before the first floor of a
building."
The following resolution concerning documentary evidence was
adopted:
"Resolv ed, That in order to comply with the requirements of jurisdictions requiring documentary evidence as a prerequisite for examination of visitors, in addition to tests already prescribed, that this Grand
Lodge furnish to the particular Lodges a card receipt for dues, to be
issued under the seal of the Lodge having upon the reverse a certificate
attested by the seal of the Grand Lodge, that the Lodge issuing the
card is a regular Lodge holding a charter from the Grand Lodge of
Florida. This card to be furnished without expense to the Lodges or
their members.''

"In connection with the passing and raising of a brother of Lodge

"Ques. Is it un-Masonic to use the name of Jesus Christ in. a
Masonic prayer? Ruled: That it is not. Masonry does not conflict
with the duty we owe to God. The form of prayer is a matter between
he who prays and Him to whom the prayer is offered: If my prayer
must have the name of Jesus in it to constitute it prayer, and if it is my
duty to pray to God, then to compel me to eliminate the name of Jesus
from my prayer would interfere w.it~ a duty I owe to Go~ .. Masonry'
requires no,sucli sacrifice.from Christian Masons. The C~ns~1an Mason
has no right to require his Hebrew, Mohammedan or Umtanan brother
to broaden his prayer and use the name 0£ Jesus, and they h~ve no
right to require the Christian Mason to eliminate what he conceives to
be the most important and vital element of prayer, 'in the name and for
the sake of Jesus Christ.'"
This jurisdiction is certainly prolific of new Lodges. At the previous Annual Communication, charters were granted to 31 new Lodges.
These were all du1y constituted by the Grand Master during the year.
Ten so-called "occasional" Grand Lodges were held in the year for
the purpose of laying corner-stones, etc., and 22 charters were granted
for new Lodges at this Communicat!on.

"Among the many allies of right in this continuous battle, next to
the Church of God, Freemasonry stands forth the most ancient and
the most helpful of them all. Her sons are called the 'Sons of Light'·
her mi~sion is to dispel the darkness of _humanity; her. message to th~
world 1s the Brotherhood of Man. She 1s the hand-maiden of religion.
"Hand in hand with the Holy Bible, as a lamp to their feet, the
two walk the rough and rugged pathway of human life. Freemasonry
teaches morals. .Re.ligi~n offers the c~p of salvation to thirsty souls.
Freemasonry, behevmg m the resurrection of the body and the immortality of the soul, teaches upright living. Religion, believing the same
teaches how to attain immortality in the great beyond.
'
"Masonry, with her beautiful ritual, impressive ceremonies and the
glory of centuries clustering about her brow, stripped of her moral
character, would lose her greatest charm, her most precious jewel. For
morality is her foundation, Truth and Virtue her pillars, and Brotherly
Love the high priest that ministers at her altars. To be 'good men
and true' is the first and most important lesson taught wiihin her sacred walls. Every step of the candidate, from his preparation to the
last solemn scene, as he passes through her beautiful ceremonies and
is inducted into her mysteries, leads along a pathway strewn
with fragrant flowers of truth, while diamonds o-f virtue sparkle about
his feet, illuminating the one mind with moral light flooding the
heart with a celestial glow of divine principles, inspiring the soul and
leading up to a higher plane of holy, upright living.

"For centuries Masonry has stood 'like ~ome massive ;~ck based

"Every Mason is professedly on the side of good, having wandered
in darkness, we now have the light. Darkness is the type of evil; 'men
love darkness because their deeds are evil'; when by good deeds and
good words of purity, honesty, uprightness and charity we let our light
shine, evil flees away as darkness flee• before the light of the rising
sun. The possibility of doing good by letting our light shine in the
practice of all the beautiful lessons taught in the several degrees is
limited only by our opportunities, and who can limit them? At home
abroad, in our various avocations, among friends or with strangers'
these opportunities rise about us with every· hour of the day. Our in~
fluence will be felt for good or evil, with or without our knowledge or
consent. We will impress in some way those with whom we come in
contact. No man is without influence of some kind. How essential
then that we guard well the portals of this earthly temple in which
our s.ouls have their dwelling place, an.d in doing this guard and guide
the hv_es of others. Then use your mfluence for good with all you
meet, though the meeting be ever so brief."

IDAHO, 1910.
The Forty-third Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted Masons of Idaho, convened in Masonic Hall in Boise, Idaho, the 13th day of September, •
1910, the M.'. w:. George F. Gagon, Grand Master, presiding.
The Grand Master in opening his address says :
"The large immigration of Masons, 'good men and true,' who .have
come into our jurisdiction the last few years and who have bu1lded
homes among us has placed us at high tide. The year's endeavor
speaks eloquent!; of results, showing ha;~?ny and contentment, as
well as a wonderful growth of membership.
The Grand Master laid corner stones of four public buildings
and administered in a businesslike manner during the preceding years
the affairs of the Grand Lodge.
He answered, so he assures us, a great many questions concerning
law and jurisprudence, a few of which we quote as follows:
"Q. Is i1 necessary for the Worshipful Master to s_ubmit. the report of the investigating committee to the Lodge for cons1derat1on?
"A. It is proper that a motion be made and carried, that the report be received and the committee disch'.lrged, .or refe.r red back for
further consideration. vVhen the report 1s received, the ballot must
be spread by order of the Worshipful Master."
"Q. If a vacancy has been created, may we appoint and install
a new Chaplain, without a dispensation?
"A. The office being vacant, the Worshipful ll:faster may appoint
a Chaplain pro tern at each meeting, but n~ Chaplam ~an be ~ppomted
and installed to fill the unexpired term, without a Dispensation from
the Grand Master."
"Q. Can a Lodge in this jurisdiction make a Mason ?f t.he rejecte~
material of another Lodge, without the consent of the reiectmg Lodge.
"A. · Every Lodge in this jurisdiction is an. in~ependent body, subject only to the Grand Lodge, and is the exclusive Judge of the persons

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

27

who shall compose its membership. I may add, however, that i·t is not a
•'ommendable policy for a Lodge to make up its membership from the
!'ejected material of another Lodge, and particularly over the protest of
the rejecting Lodge."
"Q. Two Lodges located in the same city or town, said Lodges
having conC'Urrent jurisdiction over the applications for degrees, can
,•lther Lodge make Masons of the rejected material of the other, without the unanimous consent of the rejecting Lodl!'e, even if six months
h11ve elapsed since the application was rejected?"
"A. Where there are two or more Lodges in the same city, the
Secretary of each L odge shall notify the other Lodges in such city of
1111 petitions for initiation or membership, which notice shall be read to
the Lodge to whom sent at the next regular meeting. Such Lodges
huve concurrent jurisdiction over applications for degrees and for
membership, but this does not give to one Lodge the right to dictate
who shall constitute the membership of the other Lodge. The required
notice, I take it, is merely of an advisory nature, to permit the Lodge
receiving same to present objections to any petition and to furnish information relative to the character of the petitioner that other Lodges
may not possess."

ILLINOIS, 1910.
Number of Lodges, 777. Number of Members, 101,692. Gain, 5,703.
The Grand Lodge of Ancient, Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of Illinois, held its Seventy-first Annual Communication in
Masonic Temple, in the City of Chicago, October 11th, 12th and 13th,
1910, M.'. W .'. Albert B. Ashley, Grand Master, presiding.
The Grand Master in his address states that it is a matter of
congratulation that peace and harmony prevail among the Lodges and
hrethren of his great state, and in addition to this, that the relations
of his Grand Lodge with the 71 Grand Lodges with which it is in
fraterna,l correspondence, are most cordial and friendly.
Before passing to the details of the work of the year, the Grand
Master called the assembled brethren of the Grand Lodge to their feet,
nnd with bowed heads, they stood in memory of those workers in the
quarries of life who had ceased, during the preceding year, to be the
earthly companions of their brethren and had gone into eternal rest
and refreshment incident to the paradise of God.
Special reference is made to the death in the year of Past Grand
Master John M. Pierson, and R.'. W.'. Brother William Berry Gromes.
The work of the year was represented by the constitution of seven
Lodges, which received their charters at the previous Annual Communication; by the issuance of dispensations to form eight new Lodges;
by the dedication of numerous Masonic halls, and by the placing of
several corner-stones of public bu51dings.
The event of the year was the ceremony of laying in due and
ancient form the corner-stone of the new Orphans' Home at LaGrange.
There were in line upon this occasion a great many Masonic bodies,

consisting of Commanderies of Knights Templar, Royal Arch Chaptei;s,
Masonic Lodges, Eastern Star Chapters, etc. M .... .w:. Brother George
M. ·Moulton acted as Grand Marshal.
Illinois has fallen in line with a number of important Grand jurisdictions,. like :Kentut:ky, 'I'exas, California, and others, in providing
separate homes for children and the aged: The home for the children of
Illinois, tci be at LaGrarig~;~!he children being temporarily sheltered,
while the LaGrange Home i~f\j~ process df e'rection, in Chicago, and
the aged Masons are provided for at the Sullivan Masonic Home.
Concerning the Masonic Homes, the Grand Master has this to say
in •his report : ·
"Little need be said of the great work being ddne for our dependents in our two Homes. Both are running smoothly artd satisfactorily, as all know who · have taken opportunity to visit them. The
superintendents, Brothers Hovey and Bassett, assisted by their wives,
are keeping everything in excellent condition. It has been my privilege
and pleasure to visit these homes several times during the year and
to know personally of their condition. The craft is to be congratulated that the task of managing t,hese difficult trusts and responsibilities
is being performed in a highly satisfactory manner. The work at
Sullivan has gone on without much variation from ordinary routine.
The Orphans' Home, in its temporary quarters, is in a high degree
of efficiency. All are waiting patiently for the new Home at LaGrange.
The building has progressed rapidly and will soon be ready for occupancy. The report of the Board of Trustees will furnish details of
both Homes. The unselfish services rendered by the members of the
Home Board and the executive committees call for large gratitude
from the brethren whose capable servants they are. I commend these
great charities to your hearty ·consideration and active interest."
In order to guard against the intrusion into regular Lodges of
spurious Masons made in clandestine bodies, the Grand Lodge of
Illinois, in common with most ju_risdictions at the present day, demands "documentary evidence," consisting of
Certificate of Good
Standing, attested by the Grand Secretary of the jurisdiction, etc., as
a prerequisite to the admission of visitors.
The Grand Master in his report refers to the "Baltimore Conference" of Grand Masters, and to the active participation in that Conference of Past Grand Master Alexander H. Bell, who represented
the Grand Lodge of Illinois.
It was Past Grand Master Bell's resolutions which were unanimously· adopted by the Baltimore Conference, which so effectually put
at rest the suggestion or suspicion that the several conferences of Grand
Masters held within· the last two or three years, notably those at Philadelphia and Baltimore, were intended as preliminary steps to the formation of -a so-called National Grand Lodge.

By v~rtue of a Special Report from the Committee on Correspondence, which was adopted by the Grand Lodge, recognition was refused to the National Grand Lodge of Egypt, and another Special Report from the Committee on 'Correspondence expresses the attitude of
the Grand Lodge of Illinois toward the Grand Lodges of Mexico. The

32

,

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

report, possessing something of more than ordinary interest, is herewith
quoted in full;
"Had this Grand Lodge at its last session recognized the Grand
Lodge Valle de Mexico there would now be a serious complication.
Official notice is at hand .that in consequence of dissatisfaction over
the election of the 'Gran Maestro' (grand master) eight of the thirtytwo Lodges composing that body have seceded. They have set up a
new Grand Lodge of their own and call it also 'Grand Lodge Valle de
Mexico.' Hence, there are two bodies bearinl? the same name and
assuming supreme control over the same territory, viz: the federal
district of the Republic of Mexico. The seceders took with them
the Grand Secretary and all the records, papers, archives, seal and other
equipment of the grand body originally known as Valle de Me?cico.
The official notice received says: 'It is quite probable that other Lodges
of Mexican membership and working the Scottish ritual will secede
from the regular Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico.' The notice further
states that 'the irregular body has requested the recognition and support of the Supreme Council 33°, A. and A. S. R., and at the meeting
·
July 5 that body took steps to grant the request.'
"From this it will be seen that the body heretofore bearing the
name Valle de Mexico was of a mongrel constituency where Ancient
Craft Masonry had little consideration or influence. The territory emhraced in the jurisdiction over which these rival factions are fighting is
the federal district, an oval shaped valley about 30x45 miles, between a
wall of mountains. A half dozen other irregular and clandestine grandbodies exist in the republic of Mexico.
"One of these, known as 'The Grand Lodge Unida Mexicano de
Vero Cruz,' has ·recognized the seceders as regular. This body claims
jurisdiction over the entire republic of Mexico. The foregoing facts
indicate the good fortune of this Grand Lodge in avoiding entangling
alliances with such questionable bodies as are shown to exist in the.
Mexican republic. In order that the Grand Lodge of Illinois might
be informed of ,the situation this report is made. No action is required.''

motion, the Grand Lodge extended to the orator its deepest gratitude ·
for his able, eloquent and profound Masonic address and ordered a
copy of the same printed in the Proceedings.

That Indiana is yielding to the trend of Masonic thought of recent
yrars in the matter of "physical qualifications," and is growing in the
hrlief that it is more important that a candidate for Masonry should
hnve a sound and wholesome moral character than an absolutely flawless physical body is shown in the approval of the report of the Committee on J u·risprudence, who had up for consideration the following
nmcndment to one of the General Regulations:
"Provided, That the Grand Master may, with the consent" of the
C immittee on Jurisprudence, allow Lodges to receive and ballot on
prtitions for membership of those who can, by the aid of artificial
appliances, conform to the ceremonies of the Order.
"By adhering too strictly to the physical requirements we might
render nugatory the equally vital principle of our beloved institution,
that it is the internal and not the external qualifications that make the
Masons who are revered in our memories and cherished in our hearts.
We must not forRet that the letter of the law too often killeth, but
the spirit giveth life. Let us not forget that character is more priceless than rubies and is the great desideratum of the twentieth centttry Masonry. If Masonry has progressed along any one line more
than another since its organization in Indiana, it has been along the
line that each year there has been a compelling insistence for the raising
' f the standard of him whose knock at our portals receives a satisfying resp onse. We are proud of the men who shed moral and intellectual lustre upon our Order, and yearly this Grand Lodge is becoming
more and more sensitive to the criticism which may come to it be' Ruse of the conduct of unworthy members.
"Keeping all these things in mind, it is not surprising that we
hesitate to bar the door to the lofty mind and the great heart who
may be fully equipped to do big things for our Order, for the reason
ulDne that misfortune overtook him and made the race of life harder
for him, but who, in spite of Dame Fortune's frown, rose above all
difficulties and stands erect, loving and being honored by his fellowmen."

The particular pride of Iowa is its Grand Lodge Library, which is
located at Cedar Rapids, the city in which this Annual Oimmunicatlon was held.
The Grand Lodge Library is probably as complete a Masonic
library as there is in this country, and the Grand Secretary, R.'. W.'.
Newton R. Parvin, is also Grand Librarian, and his report as Grand
J,ibrarian discloses the fact that he manifests particular interest in
that department of his work.
Concerning "Masonic charity," the Grand Master has the following to say in defense of the Iowa system of dispensing charity to its
distressed and needy members, the :Masonic Home idea not having
been adopted in Iowa :
"Our system of supplementing the local resources for charity, when
needed, through our Trustees of the Grand Lodge Charity fund, has
proved to be most successful. It is more economical than caring for
Clependents through a Masonic Home, and at the same time more
desirable. The destitute one is cared for under our system in his own
town, in the home of some relative or friend, among friends of long
atanding, without public knowledge of the aid received, unostentatiously,
nnd that is the proper way to dispense charity."
Iowa is one of possibly a half dozen important jurisdictions in this
country that has no Masonic Home.

Iowa has the fashion of electing each year from the body of the
Grand Lodge a full corps of Grand Officers, and the law of progression
in this jurisdiction is not recognized. In other words, the fact that one
this year fills the office of Senior Grand Warden is no implied pledge
that next year he will be advanced and fill the position of Grand Master,
the office of Deputy Grand Master in this jurisdiction being an ap- ·
pointive one; and the election of Grand Officers in the afternoon of
the second day of the ~es sion resulted in the elevation of an entirety
new list of names so far as the principal officers of the Grand Lodge
were concerned.

A special committee was appointed at the previous Annual Communication on "Recognition of Grand Bodies," and this committee
made at this Communication an exhaustive and comprehensive report, .
which was unanimously adopted l:zy the Grand Lodge, and, inasmuch
as its findings are so clearly set forth, and so nearly in accord with
the views of so many Masonic; students, we take the liberty of quoting
quite liberally from the report as follows :
"With this conclusion as to the effect of a recognition, that is,
that it is an ackn owledgment of legitimacy in organization, we come
to the much mooted question of what is legitimate in Grand Lodge
organization?

"Different claims on the subject are: First, that as the Grand
(,edge of England was the first organized Grand Lodge of the world
nnd came into being by the joint action of four subordinate lodges of
the realm in 1717, and most of the 9rand !°--od_ges of the world are
it direct or indirect descendants, tracmg their title thereto, no Grand
l,odge springing from any other source is legitimate. .Second, in sc;>me
•>f the countries, what is known as the Supr~me Council of t~e Af!c1e_nt
nnd Accepted Scottish Rite aJ?d Grand Orients, have exerpsed iunscliction over the three symbolic degrees, Entered Apprentice, FellowC'raft, and Master Mason, and subordinate and Grand Lodges have
heen organized by their authority; an~ there is a c.l'!im that wher~ these
rites are dominant, Lodges so orgamzed, are leg1t1mate. In this connection the 'Universality of Masonry' is a much used and much abused
, •. pression. No ~ntelli,gent Mason ca~ claif!l that, in point of memhcrship, Masonry. is universal. The umversahty of Ma.sonry was taught
when Masons were to be found on but a small fract10n of the globe;
hut then, as now, Masonry was universal in the comprehensive sense
of its spirit, teachings, influence, and adaptation to the needs of all
mankind. Like the spirit of religious liberty and practice, it is world
wide, and while its membership may be circumscribed,· its teachings
nnd influence are not.
"Referring to the claim that Supreme Councils and Grand Orients
possess authority and jurisdiction over ~~bolic Masonry to t~e ~xtent
of granting charters for Lodge oriramzatlon, we meet the s1g01ficant
query, from what source came such authority? .We co~fidently assert
that in a legal and fraternal sense they are foreign bodies. They did
not spring from Symbolic Masonry, as organized bodies, but came i~to
heing in ways that we need not consider, as we would be traveling
through a maze of disputes and doubts, unprofitable and unimportant
for our present purpose.
"We may state, as an axiom of Symbolic Masonic law; that Symbolic Masonry, in its organizations and workings, is a law unto itself,
in that it looks to no higher or foreign fraternal source for authority,
sanction, or guidance, but is the creative power within itself of all
needful agencies, and to this end the subordinate Lodge is the primal
source of authority and the only source from which can spring a legitimate Grand Lodge, and hence the legitimacy of a Grand Lodge depends, in the first instance, on the legitimacy of the Lodges that gave
1t birth, and, of course, in addition thereto, it must meet the limitations
and requirements of the ancient landmarks of the order.
"We come, then, to the pivotal query, is there more than one primal
source of authority for the creation of subordinate Lodges, or, in
other words, do we sanction a plural system of authority by which
each country of the globe may bring into being its own system of
lodge creation and government, and we are to accept it if character17.ed as Masonry? We take our lineage from the Grand Lodge of
England, as do all Lodges of North America, as well as many other
countries, and throughout the Masonic world their regularity is unquestioned.
"It may be of interest to say that there are, approximately, 131
Grand Jurisdictions in the world, . of which 58 . are in North America,
nnd of the 131 jurisdictions all but 21 are regular, that is, trace their
lineage from the mother Grand Lodge of England. In some of the
110 jurisdictions that we speak of as regular, it is true that there are
Lodges autho rized by Councils and Orients, but they are small, both

your action, your committee make the following recommendations:
"First. That it is the judgment and conclusion of this Grand
Lodge that Grand Lodge authority and legitimacy is derived from
the consent and action of Subordinate Lodges.

We make one or two quotations from Brother Porter's address as
follows:
"The principal point I wish to impress is the fact that Masonry
has always been compatible with every form of civil constitution. The
civil authorities when they became acquainted with the mysteries of
the Order found in them nothing to justify hostility on the part of the
State. To put it more broadly, Masonry has always stood for the
established order and has favored the existing form of government,
whether that government was monarchial or republican."
·
0
"I have wandered considerably from my text and digressed a good
deal from the th ought which I have endeavored to emphasize, which is
that Masonry has always stood upon the side of conservatism and
toleration and has favored the established order."
·
"There is such a thing as mo ral patri~tis~-the courage of one's
moral convictions, and courage to act in accordance with those convictions, and need for that kind of patriotism in the breast of the humblest
citizen who lives on a quiet side street of a country village in ·-times of
profoundest peace. The stability of our government and the permanency of our institutions are threatened constantly by the indifference
to what are termed conventional infractions of law. Masonry does not
seek to control the business or private affairs of its members, but
there ought to be no place in a Masonic Lodge for the dishonest man
who uses false weights and measures, who gives or accepts a bribe,
who knowingly traffics in adulterated foods injurious to public health,
or who sells for filthy money over his counter poisonous drugs to unfortunate persons addicted to their use ..
"The obligations of a Mason as a citizen are no different from
those which every citizen owes to the State-faithful allegiance and
patriotism. A man in order to become a Mason must, theoretically
at least, be better than -the average man. The obligations he takes before he becomes a Master Mason will not of themselves make him a
better husband, father, son or brother, but if he absorbs the principles
of Masonry and lives the life a true Mason ought to live, he will be a
better man in all of these respects; and if he squares his conduct with
the traditions of Masonry he will cultivate a spirit of true patriotism,
and always be found on the side of law and order."

His ideal as to what Masonry should be has not been fully realized

distasteful may be the duty I consider it imperative to speak the truth.
The burden of my work during the present year has been to bring the
brethren to the better realization, to a clearer conception of their
obligations, and duties to themselves, to the great fraternity in which
they hold membership and to the social body of which every individual
man and Mason is part and parcel."

MAINE, 1910.
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of Maine met in Annual Communication in Corinthian Hall, Portland, Maine, Tuesday, May 3, 1910-Grand Master
Edmund B. Mallett, presiding.
In addition to a full staff of Grand Officers there were present 259
delegates representing 196 of the 201 chartered Lodges, a notable representation, and it is also worthy of comment that eight of the living
Past Grand Masters were present.
GRAND MAS'tl!R'S ADDRESS.

The Grand Master's Address discloses a condition of peace and
harmony throughout the jurisdiction. The membership during the
preceding year increased 464, increasing the _total membership to 28,328.
Two Special Communications of the Grand Lodge were held in
the year for the purpose of dedicating Masonic Halls, and two Special
Communications for the purpose of placing corner stones of public
buildings.
Especial comment is made of the celebration of the Centennial
Anniversary of Maine Lodge No. 20, at which there was a large and
Pnthusiastic gathering, which was graced with the presence of distinguished visitors from abroad, including the Grand Master of Masons
of Massachusetts, and other officers of that jurisdiction by which Maine
I.edge was evidently originally chartered.
Dl!CISIONS.

The Grand Master reports that while many questions were propounded to him during the preceding year, they were all answered
by reference to the Constitution and Masonic Text Book, and that
no formal decisions were actually rendered by him.
In conclusion the Grand Master expresses his deep appreciation
lor the honor conferred upon him by the Fraternity and voices the
hope that his administration of two years as Grand Master has resulted
in a certain measure of benefit and good for the beloved institution
which it had been his great privilege and pleasure to serve.

MANITOBA, 1911.
The Thirty-sixth Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of Manitoba, Ancient, Free and Accepted Masons, was
held in the City of Winnipeg, June 14, 1911, the M.". w:. George W.
Baker, Grand Master, presiding.
That he entertains vast appreciation of the Great Light in Masonry
may be judged from the following exerpts from his address:
"The Great Giver of all good has bestowed upon us an intellect, a
thing to use, for by its use it strengthens and with it we can the better
discern our Lodge literature, for every word has a meaning pregnant
with thought and based upon the soundest philosophy, and, besides, elevating us beyond the sordid affairs of every-day life. This literature
is of the purest English, written about the period when Shakespeare
penned his immortal work, and when those eminent men put fortn
the great authorized edition of the Volume of the Sacred Law-}Vritten, too, at a period when men like·. Addison, Steele and others wese
doing literary work which delights and instructs us at this day-with
all its sublimity of thought and couched in purity of language beyond
compare. Can we not then feel that we have a heritage in a literature
in which we may justly hold a great and honest pride, and endeavor in
some small and humble way to show an appreciation by living up to
those teachings which that literature contains? The man who has
killed all his spiritual and intellectual faculties while he has been
gathering together a heap of material dross is a pitiable object. His
happiness lies not in his own self but in that gathered dust heap which
a passing wind may blow away. But the man who can wander at
will in the world of 'knowledge, or art, or beauty, or imagination, is
ever and always the King of the Universe and the Master of Faie.
Whether riches shall come to him or poverty, he has within himself a
touchstone of happiness which he would not barter for the wealth of
Croesus."

His ideas upon the subject of "emblems" and the tendency on
the part of certain Masons to wear the same in such a manner as to
make an ostentatious display, are exceedingly sound and expressed in
an incisive and forcible manner thus:
"From observations extending over some years, I have noticed a
decided tendency to exhibit an undue display of emblems worn in
various ways upon the person of the brethren. This should be deprecated, as being contrary to the spirit of true Masonry. It needs but a
little consideration to see that a mere metallic ornament can hardly
be sufficient to announce to the world that we belong to a society which
Is based on a morality. Something more is necessarily required of us.
What, then, should be our emblem? Should it not be character and
deportment and becoming dignity, fitting to those principles which are
our bulwark and pride.

"The brother, then, who makes a great metallic display and forgets, by his tenor of life, that he belongs to our Order, not only brings
disgrace upon himself, but stigmatizes our whole system, and casts an
odious reflection on every member of the Craft. Our responsibility,
therefore, is very great to the Order."
The jurisdiction of Manitoba is in a prosperous condition, the net
Increase in membership during the preceding year having been 468,
advancing the total membership to 5619.
John Wemyss, Grand Master, Neepawa.

As stated, the Brethren surrendered this right and privilege, but

Under Michigan, in our last year's report, we cited six cases from
the Grand Lodge of England's proceedings, where the so-called prerogative of making Masons at sight was exercised by Grand and Deputy
Grand Masters, extending from 1731 to 1787.

MASSACHUSETTS, 1910.
The regular business of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts is
transacted in four so-called Quarterly Communications, held each
year in the months of March, June, September and December, the
Quarterly Communication of December being in a sense an Annual
Communication, as at this time the regular annual address of the
Grand Master is rendered, also the annual reports of the various
Grand Officers.
The regular Quarterly Communication covering also the business
of the Annual Communication, was held in the Masonic Temple in
the city of Boston, December 14, 1910, M.". W.". Dana J. Flanders,
Grand Master, presiding.
A large number of Special Communications of the Grand Lodge
occurred during the year, two being for the purpose of constituting
l.odges which had received charters at the previous Annual Comnmnication. Several Special Communications were held for the purpose of participating with particular Lodges in the celebration of Centennial and Semi-Centennial Anniversaries.

"Like all great and meritorious projects of this nature, the important question is one of financing. The plan proposed is to organize
in each jurisdiction and to appeal to the brethren or local Lodges for
funds with which to build the Memorial. It is unfortunate that this
method should be necessary in a fraternal organization founded on
benevolence, particularly where it is the pride of brethren to point to
the distinguished men who have honored it by membership. It will of
course be necessary to bring the matter to the attention of the brethren,
but unfortunately to collect funds it becomes necessary to go into
'team work' with a sort of genteel 'stand and deliver' attitude to accomplish results.''
"Your committee therefore forbear to make any recommendation
on that phase of the communication relative to the collection of funds;
but we most heartily recomn:iend an approval of the object and hope
some future Grand Lodge will be able to co-operate in some plan that
a carefully considered business sagacity, based on experience, will commend. In our own State, with the present campaign to procure funds
for the opening of our Masonic Home on our hands, it will not be feasible or practical to attempt to raise any substantial amount among the
Lrethren for. the purpose purposed.
"We recommend the passage of the following resolution:
"'Resolved, That the Master, Wardens and members of the Grand
Lodge of Masons in Massachusetts heartily approve and endorse the
principle of a Memorial to Washington the Mason to be placed in
Alexandria ; we commend the zeal and work of the officers and brethren
of Alexandria-Washington Lodge, to whom the Craft is so much indebted for the good work already done in forwarding the object; we
would fully endorse any practical or feasible plan for financing the
1mdertaking in the future, but at present do not feel justified in
pledging the co-operation of the brethren in the matter of subscriptions.
" 'Resolved, That the Grand Master be authorized to name a representative of the Grand Lodge to the National Organization.'"

MEXICO, 1910-11.
At the Fiftieth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge Valle
De Mexico, held in the City of Mexico, March 24, 1910, a new Constitution was adopted, and immediately thereafter an election was held
in the regular manner for Grand Officers, and promptly upon the
result of the vote upon Grand Master being announced, Brother Jose
J. Reynoso having been re-elected Grand Master, one of the Past Grand
Masters, together with the representatives of seven of the subordina~e
Lodges, rushed out of the Grand Lodge, without sign or ceremony, and
in great discord expressing their non-conformity with Brother Reynoso's election.
Twenty Lodges remained, and these, constituting a majority, continued their labors and the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
was conducted in regular manner, and at its conclusion closed in Ample
Form.
The seceding seven Lodges have attempted to set up an opposition
Grand Lodge, and inasmuch as the old Grand Secretary was one of
the seceders, all of the records of the old Grand Lodge were purloined
and taken away; and the seceders have appropriated to themselves the
name of the old Grand Lodge, calling themselves Grand Lodge Valle
De Mexico; and the legitimate Grand Lodge of Mexico has adopted,
by constitutional amendment, a new name, called the, York Grand
Lodge of Mexico, and the Fifty-first Annual Communication of this
Grand Lodge, which is the legitimate successor of the former ~rand
Lodge Valle De Mexico,· was held in the City of Mexico, Apnl 13,
1911, M.'. w:. Jose J. Reynoso, Grand Master, presiding; William
Thompson, Grand Secretary.
The Lodges remaining after the seceders withdrew are, as a
rule, possibly entirely so, Lodges that work in English, and we believe,
it is the intention of the Grand Lodge, which has now been purged
of the disturbing element, to work in the English language.
The seceders have been making an effort, which possibly may be
successful to obtain recognition as the legitimate Grand· Lodge, from
the Supr:me Council of the Scottish Rite in Mexico, and if they are
successful in achieving this end, a rather perplexing condition will be
presented to the Supreme Council of the 33rd Degree Ancient and
Accepted Scottish Rite of the Southern Jurisdiction of the United

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

69

States, which may be forced into the position of either refusing to
countenance the action of the Supreme Council in Mexico, or discrediting the legitimacy of the real and genuine Grand Lodge of Mexico
which has now adopted the title of The York Grand Lodge of Mexico. '
Mexico, as we know, has been in a turbulent political condition for
several years last past, which resulted in the successful revolution·
within the past twelve months, and this spirit of turbulence has apparently spread so as to even include Mexican Masonry.
There is, however, we believe, no difference of opinion among
Masonic commentators, where the regularity of Mexican Masonry is
conceded at all, that the present York Grand Lodge of Mexico, F. & A.
M., is the legitimate successor to the old Grand Lodge Valle De Mexico, .
and is the only Grand Lodge in the Federal District entitled to recognition; and at this Grand Lodge at the Annual Communication of 1911,
Brother H. W. Seamon was elected Grand Master, and Brother F. E.
Young, Grand Secretary.
MICHIGAN, 1911.
The Grand Lodge of Masons of Michigan met at Port Huron in
the Sixty-seventh Annual Communication, on the 23rd day of May,
1911, M.". W.'. G. Roscoe Swift, Grand Master, presiding.
After the Grand Lodge had been opened in Ample Form, it was
called from labor to refreshment, and at the opening of the afternoon
session of the first day, the first business attended to was the calling
of the Roll of Honor, being a list of the Grand Masters of the jurisdiction who had pf!ssed to their reward.
General Lewis Cass heads the list, Grand Master 1826-9.
There was one addition to the Roll of Honor since the last Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge, it being the name of William D.
Wilson, Grand Master in 1888, who died January 24, 1911.
The Grand Lodge was welcomed to the dty of Port Huron by the
Mayor, Past Master John J. Bell. His welcome was extremely cordial
and was followed by an address by Past Grand Master Mitchell, the
oldest Grand Master in the jurisdiction of Michigan, he having
arrived at the ripe age of 94 years, still hale and vigorous.
The Grand Master's address occupies something like 120 printed
pages of the Proceedings, and is in this respect something of a record
breaker.
The year was one of extreme activity in apparently all departments.
Dispensations were granted to form three new Lodges.
Several Lodges were constituted which received their charters at
the previous Annual Communication; a very large number of dedications of Masonic halls and buildings took place; corner stones were

REPORT ON CORRESPONDlljNCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

placed to ~ number of public buildings; official visitations were numerous, and correspondence was exce~dingly voluminous.
There were practically no decisions of Masonic law, "nearly all
of the questions submitted to me," says the Grand Master, "during
the year have been answered by simply reference to the 'Book of the
Law,' the 'Blue Book.'"
Palestine Lodge, in this jurisdiction, has a membership df over
1,600, being the largest Masonic Lodge in the world, it having passed
Genesee Falls Lodge, located at Rochester, N. Y., about three years
ago. Genesee Falls Lodge enjoyed the distinction prior to that time
of having been numerically the largest Masonic Lodge in the world.
The Grand Lodge this year turned down a request of Palestine Lodge
to obtain a charter for a sort of an "annex," a wheel within 'a wheel,
as it were, a Lodge intended to serve as an adjunct to Palestine Lodge,
to help that Lodge grind out its grist of applicants, ostensively working by virtue of an independent charter,' but in reality working simply
for Palestine Lodge, the Masons thus created being added ,to the membership roll of the last named Lodge.

He complained to the Grand Master of Michigan, who instead of
admitting that a technical invasion had taken place and diplomatically
apoligizing, failed to disavow the act of the Lodge of his jurisdiction and conducted his correspondence from rather an independent
attitude, which finally resulted in the Grand Master of Canada issuing
an edict of non-intercourse with the Grand Lodge of Michigan, thereby
placing the two jurisdictions upon the basis of non-recognition.
At the Annual Communication there were evidently influences of
a calmer nature brought to bear, and the differences were adjusted,
the tempest in a teapot subsided, the edict of non-intercourse was
rescinded by the Grand. Master of Canada and diplomatic and cordial
relations restored.
The Grand Master reports at great length his visit to Alexandria,
Va., upon the occasion of the organi'zation of the George Washington
Memorial Association, and the purposes of that Association are very
fully set forth in the Grand Master's report, together with a copy of
the Constitution and By-laws of the organization, etc.
At this session, the Grand Lodge, duly and officially accepted
the gift of Ammi W. Wright, of Alma, Michigan, of what was known
as the Alma Sanitarium for a Masonic Home. The gift was valued
at many thousands of dollars and was accepted with the thanks of the
Grand Lodge and a memorial tablet ordered placed in the Home to
commemorate the donor's generosity, who, by the way, is not a Mason,
but who has a high regard for the institution, and especially its charitable work.

70

Michigan appears to have a cipher code, the Grand Master referring to "ritualistic changes" as follows:
"It is conceded that certain errors still exist in the Cipher Code,
and that certain changes are desirable in addition before new rituals
are printed. It is a very expensive matter to issue new editions of the
code. It is therefore desirable to have the code in proper form before
the new edition is published.''
Possibly the most exciting incident which occurred in this jurisdiction in the year was the rupture of fraternal relations with the
Grand Lodge of Canada in the Province of Ontario. The cause of
the trouble arose from the fact that one of the Michigan Lodges located
at Port Huron, had a member who had been ill in a hospital situated
on the other side of the river, the river forming the boundary iine
between Michigan and Canada. The member of the Michigan Lodge
finally died. Immediately prior to his decease, he expressed a desire
for a Masonic funeral.
The Michigan Lodge, instead of requesting one of the Lodges on
the opposite side of the river to perform the ceremony, and without
requesting the permission of the Grand Master of Canada, who, as
a peculiar incident in the affair, happened to live in this town in which
the death occurred, proceeded to conduct the funeral itself, the Michigan Lodge having opened in Port Huron, and then marched across
the river and conducted the funeral according to the Michigan ritual.
There was unquestionably a technical invasion of the Canadian
jurisdiction, and the Grand Master of Canada apparently felt that due
deference had not been paid to his jurisdictional rights.

71

The following are the closing words of the Grand Master's address:
"Masonry to-day stands as one of the greatest forces in society for
good, and by the practice of the tenets of her noble profession in our
individual lives we may assist in hastening the dawn of the day heralded by the 'Watchman on the Tower,' when
"'He sings of brotherhood, of joy and peace,
Of days when jealousy and hate shall cease.
When wars shall die, and man's J>rogressive mind
Soar unfettered, as is God's design.'"
From the comprehensive report of the Grand Secretary, we learn
that the jurisdiction is in an extremely prosperous condition, financially and otherwise, and that the splendid work of Masonry is going
forward in a most gratifying manner in all portions of the jurisdiction.
Fraternal recognition was extended to the several German Grand
Lodges, the regularity of whose origin seems well established, as well
as their conformity to the Ancient Landmarks.
From the report of the Committee on Masonic H"me, one concludes that the Institution is performing its work well and that it
shelters at tliis time about sixty beneficiaries.

MISSISSIPPI, 1911.
The Ninety-third Annual Grand Communication of the Grand
Lodge of Mississippi, Free and Accepted Masons, was held in the city
of Gulfport, Feb. 21, 1911.
The formal opening of the Grand Lodge was preceded by a public
reception at which apparently the entire city of Gulfport was present,
and a program of addresses and music was rendered to the apparent
pleasure and profit of all.
The Grand Master presents a splendid businesslike statement of
his administration, it being particularly noticeable that ten new Lodges
were constituted, and dispensations issued to form several others.
Mention is made of the dedication of the new Masonic Temple at
Lexington, Mississippi, the event being an important one in the history
of Masonry at Lexington, as the event took place upon the Fiftieth
Anniversary of Lexington Lodge No. 24.
Corner stones were placed to a number of important public buildings, and the Grand Master refused to place corner stones of other
buildings because the walls thereof had been too far advanced.
Certain decisions upon local questions of Masonic law were rendered, all duly approved by the Grand Lodge.
Particular attention is drawn to the proposed memorial to Washington, the Mason, at Alexandria, Va., with recommendation that the
same receive the favorable consideration of the Grand Lodge, which
recommendation received in due time the approval of the Grand Body.
The Masonic Orphans' Home is one of the objects of especial solicitude to the Grand Lodge of Mississippi, and the home is receiving
the cordial and enthusiastic support of the Masons of the State.
The assets belonging to the Institution appear to aggregate $100,442.42.
The report on Foreign Correspondence is by M.'. w:. Harry T.
Howard, Past Grand Master.
California, 1909-10, is courteously considered.
John S. Brooks, Grand Master, Lula.
Benjamin V. White, Grand Secretary, Meridian.
MISSOURI, 1910.
The Ninetieth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Ancient Free and Accepted Masons of the State of Missouri, was held
at St. Louis, Sept. 27, 1910, M.'. w:. William A. Hall, Grand Master
in the Grand East.
The Grand Master is pleased with the general state of the Craft
throughout his jurisdiction, and he gives expression to his pleasure
llt the opening of his address as follows :

74

"I am glad to report that throughout our Grand Jurisdiction the
spirit of true fraternity is in abundant evidence, and . peace and harmony prevail and have prevailed through all the year. Scarcely a ripple
has appeared on the calm surface -of events and the only coqtention
known to your Grand Master has been 'that noble contention. or rather
emulation, of who can best woi:k and best agree.'
"And very naturally and logically related to this condition is a
manifest, if n ot remarkable, growth and progress in our Order.• Our
Institution is accepted on every side, and almost without dissenting
voice, as being not only the oldest but the greatest, grandest and most
dignified of all fraternal or benevolent institutions-only excepting the
Church of the Most High. Because of this and accompanying the general
prosperity of our great State and Nation, a ceaseless procession has
sought and obtained permission to enter our Holiest of Holies, participate in the labors and enjoy the privileges of our Order. From our
Grand Secretary, we learn that OUJ" gain in membership from June, 1909,
to June, 1910, has been 1,998, the largest in our history as a Grand
Lodge.''
A degree of activity in public functions of the Grand Lodge was
manifested in the placing of corner stones to no less than sixteen

Dispensations were granted to form four new Lodges, all of which.

conceived in the heart and brain and builded and fostered by the strong
hands of the noblest among us, many of whom have already entered .
into the reward that awaits the faithful Craftsman on high. The
Home, in all that it proposes and represents, ought to be enshrine4 in
every Masonic heart I'

Masons of Missouri are now engaged in the most laudable project of
raising a fund of not less than $100,000 to build and equip a hospital,
or infirmary, for the proper care and treatment of the ill and infirm
among the residents of the Home, and toward this $100,000 fun~ a
very substantial amount, possibly half of it, has already been secured,
and so absorbed ;:ire the Maso.n s of Missouri in this enterprise that they
are not inclined t o give approval to any other undertaking such as
the proposed memorial to Washington, the Mason, at Alexandria,
Va., that may call upon them directly or indirectly for financial assistance; and apparently for that reason a special committee, appointed
on "Washington Memorial," passed out s·ome platitudes as follows:

The Masonic Home, recently opened in Montana, has thus far
proven rather expensive, the per capita cost of maintenance for the
limited number now sheltered at the Home amounting during the preceding year to nearly 1,200, but a reorganization and readjustment of
the Home promises more satisfactory and economical results from
now on.
The Fraternity is in a prosperous condition, the total membership
now amounting to 5,957, a gain of 472 over the preceding year.
The report on Foreign Correspondence is prepared by Past Grand
Master H. S. Hepner. He reviews intelligently the Proceedings of
the usual American and Foreign Jurisdictions, California, 1909, being
fraternally considere9.
The following inspiring sentiments are quoted from his Conclusion:
"The volumes of proceedings speak from every page the language
of fraternity and love and humanity; the mind becomes surcharged with
nobler thoughts, higher ideals and better impulses and· we almost regret to tear ourselves away from these elevating surroundings.
"They show an army of a million and a half human beings arrayed
in the habiliments of war against inhumanity, vice, ignorance and superstition, and standing in defense of human rights, virtue, morality
and all those glorious attributes of Divinity that tend to help make man
in the 'image of his Creator.'

MONT AN A, 1910.
The For.ty-sixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, A. F.
& A. M., of Montana, was held in the Masonic Temple in the City of
Helen~, commencing Sept. 21, 1910, M.'. W.'. John L. Carroll, Grand

Master, presiding.
An optimistic note, characteristic of the rugged and virile West,
is soumled by the Grand Master in one of the opening paragraphs of
his address, as follows:
"The Chartered Lodges have all increased their membership, young
men with the world before them, are coming in to learn the lessons
of Masonry; to assume its duties, and extend its useful_ness ~till more
and more through each succeeding year; and as the fertile soil and ~he
well nigh inexhaustible mines and forests of this great State .are callmg
into existence new and thriving towns, they too are knocking at our
doors for Masonic privileges."
·
Dispensations were granted to form seven new Lodges, which is
one of the evidences of the progressive movement of Masonry in the
Grand Jurisdiction of Montana.
The Grand Master refers to the Special Communications of the
Grand Lodge held in the year; one for the purpose of dedicating the
Masonic Temple at Missoula, one for dedicating the Hall of Manhattan
Lodge at Manhattan, and the other for dedicating the new Masonic
Temple at Billings.
The Grand Master paid a number of official visitations to Lodges
in different portions of the Grand Jurisdiction, greatly to the benefit
of the Craft.
From the recommendations of the Grand Master, we quote two
as follows:
"I recommend that the Worshipful Master remain uncovered at
funerals, and upon all occasions when the public is admitted; to the
end that our customs and usages may not become known to the profane.
.
"2. I recommend that the. constitutional number of signers for the
formation of a new Lodge be increased from seven to fifteen. We are
all more or less inclined to entertain optimistic opinions of ot~r own
town and subject to errors of judgment. A Lodge started with ten
members even, must grow rapidlv not to bec~me a trial and an undue
expense to its membership. No Lodge can exist properly for any great
length of time with less than twenty members."

"Ye brethren· of the Craft, gird up your loins and become active
participants in this holy warfare; forget the burdensome tasks of life,
though for a brief moment, and do your share of duty in bringing rays
of sunshine into darkened hearts; put your hands to your human
brother's back and buoy up his failing strength; whisper in his ears,
while he can hear those tender words of love and eulogy which you
may say when he can hear you not; help him bear the heat and burden
of the day; and the softening glance of his eye, the murmured whisper
of his lips, and the tightening grip of his handclasp will make your
own lives more noble, glorious and sublime."

Under the heading of "Decisions" the Grand Master comments
as follows:
"It is the opinion of your present Grand Master that the less law
made by Grand Master's decisions the better. The Grand Lodge should
be the power to enact and promulgate the all-important matter of
jurisprudence, except in cases of absolute necessity. Nor do I consider
it a Grand Master's prerogative to make formal decisions upon questions that are already covered by the law,"
This view of the matter of "decisions" is somewhat at variance
with the view taken by a Grand Master of this jurisdiction several
years ago, who dignified as decisions such announcements as "a Master
Mason under suspension ~annot object to the initiation or the advance-·
ment of a candidate," "a petitioner who has lost one leg may not be
made a Mason," and twenty other statements of a similar character.
The writer of the California Correspondence report, in commenting upon these intellectual scintillations, entered under the ponderous heading "Decisions" used in describing them the unsympathetic
word "non-sensical."
There was really no discourtesy intended to the Grand Master, but

In the Grand Master's address, delivered at the Annual Communication in June, he refers to the Semi-Annual Communication in the
following language:
"At the Semi-Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge in
Manchester on December 27, 1910, the attendance was very large and
the loyalty and enthusiasm of the Masons of New Hampshire were
never more strongly manifest. In my opinion it would be a sad
thing for this Grand Lodge to take any action which would in the
least tend to lessen the interest in this yearly meeting at Manchester, the importance of which to the Craft can never be equaled by any
other gathering. Whatever action may hereafter be taken on the matter of holding district meetings for instruction in the work, still the

"At this meeting of Grand Masters, presided over by the Grand
Master of Virginia, there were present the Grand Masters, or their
representatives, of thirty-three different Grand Jurisdictions. The obje.ct of this association is, briefly, this: To erect and maintain a suitable Masonic Memorial to George Washington the Mason in the form

Shryock, Grand Master of Maryland since 1885. The association, just

dollars towards defraying the necessary expenses incident to the formation and to the maintaining of this association. I recommend that this

purpose. Alexandria-Washington Lodge No. 22 has a very interesting
hi~tory, and in this connection I crave your indulgence while I briefly
speak of it. This Lodl?e 0btained its first charter from the Grand
LodQ'e of Pennsylvanfa in February. 1783, and was named and numbered Alexander No. 39. under the Pennsylvania jurisdiction. In 1788
the Pennsylvania charter was surrendered and a charter was obtained
from the Gr~nd LoMe of VirQ'inia, of which Edmund Randolph was
then Grand Master. George Wa~hin!lton was appointed the first Mas·
tf'r t'w1,.,. the Virnfoia jurisdiction and served as such until the expiration Qf the appointive term, when he was elected by the Lodge to succeed himself. After the death of the General, and in his honor, the
Lod!le's name was chan1?ed, in 1805, to Alexandria-Washinl?ton Lodge

the Lod11'e possesses an almost priceless collection of Washington relics.

Washington's bed chamber clock, his wedding gloves, farm spurs, field
compasses and numerous other genuine relics. The Lodge feels that

NEW MEXICO, 1910.
Total Membership, 2,572. Gain, 191. Lodges, 38.
The Thirty-third Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge F.
& A. M. of New Mexic,o was held at Roswell, October 17, 18 and 19,
1910, M.". w:. Frank Johnson, Grand Master, presiding.
The Grand Master's address' is a straightforward businesslike statement of the work of the Grand Lodge during the preceding year.
A large number · of Special Communications were reported by him
as having been held for the varinus purposes for which Special Com·
munications are convened, that is, the laying of corner stones, dedi
eating Masonic halls, etc.
One dispensation to form a new Lodge was issued by him and a
number of decisions upon the Masonic Law in this jurisdiction rendered, of which we quote the following:
"A Mason holding a dimit can apply to any Lodge of his choice,
irrespective of his residence, nor is it necessary ·that he be recommended by any of the brethren, as the dimit accompanying the petition is in itself a recommendation and no other avouchment should be
required."
"A brother cannot be tried for an offense committed before he
became a Mason, as this matter should have been looked into by the
Investigating Committee.
"Where a Lodge desires to hold public installation of its officers,
the Lodge should meet in advance of the assembling of the public,
should open its Lodge in regular form, admit the public, install its
officers, dismiss the public, and then close in regular form. It is in
form that a Lodge open on a Master Mason's degree some time in
the afternoon, so as to have everything in readiness, call off, bearing in
mind that they are at labor until after the installation ceremonies are
over, after which, and at some unnoticeable time, when the families
of the brethren and the public are out of the Lodge room, the brethren
shall return to the Lodge and close in Due Form on the same day."
The following paragraphs are taken from the "Conclusion" of the
Grand Master's address to#show that the condition of Masonry in
New Mexico is in a prosp~ous and satisfact9p- condition:
"It is with pleasure that I am able to report to this Grand Lodge
that the interest in Masonry in New Mexico for the past year has
been harmonious and shows a large increase in membership, as well
as a healthy financial condition of the Subordinate Lodges.
"Nothing has occurred to mar the harmony, and the Brethren are
imbued with that true Masonic spirit which should ever abide in the
hearts of all faithful Brethren of dispensing Masonic Light and Charity."

More than $1,000,000 is now being expended for the improvement

maintain the Masonic Home at Utica and provide means of its necessary expansion to keep pace with the growth of the fraternity in the
future.
Reference is made by the Grand Master to the Masonic Home,
and from the various reports concerning this Institution, we learn
that nearly 500 residents are sheltered there, the Institution exceeding in magnitude at the present time any o'ther similar institution in
the world; and, in fact, from many standpoints, numerically included,
New York is the greatest Masonic Jurisdiction in the world.
It has a membership at the present time in round figures of 168,000
Masons, the Grand Lodge of England, with all of its dependencies
numbering considerably less.
That New York does business with a "big auger," we may conclude from the fact that the ordinary income . of the Grand Lodge
from fees, dues, etc., exceeds $200,000, and the funds in the hands
of the Treasurer of the Masonic Hall and Asylum Fund are about
$392,900.41, with Grand Lodge properties valued, as previously stated,
at probably $4,000,000 or $5,000,000.
From .the report of the Superintendent of the Masonic Home,
we are justified in concluding that that Institution is performing most
capably its functions, and fulfilling in an admirable manner the duties
imposed upon it, with an average cost per capita for maintenance of the
residents sheltered there during the preceding year, of $208.58, about
the same cost per capita for maintenance as that of our California
Home.

NEW ZEALAND, 1910.

T~e Tw~nty-first Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of New Zealand was held at Wellington
May 11 and 12, 1910, the M:. w:. Brother Oliver H. Nicholson,
Pro-Grand Master, presiding.
The Grand Secretary read the following letter from His Excellency Lord Plunkett, Most Worshipful Grand Master:
"Man proposes but th~ Great Architect disposes, and what was
to have been, I believe, the most enthusiastic meeting of the Grand
Lodge, is practically a Grand ,Lodge of mourning I
"As loyal citizens and Brother Freemasons, I know that every
member of the Grand Lodge joins with me in heartfelt lamentation
for the calamity which has fallen upon our Empire, and for the loss
of the Patron of our Craft.
"At such a moment it is impossible for me, remembering my public
capacity, to take part in any ceremonies save those connected with the
Sovereign, and I cannot, therefore, be present with you today.
"This I deeply regret, as I had hoped to have personally thanked
the Grand Lodge again for the trust it so long reposed in me, to have
offered my congratulations and paid my respects to your new Grand
Master, and to have said some words of farewell to my New Zealand
Brethren.
"Nor can I feign ignorance that the proceedings were to have included the presentation of a substantial expression of the Brethren's
kindly regard towards myself, and I am much disappointed not to be
able to receive this generous gift during the Session of the Grand
Lodge and amongst representative Brethren from all parts of the
Dominion.
"I can only assure my Brethren that I am with them today in
spirit and in sympathy; that I shall never forget their loyal support
and constant good will, and that the progress of the Craft in New
Zealand will remain of deep interest to me throughout my life."
At the opening of his address the Pro-Grand Master referred to
the death of His Majesty King Edward VII, which occurred only a
few days prior to the opening of the Grand Lodge, as follows :
"Brethren, before proceeding with the ordinary business of this
Communication, I desire to make some reference to the great loss
which we have sustained through the death of our Illustrious Brother
and August and Beloved Sovereign King Edward VII. The suddenness of the news of His Majesty's death came as a great shock to the
civilized world, and left the British Empire, whose destiny he so ably
watched and directed, and over which he so beneficently ruled, stunned
and depressed under a sense of the magnitude of the loss it has sus·
tained.
"As Freemasons, his death directly affects us, for at the time of
his decease he occupied the position of Patron of our Grand Lodge,
and held the title of Protector of Freemasonry. I would remind you
Qf the statement made by him on his accession to the throne, when
resigning the position of Grand Master of English Freemasons and

Concerning the Grand Master's decision as to the ~urisdiction in
which a brother guilty of a Masonic offense may be tried, we would
say that we believe the usual rule to be that an offender may always
be tried by his own Lodge, regardless of where the o~ense may have
been committed; and, that an offender may also be tried by a Lodge
in whose jurisdiction he resides.
. . .
It is also true, we believe, i~ certain Grand Jurisd1ctto.ns that a
Lodge in whose particular jurisdiction the offense was comm1tte~, may
also try the offender, and the decision of the Grand Master above
quoted that the Lodge in whose jurisdiction the offense was com~

from authority to try the offender both the Lodge to w?1ch the offender
belonged, and the Lodge in whose jurisdiction he resides, u~less they
coincide with the jurisdiction where the offense was committed,

square.' There is not hing 'square' about such conduct, but, on the

"Now, the fact is, we are t oo liable to shirk our duty, and by

Is it any wonder, then, that the profane world should fail to recognize us except by some mark or emblem worn about our person?
"Our Master said: 'By their acts ye shall know them.' This applies -t o Masonry as well as the church, and we should see to it that
our acts through life are just such as will bear the 'test of the overseer's square' when the time comes to apply it. Try a little more

The Grand Jurisdiction of North Carolina is in a prosperous
condition. Its income for the previous year exceeded $19,000 with a
substantial amount of assets to the credit of the charity and other
·
funds.
There are now in the jurisdiction about 21,000 Masons with 395
chartered Lodges, and 10 working under dispensation.
There was a net gain in membership during the preceding year
of 832.
The Report on Correspondence is by Past Grand Master John A.
Collins. California, 1910, is considered.
Concerning the charity functions of the Grand Lodges, Brother
Collins makes the following observations:
"Organized charities are to be .found in every jurisdiction, some
having Homes for aged, indigent Masons, widows and orphans, and
these are in the majority. A comparatively few Grand Lodges do not
take kindly to the establishment of Homes, but have ample funds
to care for the needy, and these funds continue to accumulate, so
as to be more than sufficient to meet all probably future demands."
Richard N. Hackett, Grand Master, Wilkesboro.
John C. Drewry, Grand Secretary, Raleigh.
NORTH DAKOTA, 1910.
Membership, 7,581. Gain, 444. Chartered Lodges, 93.
The Grand Lodge, Ancient Free and Accepted Masons of North
Dakota, held its Twenty-first Annual Communication at the city of
Fargo, June 21st, 1910--M.'.
Halfdan Bendeke, Grand Master,
presiding.
The Grand Master, in a brief biographical sketch, inserted at the
beginning of the published Proceedings, is described as a "typical
Viking, tall, blue eyed, etc." He was born in the old Cathedral City
of Trondhjem, Norway, July 7, 1869.
The jurisdiction of North Dakota is evidently proud of its Grand
Master of 1910 and he, no doubt, is deserving of all of the affectionate
regard bestowed upon him by his brethren.

The jurisdiction of North Dakota was sorely afflicted by the

The Grand Master, referring to this event, uses the following expressive language :

could not be a keener one, namely, that of losing our esteemed Grand
Secretary, Past Grand Master Frank J. Thompson, who died on Feb.
