OHIO, 1910.
The Grand Lodge of the Most Ancient and Honorable Fraternity \
of Free and Accepted Masons. of the State of Ohio convened in the _
Masonic Temple, Columbus, Ohio, at IO o'clock ~· .m., Wednesday, October 19, 1910--Grand Master B. F. Perry pres1dmg.
GREETINGS.

Brother D. N. Kinsman, on behalf of the Masons of Columbus,.
extended their welcome to th.e hospitality of this city. His remarkswer~ appropriate to the occasion, and particularly his reference to the
duties devolving upon all · Masons to carry out in their lives outside
of the Lodge room the principles and tenets which were taught them
around the Masonic Altar.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

103

To this address M:, w:. Brother Allen Andrews, Past Grand
Master, suitably responded.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

The Grand Master's address was a plain, straightforward, unadorned statement of what he did during the Masonic year. · He was
moved by a fitting sense of gratitude to the All Wise Ruler of the
Universe that death had not summoned any of the officers of the Grand
Lodge, although more than 1,000 members of subordinate Lodges
throughout the jurisdiction had been called from labor during the preceding year.
Twenty-three Special Communications were held during the year,
twelve for the purpose of dedicating Masonic halls, and eleven for
placing corner stones of public buildings.
The Grand Master was pleased to call attention to the fact that
there are in Ohio at the present time 520 active Lodges and 79,501
Master Masons, the net gain over the preceding year being 3,525. He
was also gratified to observe nearly a thousand representatives present
at the opening of the Grand Lodge.
The Grand Lodge of Ohio was founded in 1809 and has therefore entered upon the second century of its existence.
Application was made during the year for one new Lodge, which,
having been received too late in the year for full investigation, was
referred to the incoming Grand Master.
The three Lodges to which charters were granted at the Communication of 1909 were duly constituted during the year.
DECISIONS.

The Grand Master reports that while a great many questions were
submitted to him during the year, they were with very few exceptions
disposed of by referring the writer to the Code and Decisions and he
found it necessary to render only one so-called decision upon a purely
local question, as to fees for degrees.
In conclusion, the Grand Master calls the attention of the Brethren
to the rapid growth of the Fraternity and voices his deep conviction that
strength is determined not by numbers, but rather by the character
of membership and adds that if Masonry is to fulfill its mission among
men, eternal vigilance must be exercised to guard well the portals to its
sacred altars.
REPORTS OF OTHER OFFICERS.

The Grand Treasurer reports Grand Lodge income as approximately $60,000, with balance on hand in the general fund, after the
payment of expenses for the preceding year, of $64,528.70.
The Grand Secretary, v:. w:. Brother J. H. Bromwell, presents
his twenty-second annual report, being in the usual business-like form.

104

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

He calls attention to the fact that the first volume of the history of
Masonry in Ohio, prepared by the late Brother W. M. Cunningham.
so many years chairman of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence
of the Grand Lodge of Ohio and one of the most distinguished Masonic
writers of his day, had been issued, and copies furnished the various
Lodges, etc., and that the remaining volumes, probably two in number,
necessary to complete the work, would be compiled by Worthy Brother
J. G. Reeves, chairman of the committee.

The Jurisprudence Committee also calls attention to the circular
letter issued by the Grand Lodge of Kentucky, concerning penal jurisdiction over members of Kentucky Lodges by Lodges of other Grand
Jurisdictions into which the offending member may have removed,
and where he may have committed an infraction of Masonic Law.
We believe with the committee that the Masonic Common Law
on this subject is expressed in the Code provision of Ohio, which recites that "a Brother may be tried for unmasonic conduct either bi
the Lodge of which he is a member or by any Lodge within whose
jurisdiction he may have committed the offense, or may sojourn."

OHIO MASONIC HOMJ;;.

The great monument to practical Masonry in Ohio continues to be
the Masonic Home of that State and is the especial object of pride to
every Mason in the jurisdiction.
It shelters and provides a home indeed for 168 residents, of
which 70 are men, 49 women, and 49 children.
It is supported by the various .Grand Masonic bodies of the jurisdiction, the principal source of income, however, being a per capita
tax of 30 cents levied by the Grand Lodge. This is supplemented
by appropriations from the other Grand Bodies and by interest upon
the Endowment Fund, which was increased during the preceding year
by more than $20,000, the total fund at this Communication amounting to $125,408.21.
It is the expectation that this fund will be increased from year to
year until it reaches a sum, the income from which will maintain the
Home independent of contributions from the Grand Bodies.
The Home is located at Springfield, Ohio, and during the second
day of the Annual Communication an excursion was run from Columbus to Springfield to enable those who wished to visit the Home to
do so. There is probably no Masonic Home in our country in which
the residents are made to feel that the place is indeed a "home" and
in no sense a charitable institution more than in the great State of
Ohio.

JURISPRUDENO:.

Reference is made by the Jurisprudence Committee to the communication sent out from the State of Oregon to the various jurisdictions throughout the United States in reference to securing, if possible, a uniform system of <limits throughout the various jurisdictions.
The law of California is now practically in harmony with the
arrangement proposed by Oregon, and, we believe, this is true of
most of our American Jurisdictions, the substance of the arrangement
proposed by Oregon being that membership in the original Lodge
shall not be actually severed until the applicant's petition to the Lodge
to which he desires to change his membership has been accepted.

STATE OF OKLAHOMA, 1911.
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of the State of Oklahoma was
convened in the City of Guthrie, Feb. 8, 1911, and was opened in Ample
Form by M:. W.'. George Ruddell, Grand Master.
The Grand Master has this to say in his annual address, concerning
the condition of peace and harmony in the jurisdiction:
"I am glad to say that peace and harmony have reigned supreme
among the craft the past year, that the membership of constituent
Lodges has been largely increased, much wealth added to the institution, and the moral condition raised to a higher level throughout
the jurisdiction.

106

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

"This has been a wonderful year's work for the Grand Lodge,
and the two departments which have overshadowed all others are the
establishing of the Home at Darlington, and promulgating the ritualistic work adopted at the last session of this Grand Body."
The year was one of extreme activity, sixteen Lodges which received charters at the previous Annual Communication were duly constituted, and dispensations were issued in the year to form eighteen
new Lodges, the record, we believe, for 1910, of American Grand
Lodges.
Hundreds of questions, he states, were propounded to him pertaining to Masonic law, but with few exceptions they were easily answered by referring the inquirers to the Masonic Code.
The correspondence, which is quite extensive, is set forth between
this Gdnd Jurisdiction and that of New Jersey, over the incident
concerning negro Masons in the latter jurisdiction, with the final result
set forth in the following committee report:
"T. M. W. Grand Lodge, A. F. & A. M., of Oklahoma :
"We, your committee, appointed by the Deputy Grand Master to
report upon the Grand Master's Report in reference to the MississippiN ew Jersey incident, regarding negro Lodges, most heartily sustain and
endorse the position of our Grand Master, and recommend that the
Grand Lodge of the State of Oklahoma refuse fraternal relatfonship
with the Grand Lodge of New Jersey, and in the future refuse to
affiliate with or recognize a member from that jurisdiction so long as
the Gra,nd Lodge of New Jersey adheres to its present position upon
the negro question.
"We further recommend that the Grand Master of this jurisdiction serve notice of this action upon the Grand Master of Masons of
the State of New Jersey."
Oklahoma appears to be the only jurisdiction which has followed
Mississippi in severing fraternal relations with New Jersey on account
of the existence in the latter jurisdiction of a Lodge made up of
negroes.
The Masonic Home is referred to by the Grand Master as the one
thing that is nearest and dearest to the hearts of the Masons of the
new State of Oklahoma, and the institution which is already established at Darlington promises to be one of the foremost of its kind in
our American Grand Jurisdictions. .
A Masonic Oration, "Who Is Thy Brother?" was delivered by
William H . Talmage, Grand Orator. It was received with marked
approval and printed in full in the Proceedings.
There is a brief and discriminating report upon Foreign Correspondence in which California, 1909, is courteously considered.
Alexis Eddleman, Grand Master, Marietta.
Wm. M. Anderson, Grand Secretary, Oklahoma City.

"Half a century ago it was the tendency of Masonic thought and
conduct to give careful attention and obedience to the ancient laws
and usages of Free Masonry, as expounded by Anderson, Preston,
Webb and Mackey, who were followed and endorsed by the early
writers of correspondence, such as Drummond, Pillans, Singleton,
Vinci! and Cunningham, all now passed to the great beyond, after having served well their day and generation, and their names are household words to the Masonic student, and it is known to all that they
stood with many not named almost as one rrtan in support of the
maxims of the fraternity as interpreted by Mackay as the leading
writer upon Masonic law, history and usages. Into this school of
thought this writer was initiated, received his degrees and led his
Masonic life, having had several years active experience in each branch
of the Great Fraternity. In the early days to be a Mason was to .be
looked upon with suspicion, as the possessor of dark secrets, dangerous to public safety, but among the initiated who knew the truth it
was to hold sacred every point in the obligations and faithful practice
the tenets of the fraternity, until by the force of their exemplary conduct and worthy lives, the idle prejudice was largely removed and
Masonry became popular and thousands pave of recent years been
seeking its altars, many without the proper motif and the fraternity
is partaking of the commercial character of our age. Our leaders and
writers hold to the ancient tenets with less tenacity, it is getting to be
rare to find one who is not either the promulgator or defender of the
printed or cipher ritual; Masonic law is too far out of date, civil and
corporation law. is advocated in its place. With several correspondents, Anderso.n, Preston and Webb were romances and the inconsclastic
openly denies their accounts of our early history and are seeking to
set up standards of their own, making 1717 and Anthony Sayers the
beginning of everything Masonic, and the Grand Lodge of England all
the Masonic authority which ever existed. Pure Masonry can never be
seriously injured, no more than pure religion, but its patrons and
professors can contaminate its stream far from the fountain and render
its usefulness much less marked than it ought to be. Prethren, remember the 111otto : 'Preserve the Land Marks.' "
The election of officers resulted in the choice of Charles E. Wolverton, Portland, Grand Master; James F. Robinson, Portland, Grand
Secretary.
PENNSYLVANIA, 1910.
The affairs of the great jurisdiction of Pennsylvania are con1ldcred each year at so-called Quarterly Communications, and the
Annual Grand Communication, held on St. John's, the Evangelist
l>ay, December 27, which is the. time th~ Grand Master :enders his

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON. CORRESPONDENC~.

principal report, and when the Grand Officers, who are elected at the
Quarterly Communication held earlier in December, are installed.
The principal business considered at the several Communications
held in the year 1910, was the new Masonic Home project, in process
of development at Elizabethtown, Pa., a few miles east of the City
of Harrisburg; the purchase of a valuable and magnificent site, involving an initial cost for the land of something in excess of $136,000,
was consummated within the year, and elaborate plans for the assembling of suitable buildings to house the Masonic Home organization are
under consideration, and in the course of another two years the buildings will probably be completed, and what, in many respects, may be
considered as the finest Masonic Home in existence, fully established.
The site itself comprises 966 acres of what is considered the finest
land in Pennsylvania, and the numerous financial resources of the
jurisdiction of Pennsylvania will be drawn upon to make this Masonic
charity the ideal of its kind in the world.
The properties and funds belonging to the Grand Jurisdiction of
Pennsylvania aggregate in value nearly $4,000,000, making the Grand
Jurisdiction possibly the richest in the world.
From the Grand Secretary's report we learn that the membership
at the beginning of the year was 92,116, and that there were 477 a~tive
Lodges. The total membership is exceeded by only two Amem;an
jurisdictions, those of New York and Illinois, and there is only 0~1e
foreign jurisdiction, that of England, which has a larger membership.
That the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania enjoys a substantial income
is shown from the report of the Committee on Finance, which reports
total receipts during the year of $210,243.75.
A notable event in the year was the presentation by Brother John
Wanamaker to the Grand Lodge of an oil painting of Brother GEORGE
WASHINGTON, which is the only copy of the original painted from life
by William Williams in 1794. The original of this painting is a
precious relic, the cherished property of Alexandria-Washington Lodge,
of which George Washington was Master.
The Lodge was originally warranted by the Grand Lodge of
Pennsylvania, February 3, 1783, as Alexandria Lodge, and surrendered
its Pennsylvania warrant after the formation of the Grand Lodge
of Virginia, April 28, 1788, and received a warrant from it.
In this warrant, George Washington was named as Master and
the name of the Lodge was changed to Alexandria-Washington Lodge
by vote of the Grand Lodge in 1804.
This painting of Washington, presented by Brother Wanamaker,
was accepted on behalf of the Grand Lod&:e by Past ~ast~r Brother
Norris S. Barrett of the Committee on L1bra~y, a~d m his addr~ss
of acceptance, called attention to a number of h1stoncal matters which

arc generally very well known, but to which possibly attention may

The corner stone of the United States Capitol at the City of
Washington, D. C., was laid on the 18th day of September, 1793, with
Masonic ceremony by Brother Washington in the presence of the
Grand Lodge of Maryland in the first year of Washington's second term
as President.
Brother Barrett calls our attention to the fact that in addition to
Washington, 13 other Presidents ·of the United States of America have
been members of our Fraternity, viz., Andrew Jackson, James Monroe,
James K. Polk, John Tyler, Zachary Taylor, Millard Fillmore, Franklin Pierce, James Buchanan, Andrew Johnson, James A. Garfield,
William McKinley, Theodore Roosevelt and William Howard Taft.
We might add, also, that General Ulysses S. Grant was initiated an
Entered Apprentice Mason in a Missouri Lodge, but through stress
of public duties which crowded upon him immediately after his initiation, he was never able to complete· his purpose concerning the remaining degrees.
Brother Barrett gives expression to pardonable pride in claiming
for his Grand Lodge Museum, the position of being the finest Masonic
Museum in the world.
Brother James M. Lamberton, Senior Grand Deacon, presented
resolutions which were adopted, looking to the celebration · upon September 25, 1911, of the 125th anniversary of the founding of the present
Gran.d Lodge of Pennsyl:vania; and, embodied in the resolutions presentea by him, was one that a committee of three be appointed to
invite the presence of the President of the United States, Brother
William Howard Taft, in the Grand Lodge on their anniversary and
the committee as arranged consists of the R. ·. W. ·. Grand M~ster,
Brother George W. Gutqrie, Past Grand Master Brother George B.
Orlady, and the Senior Grand Deacon, Brother James M. Lamberton.

PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND, 1910.
Number of Lodges1 14. Total membership, 731. Gain, 35.
A combined Special with the Thirty-fifth Annual Communication
of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of Prince Edward Island was held in Masonic Temple at Charlottetown on June 23d and 24th, 1910--M:. w:. W. P. Doull, Grand Master, presiding.
. The Grand Master's address is a concise statement of his official
activities.
We quote from the opening of his address as follows:
"Like a kaleidoscope the scenes are always changing-brilliant,
sombre, variegated, but changing ever. The same picture is never
reproduced, the same circumstances and situations never recur, hence
the need of our assembling annually, to receive from the Grand Master
a resume of the past year's work, followed by a deliberation, an approval or condemnation, a lesson of exami;ile where commendable, a
note of warning where unsatisfactory and an election of someone
else to try to do better next year."

"It has been said that 'Death loves a shining mark'; also that
' He is no resp~cter of persons.' This year he has removed our Royal
Brother, our beloved Sovereign, His Majesty King Edward VII.
Brethren, no words of mine can tell his royal worth or add to the
luster of his record; nor are they needed to communicate to you
a knowledge of his history. While we listen to the cold dull thud of
'Earth to earth,' we as Masons 'cherish his memory here and commend his spirit to God, who gave it.' The grandest ruler of the
g·reatest nation the world has ever held, the foremost figure of modern Masonry has been summoned to lay aside his working tools and
enter the Celestial Sanctum Sanctorum.''

QUEBEC, 1911.
Total Membership, 6,603. Increase; 308. Number of Lodg~s~ 64.
The Forty-first Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Ancient Free and Accepted Masons of Quebec was held in the City
of Montreal, Wednesday, February 8, 1911.
A Special Communication of the Grand Lodge was held February
17, 1910, for the purpose of conducting the funeral ceremonies of the
late R.'. W.'. Deputy Grand Master William Ernest Middleton, and
an Emergent Communication of the Grand Lodge was held April 13,
1910, for the purpose of attending the funeral of the late M.'. W.'.
Brother, Lieut. Col. Alexander Allan Stevenson, Past Grand Master
of the Grand Lodge of Canada in Ontario and Honorary Past Grand
Master of the Grand •Lodge of Quebec.
A Special Communication of the Grand Lodge was held in Windsor Hall in the City of Montreal on Friday evening, the 20th day of
May, 1910, for the purpose of holding a Memorial Service for the late
M· '. W .' . Brother, King Edward VII, Protector of the Craft, who died
at Buckingham Palace, England, on May 6, 1910.
This Emergent Communication was the principal event, Masonic~
ally speaking, which took place in the year 1910 in the jurisdiction of
the Grand Lodge of Quebec.
Eloquent addresses were made by the M.'. w:. Brother, J. Alexander Cameron, Grand Master, and many others, and the many excellent
qualities of his late Majesty King Edward VII were lauded, and his
ienuine service to the cause of international peace and good will were
1et forth, together with his services to Freemasonry, his genuine
attachment to the Order; and his career as Grand Master of England
for 27 years, while he was Prince of Wales, was reviewed, and much
credit to his late majesty was discovered in his life as a man, and as

RHODE ISLAND, 1910.
The yearly business oi the Grand Lodge of Rhode Island is transacted in one so-called Semi•Annual Communication, and the regular
so-called Annual Communication and the One Hundred and Twentieth
Annual Communication of the Most Ancient Free and Accepted Masons
for the State of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, assembled
in the city of Providence on the 16th day of May, 1910, the SemiAnnual Communication having been held in the same city in N ovember, 1909.
The Grand Master reports a year comparatively uneventful, although one of gener11l prosperity. He expresses a conviction that the
true spirit of brotherhood has been the watchword in all of the subordinate Lodges, and among the brethren,, and that nothing exists to
disturb the peace and harmony generally prevailing.
The two decisions rendered by him during the year were as follows:
"Query 1. Whether the Junior Warden, by virtue of his office, has
legal right to administer the obligation in conferring degrees, either
when the Master and Senior Warden are present, or when they are
absent.
"Decision. The Junior Warden, in the absence of the Master and
Senior Warden, would, by virtue of his office, be the presiding officer
of the Lodge, and would therefore have legal right to administer the
obligation in conferring degrees."
"Query 2. Whether it is a proper procedure for the Master to
allow the Junior Warden to administer the obligation when he, the
Master, is present.
"Decision. The Master, by virtue of his prerogative, has legal
right to call upon any Master Mason fa good standing to assist him in
any part of the work of conferring degrees."
The jurisdiction has a membership of 7,464, which is a net gain of
315 over the preceding year.
At this Annual Communication one of the most distinguished
Masons of our common country was chosen M.'. w:. Grand Master,
Henry Warren Rugg,
Brother Rugg was at the time of his selection the Grand Master of
the Grand Encampment of. Knights Templar of the United States.
He was for many years editor of the "Freemason's Repository,"
also a Christian minister, and for a great many years Grand Chaplain
of the Grand Lodge of Rhode Island.
Less than a month after his election as Grand Master, the Masonic
world was called upon to mourn his death, and the announcement of
this sad event was made to the brethren of the Lodges of the jurisdiction of Rhode Island by the Deputy Grand Master, and from this an-

SOUTH AUSTRALIA, 1911.
The Twenty-seventh Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of South Australia was held at Freemasons' Hall, Adelaide, April 19,
!91t, M.". w:. Brother His Excellency the Rt. Hon. Sir S. J. Way,
Bart., P. C., D. C. L., L. L. D., Lieut.-Governor, and Chief Justice of
South Australia, Grand Master, presiding.
The business of the Annual Communication was limited to the
reception and approval of the reports of the Board of General Purposes ; the Trustees of the Free111asons' Hall property; and the election of Grand Master, which resulted in the unanimous choice. of the
Right Honorable Sir Samuel James Way, Bart. P. C., D. C. L., L. L.
D., Lieut.-Governor and Chief Justice of South Australia, Chancellor
of the University of Adelaide, etc., this being his 16th cotl.5ecutive
election which he has received as Most Worshipful Grand Master, and .
it may be added that he served the Grand Lodge as Grand Master from
the years 1884-1889, inclusive, he having therefore been elected 21 times
as Grand Master of the jurisdiction.
The Grand Master, in his brief remarks, subsequent to his election,
CO\}gratulated the Fraternity of his jurisdiction upon its marked prosperity, reflected by the granting of nine warrants for new Lodges
during the preceding twelve months.
The membership of the jurisdiction, he stated, totaled 4112, an
increase of 524 over the preceding year.
The most notable event which occurred in the year was the meeting of the Special Communication of the Grand Lodge as a Lodge of
Sorrow, held at the Town Hall at Adelaide on Sunday, May 22, in memory of his Late Majesty, King Edward VII (referred to as the Patron
and Protector of Freemasonry in South Australia).
'
One of the features of Freemasonry in all of the jurisdictions
of Australia is the high standard of business administration manifested.
There are no Masonic homes in Australia in the American sense
of that institution, but there is in each jurisdiction an Aged Masons'
and Widows' and Orphans' Fund, invested in each case in i~come
bearing securities, and the income thus realized is distributed in the
form of annuities to aged and distressed Masons and .the widows

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

"It is easy to do less than our best, but it is impossible to do
more, and I have endeavored to perform faithfully and conscientiously
the duties of this office, always with the hope tqat my efforts would
be crowned with some measure of success."

Corner stones were placed to a number of public buildings . and
numerous questions of a local character propounded to him fro~ different quarters of the jurisdiction, were answered although few 'f
any, of the answers could be justly regarded as de~isions on Mas;n;c
law.

124

With deep feeling, he. announces that
"Death, the great leveler of all, · has twice, during the past year,
invaded our official ranks. Never since the organization of the Grand
Lodge of South Carolina has the Presiding Officer been called upon
to announce within one year the sad news of the death of two of the
active officers of this Grand Body, that of the Grand Treasurer and
the Grand Secretary. Words are .inadequate to express the great loss
which this Grand Jurisdiction has sustained in the death of these able
and beloved brethren. We shall feel it more and more as time rolls on."
The subject of "physical qualifications" has been giving the Grand
Jurisdiction of South Carolina no little concern in recent years, a determined effort having developed in that jurisdiction to get away from
the exceedingly strict rule of demanding well-nigh physical perfection
from candidates seeking admission, this jurisdiction being probably the
most rigid in this respect of any Masonic jurisdiction in the world,
the slightest and, in many cases, apparently the most trivial physical
defect, acting as a bar to admission.
A certain amendment touching this question was duly introduced,
and its adoption strongly recommended by the Grand Master, but after
animated discussions the amendment was rejected, although at the
close of the Communication, another amendment of similar import was
introduced, which will come up for consideration and action at the
next Annual Communication.
The amendment referred to above, and which, as stated, was defeated, the jurisdiction preferring to hold its old rigid rule, was as
follows:
"That every candidate for initiation in this jurisdiction must be
a man, freeborn, of mature and discreet age, having no maim or defect
in his body or mind that may render him incapable of learning and
practicing the art, and who can comply literally with all the requirements of the Ritual as to initiation ceremonies, without artificial aid
or friendly assistance."
The Grand Master refers to the invitation received by him to
attend at Alexandria, Va., the meeting intended to organize the Washington Memorial Association, and he expresses his thorough accord
with the movement, accompanied by a recommendation that the Grand
Lodge give the same its endorsement, which later in the Communication was done.
Dispensations were granted by the Grand Master in the year tq
form four new Lodges, and the three Lodges which received charters
at the previous Communication were duly constituted.

SOUTH DAKOTA, 1911.
Number of Lodges, 128. Members, 8;901. Gain, 577.
The Thirty-seventh Annual Commilii.icadon of the Grand Lodge of
Ancient Free and Accepted Masons of South Dakota was held at
Chamberlain, June 13th and 14th, 1911, M.". w:. Samuel S. Lockhart,
Grand Master, presiding.
Preliminary to the official opening of the Grand Lodge an address of welcome to the Qrand Body was made by Brother Francis K.
Barry, Mayor of the city of Chamberlain, responded to by the Past
Grand Master, Brother Oscar S. Gifford.
'
The Grand Master, in the opening of his address, uses a quotation
from one of his predecessors to characterize the ideal Masons, as
follows:
·
"The ideal Mason is a full-grown man, patriotic, intelligent, reverent, devoted to home, alert to business and an unfailing friend. He
will always be found on the side of his country, his race and his
God.
"What a people we would be if all would make that short paragraph a standard and try to live up to it. His ideal is none too high.
Which one of these virtues do you not wish your boy to attain? Name
it. If he should attain all, why not you?"
The Grand Master refers with deep feeling to the great affliction
suffered by the Grand Lodge during the preceding year in that the
Grim Reaper had called in that time three Past Grand Masters of the
jurisdiction to their reward-M.". w:. William Clark Allen, M.". w:.
Henry Harrison Blair, M.'. w:. Fred'k H . Files.
A degree of Masonic activity was manifested throughout the year.
Various corner stones of public buildings were placed; certain dedications of Masonic Temples were made under the supervision of the
Grand Lodge, and certain Emergent Communications of the Grand
Body held for other purposes.
A large number of questions concerning Masonic matters were
answered, although nothing entitled to the dignity of a so-called decision was rendered.
Reference is made by the Grand Master to the proposed George
Washington Masonic National Memorial Association, which at this
Annual Communication received the endorsement and approval of the
Grand Lodge.
An eloquent address was delivered by Brother M. F. Montgomery,
Grand Orator, the theme of his very interesting effort being the imperative need of the "soundness"· of material to form a permanent and
lasting structure, particularly the need of soundness of character in
the Masonic edifice.

The Seventy-fifth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Texas was held at Masonic Temple in the City of Waco, December

Masonry is experiencing a marked growth within the vast jurisdiction of Texais, and the Grand Master's report discloses interesting
information along these lines, it appea·ring that during the year 1910
twentyrseven Lodges were constituted, and at the Annual Communication under review twenty-three Lodges U. D. received charters.
The finances of the Grand Lodge are in excellent condition, and
its Masonic Home at Fort Worth is one of the foremost institutions
llf the character in this country. The present home is designed to
shelter the widows of Masons, and Masonic o·rphans, and at this
Communication plans were consummated for the erection and maintenance of a home for aged Masons at Arlington, the purpose being
to shelter at this home aged M;i,sons and the widows of Masons, leaving the Fort Worth Home free for the exclusive care of children,
this plan having already been adopted in a number of jurisdictions,
including our own jurisdiction of California.
Brother A. W. Houston, Grand Orator, delivered an address on
"OUR OBLIGATION."
The Reverend Brother A. E. Eaten delivered an address also to
the Grand Lodge on the subject, "THE BIBLE AND THE MASONIC
BROTHERHOOD."
The "Traveling Silver Trowel" made its appearance at this Grand
Lodge at this time, its reception being attended by an interesting
and somewhat elaborate ceremony. It will be recall~d by the members of the Grand Lodge of California that the "Traveling Silver
Trowel" was received in our Grand Lodge two years ago. Accompanying this trowel is a record showing the dates and places of its
presentations, which record contains appropriate emblems and symbols of the local jurisdictions with names of officers and committees
presenting and receiving the trowel.
When the trowel shall have finally circled the globe, as is the
intention, it will indeed have acquired a great historic value and become a treasured emblem in the archives of the Justice Lodge No. 753
of New York, which sent the trowel upon its fourneyings,some five
or six years ago.
In the controversy between' the regularly estabHshed Grand Lodge

resolutions from the Committee on Foreign Correspondence, recognized the original Grand Lodge, of which Brother Jose J. Reynoso
is Grand Master, and Brother William Thompson, Grand Secretary.

UTAH, 1911.
Total Number of Members, 1,779. Increase, 141.
The Fortieth Annual Communication of the M:.
Grand Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons of Utah was held at the Masonic Temple,
Charles Bruerton
Salt Lake City, January 16 and 17, 1911, M:.
Jack, Grand Master, presiding.

w:.

w:.

The Grand Master opens his address as follows :
"Brethren, we are at the close of another year. It has been my
good fortune to succeed most efficient Grand Masters and to find
the work organized, the Brethren interested, the Lodges in good hands.
"Moreover, this is a period when an awakening to the greater
realities of life has been sweeping over the world. In every counl!ry
men are raising their voices against fraud, oppression and injustice;
calling for 'personal purity, corporate honesty, national patriotism and
civic enterprise. Such a wave, like everything in life, has its ebbs .
and flood tides; and when it surges through a nation it reaches every
corner, affects each individual.
"In every Lodge of our jurisdiction we have found an ambition
to do exact ritualistic work, combined with an earnest desire to dis.play that true spirit of Masonry which your Grand Officers have at all
times and on every occasion sought to emphasize and inculcate."
.
The Grand Master felicitates the Grand Lodge upon the fact that
the gain in membership in the year that had just closed was the largest
in the history of the Grand Lodge, with the single exception of the
year 1874.
The. Grand Ma-ster reports that during the year he visited each
constituent Lodge at least once, surely a good record.
Five decisions were rendered, of which we quote the following:
"Labor may be suspended in the Master Ma.s on's Degree and a
Lodge of Entered .Apprentices opened in lieu thereof without passing
through the Fellow Craft Degree. But all Lodges opened must be
properly closed.
"If the Worshipful Master elect be not qualified for installation,
none of the officers can be installed; A LodP."e starts anew each year,
and if it has no member qualified to serve as Master, or does not see fit
to elect such a Brother, it mu.st cease work."
Apparently there could be no tibjection to the first decision quoted
above, but the practice of the jurisdietion of Utah has not been in
accordance with that decision and the Jurisprudence Committee supported by the Grand Lodge refused to approve the same.
Pa·rticular reference is made by Grand Master Jack to the Golden
Wedding,_ which took place in the year, of Grand Secretary Christopher Diehl, and in view of the fact that the Grand Lodge of Utah
and Brother Christopher Diehl are almost synonymous, there was
no impropriety in the Grand Master elaborating in his annual address

VERMONT, 1911.
Membership, 12,931. Number' of Lodges, 103. Net Gain During the
Year, 204.
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of Vermont, held its One Hundred Eighteenth Annual
Communication at Burlington, June 14th and 15th, 1911, M:.
Henry L. Ballou, Grand Master, presiding.
The Grand Master at the opening of his address manifests a strain
of sentiment in a backward glance to "Fifty Years Ago," thus:
"While in the enjoyment of life, liberty and the oursuit of happiness to an extent seldom if ever attained by the fathers, we are reminded that such was not the case when our brethren convened fifty
years ago in Grand Lodge. The sky above us to-day that has scarcely
a cloud to mar its beauty was then shot with darkness from North to
South, a sad foreboding of the coming storm that was to rend and
tear our fair land with bitterness, destruction and death. The words
used in his annual address in January by the venerable Grand Master
Philip C. Tucker portray for us the situation. They were in part:
'Brethren of the Mystic Tie: We meet, upon the present occasion,
with a cloud of gloom hanging over our beloved countrv. One of the
stars in our national flag has been torn from its place ; our flag itself,
as to one portion of our national soil, no longer spreads its folds to
the breeze, to typify to all eyes the unity of national freedom, but where
it once so proudly waved now appears the palmetto and the rattlesnake, sad substitutes indeed for that glorious banner which has heretofore commanded respect in every country where human foot has
trod, and in everv sea which has borne upon its waves the keel of
an American vessel. We are a divided republic, and the last resting
place of republican liberty on earth is no longer one and indivisible.'
"No wonder his· great heart ached as he contemplated the situation.
His only son, who bore the same proud name, Philip C. Tucker, and
who was destined to become, like his father, a great leader in Masonry,
dying at the head of the oldest Supreme Council of Scottish Rite
Masons in the world, was then living in Texas and was in the coming
struggle to draw his sword in defense of his adopted State and in
desperate battle oppose the friends of his boyhood and youth. Two
days before Fort Sumter was fired upon the spirit of this prince among
our Grand Masters took its flight from this 'transitory existence' to a
state of endless duration.' Thankful indeed should we be that the days
of '61 are fast becomin~ ancient history. Long ago God's grass healed
over the scars that cannon balls had made, and spread its carpet of
green over hillsides billowy with the dead; and now fifty years after the
forces at work for unity have accomplished the same miracle in the
hearts of those whose feelings seemed to be torn for all time. Among
these forces and to the very front is to be found the institution of
Masonry."
He reports a sound and healthy condition of the Craft with a
reasonable degree of growth during the preceding year.
He expresses the hope, which may reasonably be cherished by
everyone, that the ever-widening circle of Masonry may ultimately

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

"As to Masonry in Russia, the Canadian Correspondent, M.". w:.
Brother Henry Robertson, presented an interesting story in 1900, at the
time of his retirement from the round table after long and most efficient service, from which the following:
" 'When we were asked to write an article on Freemasonry in
Russia, the reply naturally came that it would be similar to that celebrated historical chapter on the Snakes of Ireland, which consisted of
six words : "There are no snakes in Ireland." '
"'There may be Freemasonry in Russia but it is not visible. There
was a time when it existed there, but it never flourished to any great
extent. The capacity to understand and appreciate the genuine benefits of the craft was lacking, and there was no bond of community
between the Lodges. The Orthodox Party of the Greek church were
its enemies, and their methods of persecution differed but little from
those of the Clerical Party in Roman Catholic countries. Although
assassination was not often resorted to, the brethren were imprisoned
and exiled and their property confiscated, all in the name of religion
and to the praise and glory of the God of Mercy.'
"The popular supposition has been that Peter the Great introduced
Freemasonry into Russia from England, but Brother Robertson says
the first Lodge there was formed in St. Petersburg, March 27, 1771,
during the reign of Catherine II, by Brother Von Reichell, a German,
and under the German system. A second Lodge was opened in St.
Petersburg in June following· under English patronage. The earlier
Lodge, with characteristic English assumption, was promptly declared ·
illegal, a message having been sent from London to Berlin that 'the
London Grand Lodge had the exclusive right of constituting other
Lodges in the whole world.' The earlier Lodge suspended labor, but
Von Reichelt founded another Lodge in 1773 (with a Russian Prince
at its head) , the old body was reopened and three other Lodges were
formed. Continuing, Brother Robertson wrote:
"'In 1774 the English organized five Lodges-three in St. Petersburg, one in Moscow, and one in Jassy-and the fight went merrily on.
The result was, that in 1776 the English representative finding the
court influence against him, abandoned the English system and went
over to the German system, taking with him the whole of his Lodges.
In 1777 there were eighteen Lodges working under the Provincial
Grand Lodge of St. Petersburg, according to the Swedo-Berlin s_ystem. For a few years Freemasonry was 'fashionable' and the Lodges
and the membership and the systems all increased.'
"But the 'fashionable element' soon grew tired ~f their diversion
and quit. Quarrels between the different systems followed. The charlatan Cagliostro with his 'Egyptian mysteries' brought reproach upon
the craft, and the French revolution was attributed to them. The
crowned heads of the continent were filled with dread and suspicion,
and then Brother Robertson says:
·
"'The blow fell in January, 1794, when Empress Catherine issued
a decree forbidding all assemblages of Freemasons, and in a few
months no Lodges were to be found within the Empire. This decree
was renewed by Catherine's successor, Paul I, in 1797. Under Alexander I a few Lodges were reopened, and in 1810 they received official ·
recognition and confirmation. Then ensued a revival. Within ten
years there were thirty-one Lodges, but their progress was again stopped
by internal dissensions. Then came renewed fears for monarchial

The feature of the volume of Proceedings for 1911 is the report

The Grand Master, on account of certain irregular Masonic Lodges
in the State of Washington, makes "this report c~cerning incorporation of the Grand Lodge:
"Having been advised that irregular Masonic Lodges were being
organized in the State of Washington, and that according to the law
of this State there is nothing to prevent these Lodges from incor- ·
porating under our law and thus robbing us of the use of the name
that has so long distinguished the craft (as the law provides a penalty
for wearing an emblem or using the name of a society first incorporated), I proceeded with the incorporation of this Grand Lodge under
the law of the State of Washington on April 1, 1910. I felt that it
was imperative to take this step rather than to wait for this Communication of the Grand Lodge, I trust that you will not think I was
too hasty in this matter, as II felt that an emergency existed and immediate action was necessary."

WASHINGTON, 1910.
Number of Active Lodges, 165. Total Membership, 14,473. Average
Number of Members per Lodge, 86.
The Fifty-third Annual Communication of the Most vyorshipful
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of Washington convened
in the City of Tacoma, on Tuesday, the 21st day of June, A. D. 1910,
A. L. 5910, and was called to order at the hour of 10 o'clock a. m.,
Wm. R. Baker, Grand Master, presiding.
As to the condition of Masonry within his jurisdiction, the Grand
Master in his amTual address has this to say :
·
"The past year has been one of great prosperitv for this Grand
Lodge and the Grand Secretary's report wil! show. a material increase
in our membership. While we have numerically mcre~sed, I can say
with confidence that the personnel of the new members 1s ex~ellent and
that our Lodges are receiving members of w~om we can J~Stly t~el
proud· which proves to the world that we receive none knowingly into
our r;nks but those who are moral and upright before God."
The activities of the Grand Master were manifested in tlie year
by the constitution of certain Lodges which received charters at the
preceding Annual Communication; by dispensations to form four new
Lodges ; by the placing of corner stones to s~ven public buildings and by
the issuance of numerous dispensations for a variety of purposes.
One decision of Masonic law of a purely local character was rendered.

He makes reference as· follows to the short-lived effort in a certain
quarter concerning a National Grand Lodge:
"I have been importuned on several occasions, the past year, to
give my ideas and the views of this Grand Lodge on the question of a
National Grand Lodge. To these requests I have replied that this
Grand Lodge several years ago had gone on record as being opposed
to a National Grand Lodge and that personally I was averse to the
plan. I am, however, in favor of a National Convention of Grand
Lecturers, as I feel that a great de.a l of good could come from a convention of that kind."
A learned address was delivered by the Grand Orator, Worshipful
Wm. J . Sutton, which was greatly appreciated by the Grand Lodge
and ordered printed in full in the Proceedings.
The establishment of a Masonic Home is receiving the serious consideration of the Grand Lodge of Washington at this time, and the
following resolutions concerning the same were duly adopted:
"To the M.". W .". Grand Lodge of Washington:
"In the matter of the establishment of a Masonic Home, which has
been referred to your committee, we beg to submit the following recommendations :
"That the incoming Grand Master appoint a committee on Masonic
Home, consisting of five members.
"That such committee communicate with all the Lodges in this
jurisdiction, inviting proposals for location of said Home.
"That the committee be empowered to investigate all sites offered,
and that the actual traveling expenses that are incurred in investigating such sites shall be paid by Grand Lodge.
"That the committee be requested to submit their report to the
Grand Lodge convening in June, 1911, together with their recommendations, with a view to establishing such Home ; and to recommend a complete plan of organization and administration for the
government of said Home."

The Grand Lodge of Western Australia has not only advanced
substantially in membership, but it also has developed a wonderful
financial strength, considering its comparatively recent organization
and the sparsely inhabited country in which it is located, its vested
funds amounting in round figures to the equivalent of $125,000.
It has developed a splendid charity organization, which enables
it to fulfill in an efficient manner its obligations to the distressed among
its membership, and it is worthy of comment that its Charity Fund is
in process of yearly substantial growth.

At each of the Quarterly Sessions, the Grand Master rendered
a concise and illuminating report of the affairs of the jurisdiction
and of notable events that occurred from time to time during the year.
Especial mention is made of the extreme pleasure experienced by
the Grand Master of welcoming, on behalf of the jurisdiction, that distinguished soldier and Freemason, Lord Kitchener, who visited the
jurisdiction and who expressed himself as highly delighted with everything he saw.
Lord Kitchener expressed no little surprise to find that the Freemasons of Wes tern Australia owned such a magnificent temple as that
which exists at Perth, where most of the Communications of the
Grand Lodge are held, avowing the opinion that such magnificent
headquarters, considering the comparatively small population, reflects
great credit upon the Fraternity.
Lord Kitchener, it appears, was made a Past Grand Warden of
England in 1897, District Grand Master of Egypt and Squdan in 1899
and District Grand Master of Punjaub in 1902, which position he
holds at the present time.
The Grand Master Brother, The Right Reverend C. 0 . L. Riley,
D. D. Lord Bishop of Perth, presided at all the Quarterly Communications ·and at the Quarterly Communication of January, 1910, wa.s
unanimously eleeted Grand Master for the sevehth consecutive term.
Masonry in Western Australia is in a sound and flourishing condition and is doing splendid Masonic work.
There is an intelligent report on Foreign Correspondence by
several members of the Committee in which California for 1909 has
a place.
C. 0. L. Riley, Grand Master, Perth.

This jurisdiction, like the other jurisdictions of Australia, has
established the system of annuities for aged and infirm Masons, and
the widows and orphans of Masons, and annual relief to the amount
of many thousands of dollars is distributed from the earnings of
benevolent funds.
This Grand Jurisdiction is in extremely good financial circumstances, the sum total of the various credit balances belonging to the
Crand Lodge, amounting to £25,720.15.10, equivalent to practically
$130,000.
There are 90 Lodges in the Grand Jurisdiction, with a total membership of 3,733, a gain over the preceding year of 43.
A suggestion well worthy the consideration of Masonic Jurisdictions throughout the world comes from a practice followed in the
jurisdiction of South Australia, and recommended at this time to the
Craft of Western Australia, in a communication from the former
jurisdiction, and because of the peculiar merit of the suggestion, the
communication referred to is quoted in full as follows :
"A Communication has been received from the Grand Lodge of
South Australia stating that the Masters' and Wardens' Association
of that jurisdiction had submitted to them the following resolution:
"'That it is advisable that some other method of candidates pledging their fidelity be adopted than by kissing the V. S. L.'
"The Communication went on to say :
"'This was not meant in any shape or form to dispense with the
Sacred Writings, but from hygienic reasons, that some other method
should be adopted than that which is now customary, viz., hundreds,
and possibly thousands, saluting the V. S. L. on the same page year
after year. A suggestion has been made that a small, inexpensive
V. S. L. be procured for each candidate, and after he has attained
his M. M. degree he should be presented with it.'
"The Communication inquired if the Grand Lodge of Western Australia had ever considered or taken any action in the matter, and a
reply was sent ti;> the effect that it had not. The Board, however, was
deeply impressed with the importance of the question, and gave the
subject its earnest consideration at different meetings, with the result
that it now submits the following recommendations to the Grand Lodge
for adoption :
"'That .Grand Lodge direct that a separate copy of the V. S. L.
be provided for each candidate whereon to take his several obligations.
"'That, in the event of the foregoing recommendation being agreed
to, Grand Lodge do supply all Lodges with copies of the V. S. L.
free of charge.' "
·
lOa

The procedure above indicated might, we believe, with wisdom
be adopted in our own jurisdiction.

"What friend like a Masonic friend. We have followed the same
pathway; we have fought the same battles; we have been assailed
with the same temptations; the same influences to evil have bubbled up
in our souls, coming we know not from whence. We have rejoiced
in the same blessings of a kind Providence. Together we have enjoyed
them all, and when clouds darken and the lightnings flash, the golden
chain of friendship is not severed. In my high school days I oft debated
the question as to which was greater, fove or friendship; but in this
higher life, are they not one? The husband and wife, who have together, in perfect harmony of spirit, braved the many adventures of
life, have lost sight of life's baser passions, making those things in
the order of nature which cloud the higher instincts of the yduth,
but incidental to that divine friendship of the soul which transcends
time and prefigures the glories of the Eternal World."
"Masonry teaches, as does no other philosophy in the world,
the true end and aim of existence, and the true nobility of labor.
Here we have been taught-to use the language of Lord Bacon-to
exercise, in prosperity, the virtue of temperance; in adversit:,i, that of
fortitude; in short, to develop character arid virtue under all the
circumstances and in all the conditions of life."

*

*

*

*

*

"Today, then, my Brethren, let us renew allegiance to the principles of the great Order to which we belong. In Masonry we find the
most splendid of all philosophies of life and morals, the concentrated
wisdom of all the generations of men who have lived and suffered
and labored, and to-night rest in dreamless sleep in quiet cities of
the dead. · So Masonry means, not only the garnered wisdom stored
up in lectures and books, but more especially that wisdom which becomes part of the life."
·
From the report of the Grand T·reasurer, it appears that the total
income of the Grand Lodge for the preceding year was $7,076.11,
and the commissions paid to the Grand Treasurer, Brother S. · N.
Myers, amounted to $498.26; two-thirds as much as the salary of
the Grand Secretary, who also fills the important position of Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence; and two and
one-half times the salary paid the Grand Treasurer of California,
with an income more than ten times the income o{ the Grand Lodge
of W est Virginia. In fact the compensation paid the Grand Treasurer
of West Virginia is neairly as much as that received by the Grand Treasurer of the great jurisdictions of either New York or Pennsylvania,
holding assets of a number of millions each, and each Grand Jurisdiction with a yearly income of several hundred thousand dollars.
The two items of $498.26, commissions paid the Grand T·reasurer,
and $250 for Grand Lodge banquet, amount to more than the total
charity expenditures, or· appropriations of the Grand Lodge.

WISCONSIN, 1911.
The Sixty-seventh Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Free · and Accepted Masons of the State of W isconsin was held in the
city of Milwaukee, June 13, 14 and 15, 1911, M.". w:. Ernest E.
Gatchell, Grand .Master, in the Grand East.
T he Grand Master takes a long look backwards of fifty years
and contrasts in the following language conditions existing then and
now :
"Fifty years . ag? to.- day the. Gra nd Lodge met in Seventeenth
A?nual Communication m the City of Milwaukee. The nation was
stirred by the . so1;1nds of martial. music .and busy preparations for one
of the most fernble wars of history: There was no . Grand Master
present. . If! explanation of this Grand Master Gabriel Bouck in a
commumcat1on to the Grand Lodge, said :
'
" 'On the 20th of ~pril, A. D. 1861, I became a member of a
Volunteer Company, which, on that day tendered its services to the
Governor of the State, and were, on the 22nd of th e same month
accepted and attached to the Second Regiment Wisconsin Active Militia'
an~ ordered to rendezvous at Camp Randall ; from the time of such
enlistment: my new engagements have demanded my sole attention
to the entire neglect of m.y private and professional business, and in ~
great measure, of the duties of Grand Master.'
• "The Gr:and Lodge was at that .time composed of 119 Lodges, and
1
a membership of 3,700. To-day ·we represent Z64 chartered Lodges
an~- a .member ship of over 26,~~. net . gain of 741 for the past year'.
It is a great pleasure and sabsfact1ort to r eport to you tha t, with this

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

large membership and all the work that this inc·rease represents, there
have been no troubles of sufficient importance to report to you for your
consideration. Surely neither envy, discord nor confusion has interrupted that peace and tranquillity which should characterize Masonic
intercourse."
From the Grand Master's decisions two are quoted as follows:
"An objection to initiation, addressed to the Lodge, mailed to the
Secretary and by him handed to the Master, should be regarded.
"A brother may be installed Master of a Lodge, though his residence at the time be in another Grand Jurisdiction."
Nine Special Communications of the Grand Lodge were held
during the year for purposes of placing corner stones, dedicating
' Masonic Temples, etc.
Wisconsin is among the fow import;mt jurisdictions in the United
States that has not approved the Masonic Home idea of administering
Masonic charity, and upon this phase of charity, and charity in general,
the Grand Master speaks as follows in his address :
"Without dealing in platitudes or attempting impossible flights
of oratory, let us consider Charity as a Masonic virtue. Charity is
the corner stone of our Masonic fabric. Charity in its broadest sense
and definition runs as a golden thread through all the warp of our
Masonic Ritual. Without it we are as the empty shell which roars as
with the roar of the ocean. The Charity to forgive them who spitefully
use us ; Charity for those who fail in the good fight and fall short
of reafo:ing the high calling-which means Charity for all men, which
each one of us asks and needs ; a broad and liberal Charity for the
needy-the unfortunate-the distressed ; with such Charity we are
Masons in fact and in deed. In so far as we are lacking in such
Charity, in so far do we fall short of our high calling.
"Let us now consider charity in the concrete-the charity of the
pocketbook. The Grand Master responded to calls for charity to the
amount of $768.12. To this amount of $768.12 should be added $50.00,
a balance left of a former appropriation, and unused. The Lodge
was permitted to use this in a case of need recently arising. This
makes a total of $818.12 appropriated under the direction of the Grand
Master during the recess of tbe Grand Lodge. Correspondence and
vouchers relating to the distribution of this amount will be found in
the office of the Grand Secretary, and may be examined by any member of this Grand Lodge. No appeal for aid was refused, and no excuse is offered for the amount appropriated.
"We are justly proud of the Home method of caring for the unfortunate in contradistinction to the institutional. Let us not forget
that our membership is growing at the rate of nearly a thousand a
year. Let us not forget that our old members are growing older.
In remembering these things, let us keep pace with them with our charity fund, so that in the future. as in the past, we may be always ready
and able to answer all legitimate calls for help. Let us jealously watch
our charity fund, so that should our annual tax per member of ten
cents not be sufficient, we may make it such an amount that within
the boundaries of Wisconsin there may be no unrelieved distressed
worthy brother and no Lodge with its treasury hopelessly depleted."

From the Grand Secretary's report the information is obtained
that a satisfactory degree of progress and prosperity exists within the
jurisdiction. A net gain in membership of 741 over the preceding
year is recorded, and the total membership Jan. 1, 1911, appears to have
been 26,421.
One of the ablest Masonic commentators at the present time i.s
Past Grand Master Aldro Jenks, Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence in Wisconsin.
He is a staunch believer of maintaining in all its purity the great
stream of Ancient Craft Masonry as it descends through the centuries,
and strongly and logically resists all attempts to merge into this stream
any of the spurious creations of modern times, especial~y resisting t~e
claims of so-called Supreme Councils of the Scottish Rite of authority
in Craft Masonry, and standing immovably upon the ground that socalled Grand Bodies tracing a genealogy of this character, are not
entitled to recognition among the sovereign Grand Lodges of the world.
Brother Jenks' views upon this subject are, in our opinion, eminently sound.
His reviews of the various Grand Lodges are both interesting and
instructive, and we take the liberty of making a few quotations therefrom.
Under the caption of Arizona, his comments upon the Grand Lodge
Swiss Alpina, are as follows :
"The Grand Lodge Alpina was duly recognized upo?. the. recom·
mendation of the Committee on Correspondence because its aims and
purposes are in accordance with the fundall!ental prin~iples of Masonry;
that it is accomplishing great good, and its regularity has ~een ful~y
established.' We think there can be no doubt of the regularity of this
Grand Lodge.
"It traces its genealogy back to the Grand Lodges of England,
Ireland and Scotland, although some of its Lodges were originally
obedient to the Grand Orient of France. That was a time, however,
before the latter body committed Masoni~ suicide by r~oving fr~m
its ritual all allusions to a Supreme Bemg and removmg from its
altars the First Great Light.
"The trouble with Alpina is that it has not always been particular
as to its associations and so respectable Grand Lodges have been averse
to extending to it the right hand of fellowship."
Under the caption "District of Columbia,'' in speaking of the
Grand Master's address, he has this to say:
"What is otherwise a good address is 1:11arred by a ~audatorv. m~n­
tion by the Grand Master of the. Masom~ Mutual .L.1fe Asso~1at1_on.
This, he says, 'has passed the ,fortieth anniversary of it.s o~ga!11zat1on
with every claim paid in full, etc. Of course, such mshtuhon.s do
great good, while they last, and are all perfectly solvent a~d reliable,
until the crash comes. Then Masonry suffers through having loaned
its fair name and credit to the enterprise, many brethren find that the
support they had counted on for their families is swept away and they

Several decisions of a local character are set forth, one of which,
showing that Wyoming is not a strict constructionist in matters of
physical qualifications, is quoted as follows :
"Question. Cao a candidate receive the degree of a Mason who
has lost the two middle fingers and the end of his thumb at the first
joint on his right hand?
"Answer. Yes. The physical tests that are required of all candidates for the degrees of Masonry can in this case be complied with."

The Thirty-sixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge,
Ancient Free and Accepted Masons, of Wyoming, was held at Rock
Springs, September 7 and 8, 1910--M.". w:. Birney H. Sage, Grand
Master, presiding.
The Grand Master's appreciation of the function of Freemasonry
in improving human character is expressed in the following words
from the opening of his annual address:
"We are factors in the work of the great army engaged in a
,grand, united effort to enlarge and improve human character, impressiing thereon great moral truths which tend so greatly to promote the
·safety and welfare of every community. In this great, noble and neverending labor none of us should for a moment falter in striving for
the betterment of humanity and all ,good works necessary in aiding the
weak and destitute, that such works may demonstrate to the people of
every community that in the face of the great competition brought about
during recent .years through the establishment of the multitude of societies now in the field, Masonry continues to pursue the even tenor of
its way, as a silent power for good and entitled to the commendation
of all fair-minded, unprejudiced people; who, as never before, are
watching and noting whether or not as an organization it is keeping
up with its profession. Every member is, or should be, vitally interested in keeping. up its prestige, and, it seems to me, one of the duties
devolving· upon each member present, when he returns home, is to impress every member· he can reach that he is personally one of tlie fac·
tors in increasing such prestige.
"The past year, like· several of those preceding it, shows· a steady,
healthy increase in membership and finances. Our Orphans' Home
fund is gradually assuming proportions which in a few years more
will insure the successful erection and maintenance of such Home.
Therefore, let us devote ourselves personally and collectively to the
great work before us and harmoniously conduct the business of this
session with reasonable dispp.tch and with an eye single to the good
and welfare of our great Fraternity."

Reference is made by the Grand Master to his invhation to attend
the meeting of Grand Masters at Alexandria, Va., in response to Alexandria-Washington Lodge No. 22's invitation to attend the meeting designed to lay the foundation of the Washington Memorial Association.
Several Special Communications of the Grand Lodge were held
in the year for the purpose of placing corner stones of public buildings.
In "Conclusion" the Grand Master returns his thanks for the loyal
support rendered him by the various officers of the Grand Lodge and
for the kindness and courtesy extended to him on all sides by the members throughout the jurisdiction.
That the veteran Secretary, W. L. Kuykendall, is the big figure
in the jurisdiction of Wyoming is shown in the following resolution
duly adopted :
"Resolved, That the picture of our Grand Secretary be inserted in
all the Grand Lodge proceedings for this and all succeeding years."
And in accordance with that resolution Brother Kuykendall's
strong and virile likeness adorns the present volume of Proceedings.
Discussions pro and con concerning the Masonic Home project
were indulged in during the Communication, with a final result that
the Grand Lodge decided to defer further action upon the location of
the proposed Masonic Home until the session of 1914.
The Report on Foreign Correspondence is by the V.". W.". Grand
Secretary, Brother W. L. Kuykendall, and he comments in an incisive
and intelligent manner upon the doings of the various Grand Lodges.
California, 1909, is considered.
Hugh Hynds, Grand Master, Laramie.
W. L. Kuykendall, Grand Secretary, Saratoga.
